GRANTED 'WISHES. Two little girls let loose from school Queried what each would be. One said, "Id be a queen and rule," And one, "The world I'd see." The years went on. Again they met And queried what had been. "A poor man's wife am I, and yet." Said one, "I am a queen. "My realm a happy household is, My king a husband true; I rule by loving services— How has it been with you?" One answered, "Still the great world lies Beyond me as it laid; O'er love's and duty's boundaries My feet have never strayed. "Faint murmurs of the wide world come Unheeded to my ear: My widowed mother's sick bedroom Suffieeth for my sphere.'! 'They clasped each other's hands, with tears Of solemn joy they cried, "God gave the wish of our young years, And we are satisfied." J onx G. WHITTIBEI.

NEW POLK BY TBNNYBOX. (The Nineteenth anew? for S,ptember contains a new poem by Alfred Tennyson. It is ins-ribed 'To Virgil," and was written, as we are told, at the request of the Mantnane for the nineteenth centenary of Virgil's death. We append a few of the versesl— Virgil, thou that singest Ilion's lofty temples robed la fire,

Ilion falling, Rome arisidg, - wars, and filial faith, and Dido's pyre; landscape-lover, lord of language more than he that sang the Works and Days. All the chosen coin of fancy flashing out from many a golden phrase Thou that singest wheat and woodland; titth and vineyard, hive and horse and herd; All the charm of all the Muses often flowering in a lonely word;
* * Now the Rome of slaves hath perish'd. and the Rome of freemen holds her place, 1, from out the Northern Island sundered once from all the human race,
I salute thee, Mantovano, I that loved thee since my day began. Wielder of the stateliest measure ever moulded by the lips of man.

How TO MARE NEW ROPE PLlABLl4.—Considerable difficulty is sometimes experienced in handling new rope, on account of its stiffness. This is especially the case when it is wanted for halters and cattle tits. Every farmer is aware how inconvenient a new, stiff rope halter is to put on and tie up a horse with. And new ropes for tying cattle are frequently unsafe, for tLe reason that they are not pliable enough to knot securely. All this can be remedied, and new rope made as limber and soft at once as after a year's con- stant use, by simply boiling it for two hours in water. Then hang it in 3 warm room, and let it dry out thoroughly. It retains its stiffnese until dry, when it becomes perfectly pitabl Farmer. Many Curious reasons have from time to time been advanced for the disappearance of the shoals; it is said, for instance, that herrings were driven from the Baltic by the battle of Copen- hagen, ant that in other localities they were frightened Pete away by the fires used in burning kelp; it is also affirmed ' by the superstitions that they at once leave a coast where bleed has been needlessly spilt. One of the quaintest reasons ever given for the .non-appearance of these fish in their weete,d haunt was given by a Member of Parliament in a debete on a little bill: the story was that a clergyman having obtained a living on the coast of Ireland, at once eig- nified his intention of taking his tithe of fish, and since that declaration was made not a single herring ha ever visited • Li that part of the coast !—God Words. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. The South-Eastern Gazette quotes a striking instance of the reduced letting velne of agricultural land in Kent. The All Hallows' Farm, near Rochester, formerly let at £9OO a year, has been in the market for two years, and has been ex- tensively advertised, yet the sole result is that a tenant has just been secured for it at an annual rent not exceeding 050. This is believed to be the greatest reduction yet made. Tag Time RENT CRiTZGE.—Au attempt has been made to collect tithe in Kent half-yearly instead of yearly, and ' has been resisted by the farmers. A distraint was made on the goods of Mr. Joseph Gibson, a farmer near Maidstone, and some implements and a stack of hay were seized. The property was sold by auction cn Tuesday, in the presence of a number of members of the Anti-Extraordinary Tithe Association, who protested against the action of the tithe- owners and their agents. Come Itrrnales.—The new Act of Parliament relating to corn returns empowers Her Majesty in Council to declare from time to time what shall be the places at which the weekly returns of the purchases of British corn are to be, made, the numbers of these places being between the limite of 150 and 200. The mode prescribed for ascertaining the average price of any sort of British corn for a week is to add I together the total quantities appearing from the Inspector's summaries to have been bought during the time, and also I to add together the total prices, and then to divide the total prices by the total quantities. The quarterly or yearly average prices are to be ascertained by adding together the weekly averages Included in the time, and dividing the total by the number of weeks; and the septennial average price by dividing by seven the sum of the average annual prices for the seven years. All these computations are to be made with reference to the imperial bushel. And in converting returns made by weight the inspectors are to estimate a bushel as corresponding to 60 imperial pounds of wheat, to 50 of barley, and of 39 of oats. The septennial average price thus ascertained is to be taken as the average price for the purposes of the Tithe Commutation Acts. London is subject to the Act in much the same way as other towns; the chief modification being that within five miles of the, Royal Exchange the persons who are required to make re- turns are limited to dealers in British corn, corn factors, and those who buy British corn within the Corn Exchange or any other building used for similar purposes. Power is given to the Board of Trade to frame regulations for the execu- Vett of the Act, which repeals and replaces the Corn Returns Acts of 1842 and 1864. STRAWBERRIES AT 3D. PER POI:IND.—A correspondent writes While North Wales has become noted as the I theatre of Mr. Kynaston's successful growth of ardent fruit the wonderful results of Mr. William Lovel'e system of strawberry growing have been wrought in North Yorkshire I —formerly at Weaverthorpe, and later at his recently settled and cultivated four-acre field near Driffield. With a long experience as a cultivator, both on the farm and in the garden, Mr. Lovel has finally adopted the strawberry as his speciality. He is now achieving an undoubted snccess In this new field of operations, for which no doubt his many previous experiments have served to prepare the way. Popular as is the strawberry, its use cannot be expected to become general owing to the hitherto high price at which the retailer pieces it before the fruit-buying public. There is no reason, thinks Mr. Loyal, why it should be either scarce or dear, nor is there any reason, in his opinion, why anybody who has even a small garden should not supply his table with strawberries of his own growth. There need be neither mystery nor difficulty about their cultivation, and wherever an amateur can succeed in growing the prosaic cabbage and potato, he may, if he will follow Mr. Lovel'e suggestions, grow the welcome strawberry. His success will depend on two or three simple requisites. He must have well-prepared soil, must choose his varieties with care, and must secure young and strong plants. This done, there is no reason why field or garden, small or large, may not respond with a crop plentiful and profit- able as any which our beginner could desire. This is to be done in Lancashire, as in the south of England or as in Perth- shire, with ease and certainty. It cannot fail to be seen that Mr. Lovel's success has a bearing which should not be over- looked by the landowner and the cultivator in these daps of agricultural unrest and severe depression. If Mr. Lovel can obtain from his field of three acres a profitable and remunera- tive return, what is to prevent the small farmer, especially If he have easy access to a large town, from doing the same on his farm of ten or twelve acres? It is the custom to abuse our capricious climate, and to let the verdict go by default. We must, we are told, go abroad for our wheat and oar fruit, and cover our -e.vn acres with stock and green crops, for meat and for dairy uses. But Mr. Loyal denies any such necessity. Our climate is, for 213, the most excel- lent which the earth presents. No climate, he says, has the abundant warmth and moisture which we obtain in England, and it is this blended summer warmth and moisture which be has turned to such productive account. No country on the earth's surface can yield the lovely carpet of green grass like our own, and none can so well produce in perfection those humbler but very acceptable products, the gooseberry and the strawberry. Mr. Lovel has a good deal more to say to the same and. The children benefit by his fruit gifts, and he has no trouble with thieves. We are confronted, socially, with not a few knotty problems and perplexing questions. We have a 'food question,' a 'health question,' a labour question,' and a land question.' To all these Mr. Lovel bears his pertinent testimony. Perhaps it would be more correct to say that he vigorously plies his sp tde and pro- ducts his strawberry. It was certainly delightful, as eaten in his garden only a few weeks ago. Like the late Thomas Rivers, the very successful champion of the orchard-house, and author of the notable book on the same subject, Mr. Lovel would have every one try the matter for himself. His reply to the inevitable question 'Will it pay' is a decided Yes.' To those who wish to make the most money from an acre of land, says Mr. Lovel, I know of co crops that answers better than early potatoes and strawberries. I have grown 21b. of fruit to the square yard—more than equal to the value of the land. With good market varieties there need be no difficulty in producing one ton of fruit to the acre, arid this, at 3d. per lb., would pay all expenses and leave a nice profit to the cultivator.' On this point I have thought It fair to quote Mr. Lover own words. The vision of etrawberrics at 3d: per pound may well captivate many a Manchester housekeeper, who would be glad enough to have such fruit at 63. if the distributor and the merchant and the railway company could be centented with the other 3d. as repayment for placing the berries early in the market. There is only one word to be added by way of caution to the amateur. In crder to taste a strawbeiry in perfection, says Mr. Lovel, 'it should be gathered at sunrise with the dew on it, and eaten to breakfast' "—Manchester Guardian.

"OUR, OLD NOBILITY,' [Published by 3fr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-street London, WC., and reprinted by permission.] THE HOWARDS. (CARLISLE BRANCH.) The lamented death of the late Mr. C. Howard, M.P., brother to the Eirl of Carlisle reminds me that I have as yet only glanced at the ducal line of that great family. Beside the Duke of Norfolk, the Earls of Suffolk, and Effingham, Lords Howard de Walden and Howard of Glossop, and the Earl of Wicklow, all bear the same famous name, and all except the last are undoubtedly descended from the same stock—an honour which the Earl of Wicklow also claims. Taking the es'ates of all these, and of three Commoner Howards, I find that this fortunate family owns more than 211,000 acres of land in the United Kingdom. The Earl of Carlisle, though not the wealthiest of the Howards, has more extensive estates than the Duke of Nor- folk himself. He owns in— Cumberland 47,730 acres.
Northumberland 17,780 „ Yorkshire 13,030 ~

Total 78,540 „ with a rent-roll of £45,602. Those who are familiar with "The Lay of the Last Minstrel" will recollect "Belted Wilt Howard," one of the prominent characters in the poem, but who, as Scott tells us in his notes, by a poetical anachronism was introduced into the romance a few years earlier than he actually flourished. It was "Belted Will Howard" who was the founder of the Cumberland branch of the family. He was a younger son of the fourth Duke of Norfolk, who was beheaded in the reign of Elizabeth, having been drawn into treason through Mary Queen of Scots. In the following reign, Lord Wm. Howard was restored in blood. It was a marriage with a Dacre heiress that made him a great landholder. The Dacres settled in Cumberland very soon after the Conquest. They are said to have been kinsmen of De Meschines, a Norman, whom William created Earl of Cum- berland, and to whom he granted the whole county. De Meschines granted the barony of Gillesland to the ancestor of the Dacres. There is a place called Deere, in Cumber- land, but it is doubtful whether the family derived their name from the place, or the place derived its name from the family. Scott says that the family took the name to com- memorate the part played by one of them at the Siege of Acre; but Mr. Howard, the author of "Memorials of the Howard Family," regards this as a groundless fiction. Be that as it may, for some centuries the Decree were one of the most powerful families in Cumberland, taking an active part in the incessant border wars. By marriage with an heiress one of tham acquired the barony of Greystoke, which also had been granted by De Meschines to another of the Norman associates. In time there appeared two branches of the Deere family—the Lords Deere of the North and the Lords Deere of the South. The title held by the latter branch still exists the heir presumptive to it being the present Speaker of the House of Commons. Lord William oward married one of the three sisters and co-heirs of the last Lord Dacre of Gillesland. Each of these sisters, by the way, married a Howard. By this marriage Lord William became possessed of Naworth Castle, the ancient seat of the Dacres of the North, and of the barony of Hinderskelle, near Mahon, in Yorkshire, on which estate Castle Howard, a mansion built by Sir John Vanbrugh, was subsequently erected. Greystoke barony came into the possession of the Dukes of Norfolk, and is now owned by one of the younger branches of the ducal house. The Barony of Deere of Gillesland was revived at the Restoration in favour of Lord William Howard's descendant, and in addition he obtained the higher title of Viscount Morpeth and Earl of Carlisle, and was at one time Ambas- sador to the Czar of Muscovy, and at another Governor of Jamaica. The third Earl was for a time First Lord of the Treasury. The fourth married the heiress of one of the co- heirs of Cavendish, Duke of Newcastle; but, as he left only daughters by that lady, I presume his share of the Newcastle property passed to them. He married, secondly, a daughter of the fourth Lord Byren—hence the connection of his son, the fifth Earl, the Byron family. / Men are sometimes kept in remembrance by the strangest

div.head: EXAMINER An
div.p: THE EXAMINER An

accidents. The fifth Earl of Cat;lisle was Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. He published some poems, which ran through three or four editions; and some tragedies, which gave rise to Dr. Johnson's somewhat toadyism remark, " that when a man of rank appeared in the character of an author, he deserved to have his merit handsomely allowed." But these things, and the Earl himself, would have been long since entirely forgotten, had not the Earl been the guardian of Lord Byron. To the Earl of Carlisle "The Hours of Idleness" were dedicated "by his obliged ward and affec- tionate kinsman, the author." But the guardian treated the ward with studied coolness, or, at any rate, the ward fancied that he did so; and in "English Bards and Scotch Re- viewers" the "affectionate kinsman" attacked the nob!e ' author of the forgotten tragedies of "The Stepmother" and "The Father's Revenge," in lines which the author himself afterwards pronounced as "much too savage What heterogeneous honours deck the peer! Lord, rhymester, petit-maitre, pamphleteer ! So dull in youth, so drivelling in his age. His scenes alone had damned our sinking stage; But managers for once cried, "Hold, enough Nor drugged their audience with the tragic stuff. Yet at their judgment let his lordship laugh, And case his volumes in congenial calf; Yes! dot( that covering where morocco shines, A-nd hang a calf skin on those recreant lines.

Byron afterwards scribbled on his copy of the book, oppo- site this passage, "Miserable record of misplaced anger and indiscriminate acrimony ;" and, in a well-known passage in " Childe Harold," he alludes to a younger son of the Earl who fell at Waterloo:—

Yet one I would select from that proud throng, Partly because they blend me with his line, An partly that I did his sire some wrong, And partly that bright names will hallow song! And his was of the bravest, and when shower'd
The death-bolts deadliest the thin files along, E'en where the thickest of war's tempest lower'd,

They reach no nobler breast than thine, young, gallant Howard. The seventh Earl, known for the greater part of his life as Lord Morpeth, was one of the most deservedly :pop:ear noblemen of the present century. His father was a member of Lord Grey's Cabinet, without portfolio. Lord MorpAh, like his: father before him, entered Parliament for Morpeth, which was then a pocket borough of the family. In 1827 he was the seconder of Sir Francis Burdett's motion in favour of Catholic Emancipation ; a little later, in an eloquent speech, he seconded Sir Powell Buxton's resolution in favour of the Abolition of Slavery in the Colonies. As early as 1832 he declared himself in favour of the remission of the Advertisement Duty and the Stamp Duty on News- papers. Throughout the prolonged debate on the first Re- form Bill, he steadily supported the popular cause, having by that time become one of the members for the great county of York. He held office in several Liberal Adminstrations as Secretary for Ireland, as Commissioner of Woods and Forests, as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and twice as Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland. It is rarely that'an Irish Viceroy can be denominated popular, but the Earl of Carlisle was one of the most popular Viceroys that have ever held office. In the Conservative reaction of 1841, he lost his seat for the West Riding of Yorkshire ; but a few years after he was re-elected to Parliament, and voted in the majority with Sir Robert Peel for the Abolition of the Corn Laws. Sanitary Reform, Factory Legislation, the Education of the People, and Mechanics' Institutes found in the Earl of Carlisle a warm and earnest supporter. He won for himself an honour- aWe position in literature. Besides his poems, he published volumes of travels in America, Turkey, and Greece; lectures on the writings of Pope and Gray, and on the importance of Literature to Men of Business; and in his elder years he evinced the same interest which he had manifested in his youth as to the Slavery Question by writing a preface to " Uncle Tom's Cabin."

The seventh Earl of Carlisle, who was never married, was succeeded in 1864 by his next surviving brother, a clergy- man who, in 1832, obtained the living of Londesborough, in Yorkshire, a little parish of 324 inhabitants. value £798 and a house, which, strange to say, he still holds. He is over seventy years of age, and has never married. Mr. Charles Howard, the late Member of East Cumberland, had an only son, Mr. George Howard, who was recently elected Member for East Cumberland. Mr. George Howard is married to a daughter of the second Lord Stanley of Alderley, and has given promise, by his consistent Liberalism, of faithful ad- herence to the principles which have niade the Carlisle branch of the Howard family one of the most popular of trie great houses.

TRADE NOTES. It would appear that the resolutions come to by the Miners' Conference at Manchester regarding wages is soon bearing fruit. In several instances tho men are seeking more wages, and will strike if their demands are rejected. A dispute 61 quite a novel character is reported to he going on at the Siemens Steel Works, Swansea. It is stated that upwards of 1,700 men are out on strike, in order to reList Sunday labour, which the employers contend is necessary to enable them to compete with Continental manufacturers. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES.—In the week ending September 9, 1882, there were 780 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 156 over those of the correspond- ing period last year ; and the failures gazetted numbered 188, a decrease of 6. The totals for portion of year to September 9, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 33 340, a decrease c-f 1.502 ; the failures gazetted number, 7,440, a decroase of 731.—Stubb's Mercan- tile Gazette. THE STRIKE IN THE CLYDE SHIPYARDS.—A meeting of the Clyde Shipbuilders' and Engineers' Association was held in Glasgow on Monday, when an offer was made on behalf of English workmen to till the places of the men on strike at the present rate of wages. The meeting appointed a depu- tation to meet represfeptatives of the workmen, in order to make the nec.ssary arrangements for the men beginning work at as early a date as psssible. WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE —At a meeting of employers oonnected with the North of England Iron Trade Board of Arbitration, at Middlesborough, on Tuesday, a resolution was adopted to give notice to the operatives for a reduction of 9d. per ton in puddling, and 7/d. per cent. in other forge and mill wages, taking effect on the termination of the pre- sent wages agreement, October 28; also suggesting the establishinz of a satisfactory sliding scale for future regula- tion.of wages. .

. uneasy feeling prevails as to the action the men may take with regard to wages and colliery proprietors are very chary about selling forward. Supplies, however, are still suf- ficiently plentiful in the market to check any general upward movement in values at present, but there is a strong tendency to stiffen, and at some of the West Lancashire collieries the better classes of hou,e coal are being put up 6d per ton, which will probably be followed by a general advance at the close of the month. The slight stiffening in house-fire coals may be said to have advanced the bisis of pit prices to about 8s 6d to Os for best coals, and 65 6d to 7s for seconds. In other descriptions of fuel quotations are without change. Shipping is moderately fair, and in house-fire coals going into Liverpool there has been an advance of is per ton, but steam coals, although stiffer, can still be bought at late rates.

THE LABOUR KARIM. The labour market•remaine generally in a satisfactory condition, and prospects in the leading industries are good. Some large sections of coal miners seem disposed to press at an early date for an ad- vance in wages, but the general strike lately advocated at Manchester is not, it is anticipated, likely to take place. Railway enterprise in the United States continues on a large sale, and affords good prospects of continuous activity for English ironworkers. At Birmingham in the hardware and other branches colonial orders remain fairly plentiful, and at Wolverhampton manufacturers are also well employed. On the Clyde the ship joiners are still unsettled; otherwise all the leading shipyards are busily employed. The bout and shoe trade at the principal centres is again increasingly busy, and at Leeds some scarcity of hands is reported. Several large railway works, including the new Forth Bridge, are under tender, and navvies are in demand in several paces. Meanwhile the Local Government Board has issued a circular letter on the new Vagrant Act, which may some- what affect migrant labour of the unskilled kind. In Corn- wall the mining market is again very depressed, and through- out the West of England no great activity in the building or other trades prevails. Emigration to Queensland on a large scale is likely to be resumed at an early date, and somewhat stringent conditions as to remaining in the colony will be insisted on in the case of free immigrants. Advices from Kimberley diamond fields indicate trade as stagnant.— Labour News.

div.p: MIDDLEWICII AND NORTHWICH AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The annual show of this society was held at Northwich on Saturday in the Drill Field. It was a very fair show in nearly all departments, and in point of extent a considerable in- crease on any of its predecessors, the area of the society having been widened since last year so as to include all the townships within ten miles of Middlewich. The horses were perhaps the most notable feature of the exhibition, the heavy classes in particular. A number of prizes were offered to cottagers, agricultural labourers, and others, but there were only a few entries for them. A prize of £1 was offered for the best" labourer in husbandry." Character and length of service were the tests of merit, but it does not appear how the judges made up their minds.. Henry Brooks, serving at Byley. got the Li, with a term of service of over 27 years. It is, however, a little hard on Mr. Brooks to enter him on the list immediately after the fat pig. Prizes were also offered for the neatest and best cultivated cottage garden, and it is to be regretted there were no entries. 'The day was tine, and there was a large attendance at the show. Mn. H. VARLET'S ELEVEN V. ST. HELENS RECREATION.— This match was played at Boundary-road on Saturday last, for the benefit of L Reaney, professional of the Recreation Cricket Club. There was a fair attendance of spectators, who took a lively interest in the matter. Mr. Varley winning the toss, sent his men in to bat, and they succeeded in putting together a total of 81. Messrs. Nichol, Chandley, T M Draper. and Varley reached double figures. After the usual interval G Barton and Pye went in to face the bowling of Nichol and Fidler. Pye was bowled when he had made three. 403arton was bowled when he had reached double figures. T Marsden and W Alton played with great care and caution for their respective s'ores of 25 and 21. Marsden was also successful in his bowling, five wickets falling to him for 19 runs Towards the close of the Recreation's innings Use excitement became rather intense, as they wanted five runs to win with two wickets to fall Every ball was eagerly wa`ched, and each bit was loudly applauded by the spectators. It is stated that the hop harvest in Kent will be one of the smallest ever recorded. In nearly every case the estimate has been much too high.
Under the will of the late Dr. J. B. Baxter, for twiny years Procurator Flsoo.l of Dundee, the collev in that, town has benefited by the sum of £lO,OOO at least.

:o an official despatch from Manilla, no rsons died Dom cholera at that place on

mmation has reached CopetL'agen that the population of Iceland, which laas suffered severely from famine, has been decimated by an epidenaic of measles. The great strike of ironworkers in the United slates has ended, and the men have returned to their work at the old rates, and against the orders of the Amalgamated Amocia- tion. Upon the occasion of the second earthquake at Panama on Saturday half the population abandoned their houses in fright, and considerable damage was done to about ten miles of ths railway.

NeWs just received from China is to the effect that the total export of tea frem that country luring the present year amounts to 91,000,0001b5., being an increase of 1,000,0001b5. as campared with last year. A great Catholic Congress, which is attended by 700 persons, is now sitting at Frankfort-on-the-Main. At the opening meeting on Monday a letter was received from the Pope conveying the Apostolic Benediction to the assembly. The Emperor of Germany received a deputation of the students of Breslau on Sunday, and, in reply to an address presented to him, declared his strong sentiments in favour of peace. His Majesty is, it is stated, in excellent health.

, The scandalous abuses in the postal and telegraphic administration of Spain have attained such serious dimensions that they are to be brought before the Cabinet with the view of effectual steps being taken to remedy the evil.

A rumour has reached Calcutta that some of the Ameer of Cabul's troops have been defeated by the Chief of Maimena. The correspondent of the Times says it is believed that Musa Khan, son of Yakoob Khan, is at Maimena, under the pro- tection of the Chief.

Another serious Indian outbreak appears to be imminent. •The Arrapahoes have gone upon the war path, the cattle herders are arming for defence, and cavalry is about to be sent to their aid. Several of the prairies have been fired, and a number of cattle have perished. The sensational report of the handing over to the Spanish authorities by the English at Gibraltar of three ex-officers of the Cuban insurrection is declared by the Spanish officials to be apocryphal. It has been ascertained that the men were caught at the Spanish lines trying to escape direct from Cadiz by land._

It was the fete day of the patron saint of the Czar on Monday, and the usual custom of bestowing decorations on the three services was observed. The Order of Alexander Nevsky was awarded to General Drenteln, Governor General of Kieff, who recently made a violent speech against the Russian Jews at Balta.

ACCIDENT TO THE PRINCESS LOUISE. The Viceregal train which was conveying the Marquis of Lorne and the Princess Louise to San Francisco on Wednesday, came into collision with an engine. The Princess was thrown down, but received no injury beyond trifling bruises. The engine of the train was so damaged that another had to be procured before the journey could be continued. The American ironmasters have met to consider what iron duties they should recommend to the Tariff Commission, and have come to the determination to leave the present duties mainly unchanged. They will, however, ask for an increase on cotton ties, tinplates, and wire rods • that iron ore duty be advanced from 20 per cent, to one dollar per ton, and that steel rails remain unchanged. An occurrence of a most unusual character is reported from New York. Just previous to the departure of the steamer Alaska from that port on Tuesday, it was found that the mail bags from Australia were on fire, and the flames were not extinguished until ten sacks of newspapers and two of letters, including some registered letters, had been destroyed. None of these bags had been opened at New York, and the only explanation of the accident that is put forward is a sepposition that some of the sacks must have contained combustible matter. THE PECQ MURDER.—The Court of Cessation has , quashed the judgments passed last month at Vereeilles in the Pecq case, and there is to be a new trial. The flaw in thepro- ceedings which was held to have invalidated the trial was the fact that one of the witnesses, Groustean, the second lover of the female prisoner, did not give his evidence 'viva voce. The court held that such a course was a violation of the law, which prescribes that all evidence shall be rendered at the trial with spontaneity, freedom, and independence. ALARMING ACCIDENT TO AN EXPRESS TRAIN—As the express train for 'Vichy was about to leave Paris on Saturday morning a violent explosion, resembling the rattle of mus- ketry, WAS heard in the luggage van. A large trunk burst into pieces, smashed a quantity luggage, blew a panel out of the van, and knocked down four railway porters. The passengers were seized with panic, but the stationmaster and some officials lost no time in examining the van, when they found that it had contained a number of sporting cart- ridges, a gun, a sword, aad the uniform of a lieutenant of dragoons, all of which articles were greatly damaged and scattered about the van. Two of the porters knocked down by the explosion are seriously injured. RECALL OF THE BURMESE EMBASSY. A Daily- News Rangoon telegram says :—The Burmese Embassy has just arrived here, and has met with an official reception. The gunboat Ranger manned yards, but little enthusiasm was manifested. The general opinion is that the recall of the ligmbassy is an insult to the Indian Government. Probably the CaRSO of the recall is that England's hands being full with Egypt there is no fear of consequences. The frontier is in a highly disturbed state. A police guard has been at- tacked within British territcry by the subjects of King Thebaw, and there is a general feeling of unquietness. PRIZEFIGHT BETWEEN "LADIES."—Some little scandal has been caused in "good society" at Columbus, Georgia, by the proceedings of two young ladies in that city—Miss Laura Morwin and Miss Della Stile—who came to high words one evening recently respecting a young man to , whom they are both attached. After much talking of an , unpleasant nature, it was agreed that the dispute should be settled "according io the Marquis of Queensberry's rules." Seconds were immediately chosen, and on the following morning at daybreak the young ladies with a select party of friends crossed the Alabama line and selected a spot for the encounter. A ring was speedily formed, and the combatants set to work without further delay. Happily the contest was not a grotracted one. Two rounds only were fought, when Miss Stile was declared the victor—Miss Morwin being " knocked out." They then returned to Columbus, where the 1 young man who was the innocent cause of the fight met them and with much emotion bade them both farewell, hav- ing been advised by his ftiends "to go West before it was eternally too late." AN EXTRAORDINARY FRENCH CRIMINAL. The Paris police have just unearthed an individual of a most extraor- dinary type. A few days ago, in the course of certain in- vestigations regarding an odious criminal offence, the police found that an old man, ceiling himself M. Leblond, was im- plicated in it, upon whom with some trouble they succeeded iE laying their hand. His miserable dress and generally wretched appearance imluced the belief that he was a home- less vagabond. The police were, however, much puzzled by the fact that he was in possession of a number ef important- looking keys. Having extracted from Leblond his address, M. Mace, the chief of police, accompanied him to the house indicated. To M. Mace's astonishment he found that this was one of the largest mansions in the quarter of the Champs Elyeeee. In reply to inquiries, Leblond stated that it had belonged to his family for over a century, and that he him- self had lived there withort any servant, male or female, for the past 15 years, his explanation being that he was a misanthrope. On entering the house and opening the shut- ters M. Mace found it full of the most costly furniture, with a collection of old pictures, books, and other objects of art.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Tha shrine of Knock, near Ballyhaunis, was visited on Saturday by large numbers of persons from all parts, includ- ing many Americans, and several miraculous cures are re- ported to have been made. The trial of the prisoners charged with the murder of the Joyce family in Connemara was on Monday re moved into the Dublin Special Commission Court on the certificate of the Attorney General for Ireland. At the Dublin Police Court, on Monday, a soldier named Baker was committed for trial for the wilful murder of a woman who kept a disorderly house. During a quarrel he pierced her eye with a stick, which entered the brain and caused instant death.

The Corporation of Limerick have passed an extraor- dinary resolution refusing, in defiance of the decision of Judge Lawson at the late assizes, to make a presentment for the pay of the extra police imposed upon that city, in con- sequence of its disordered condition, by the Lord-Lieutenant. The Lord-Lieutenant left the Viceregal Lodge on Tiles-. day, accompanied by Mr. Jenkinsou, assistant under secre- tary and director of the ()rime department; Mr. Courtney Boyle, private secretary; Major Turner, R. A, Captain Hammond, KN., and Mr. Ross, of Bladenburg, aide-de-camp, for a tour in the west.

_. ....,... ........ ......,_. . . An additional Sub-Commission under the Land Act has been appointed, consisting of Mr. Wm. Roper, barrister, as legal member, and Messrs. Thomas Smith, county Wicklow; A. B. Nolan, county Mayo; and R. B. Henston, county Tip- pearary, as lay members. Mr. Roper is a Conservative of strong views. A man remanded at the Dublin Police Court, on Satur- day, for an extensive burglary at S.immen's Court, Castle Donnybrook; is supposed by the police to have been a ring- leader in the various Fenian outrages perpetrated in the city. He is an adept in disguises, and has long eluded the police. MURDER IN COUNTY CORIK.—.,I labourer named Timothy Keefe was murdered in Newmarket, county Cork, on Satur- day night. He had been drinking during the evening with four men. On leaving the town a quarrel took place between Keefe and a man named Edward Sheehan, who attacked and murdered Keefe. Sheehan is in custody. It will be remembered that considerable alarm was eaused at Kilmainham last month by the mysterious discharge of a : number of rockets from within the gaol. An inquiry has been held regarding the affair, with the result that Mr. James Careit, a "Suspect," has been sentenced to 14 days' solitary confinement, his right to receive visitors suspended, and all his correspondence withheld. THE CONDEMNED. MAN WALSH. A Galway corres- pondent writes :—Mitch interest is taken in this district in the fate of the unfortunate man Walsh, who is condemned to be hangd on the 24th inst for the murder of the Lydens, father and son, at Letterfrack. Walsh Was visited on Wed- nesday by his mother, who remained with him for nearly an hour. Walsh takes his condition quite unconcernedly, and 1 chats to the waeders and attendants freely. He sleeps w4l, eats heat tily, and drinks nothing but port wine. BATTLE AT KASSASIN. Arabi has not waited quietly within his sandy redoubts and ieu,'renelaraents to be attacked at Sir Garnet Wolseley's ._ace _l2lue, He bad witnessed and resisted a British roconnais- m • In force, which had followed sundry reconuoitrimg itel:Mitions conducted by officers accompanied by a few rraernen, and concluded that it was time that he should re- sts ,c 1 the compliment. Accordingly at a very early hour on \:tattlirdaY Morning he disturbed the quietude of the British 4 `/IP by sending about 5,000 of his troops to the front, and lor,°,l3l3ing shells within Sir Garnet's lines. General Willis 00 time in replying. Infantry, cavalry, marines, and 47,"dery promptly turned out to repel the audacious Egyptian aVnce, and returned the enemy's fire with vigour. The 4tlllerY train with its 40-pounder in position was also run °for' and soon its shells were dropping amongst the Egyptian br,,ces• Arabi's troops showed a good deal or confidence, and °right 16 guns into play with their usual accuracy gr,fire, but as the British drew nearer and nearer they tC"tially retired. But the English advanced more rapidly than Was expected, and the Marines drew so rapidly upon ° foe that by admirable management they succeeded in 2pturing three of the enemy's guns, which had been dis- !°ted by the British fire. While the battle was thus turning et favour of the British another force of rebels was seen 4dv, . M go, "g rapidly from the direction of Es-Salihiiyeli. Sir art,er Russell, with the heavy cavalry, some infantry and **lderY, at once advanced to meet the new attack, which es, it is believed, entrusted to the best of Arabi's forces. atathis as it may, it was pushed forward with vigour, even tbe time when the other section of the attacking force 18 Seen to be in full retreat. For a time a determined stanA was made, but it was in vain. The heavy cavalry, a gun of the enemy in difficulties, swooped ch,wn ,vnn it, and captured it, with its horses and all its filuiPment, and when it was seen that tho force Tel-el-Kebir was retreating further and I,Trtaer, the flank attack from Es-Salihiyeh could no eeger be maintained. It fled, and soon its retirement l7eloped into a very hasty retreat. That ,this was not teerelY a reconnaissance in force is demonstrated by the de- advancehimaking from Es-Salihiyeli. Arabi deliberately ;,... aned his forces there with the object of making a flank .j , ;',ok while troops from Tel-el-Kebir engaged the British tront, and when the Enslish advance uponTel-el-Kebir it Possible that he may repeat this manoeuvre, in which, rWever, after Saturday's experience, he may possibly have confidence than before. He advauced on the British ;4„411), no doubt, with the intention of making a desperate ;,"ank before Sir Garnet on his part was ready either to ranee or to resist as vigorously as when all the British 4°roe had been concentrated at the front, and his complete hFfeat must have again shaken his confidence in p ability to meet the British in the open field. ~"° fighting—in which the Egyptian General had, it is said, ;Ight regiments of 20,000 infantry at his disposal, with 2,000 ePllar cavalry, 3,000 Bedouins, and 62 guns—enabled our n "Lneers to gain more exact information as to Arabi's defences Tel-el-Kebir, and the conclusion arrived at is that a direct tttank upon some of his redonbts, which are defended by as -"alrY as 12 guns, will be attended with grave danger. It flay, therefore, be at least anticipated that the enemy will his ground, though fears are still entertained lest he Zottld again run away. The losses of Arabi, whose object Os to capture the British camp, is reported at over a 7.,ondred killed and an unknown number wounded. Sir ,zarnet Wolseley's list of killed and wounded is sufficient I;,iclenCe of the severity of the engagement. The loss in tilefi was only two, but-seven are retnrned as very seriously iipladed, five as dangerously wounded, 18 as wounded, and as slightly wounded, making in all two killed and 66 meet, Arabi's losses will, no doubt, have a discouraging :.(keet, while the courage of the British force is correspond- stimulated by another success. The Guards reached trent too late to join in the battle, and the Highlanders ke left Ismailia on Saturday evening for the front had only anced 10 miles by Straday, and had suffered severely Cam sunstroke.
GREAT BRITISH VICTORY.
`I•I"I'TJRE OF TEL-EL-10IBIR AND THOU-
SANDS OF PRISONERS. PLIGHT OF ARA.BI AND HIS ARIL PURSUIT OF THE ENEMY.

The early hours of Wednesday morning witnessed what ' "1 probably prove to be the most decisive, and possibly the / °Lily, battle of the Egyptian campaign in which we are now "allge aged. Carefully planned and boldly executed, the 'otet• • 43/1 attack on Arabi's strongly fortified position at Tel- was attended with brilliant and complete success, hl resulted in the utter rout of the rebel forces. The severe tlature of the defeat is gathered from the fact that according 10 the first reports which reached us from the battlefield 40 " the enemy's guns had been captured, while fully 2,000 7tetians were killed in the assault. The actual fighting, 1411 e of short duration, was of a bloody and decisive cha- teeter. During the 20 minutes which elapsed while our t,rt'°Ps were occupied in storming the fortifications in their ;tont, the carnage was soinethimg dreadful; and once brought ,4ee to face with the British bayonets, the Egyptians—as uetter.troops before them have done on many a European aeld of battle—wavered, turned, and, panic-stricken, fled in 11'11(1de:order from the scene of conflict, leaving works, :totes, and guns in our poseession. No one from the -tat doubted the final result of the attack 31(1 Arabi's; carefully fortified position at Tel-el- ebir. With the details of the assault planned by so con- mete a tactician and yet so cautious a general as Sir A arnet Wolseley, it was universally felt that when he did .I.,eliver a blow it would be one that would shatter the oppos- :g forces and pee° the way for a speedy termination of the Vein. In this anticipation Sir Garnet has not dis- PPointed the public After chafing for some days at The I - • • a owness of the British advance, the long-expected attle has been fought and the turning-point of the cam- greached. n Arabi's troops have Leon worsted in the 4ht and retired before our cavalry thoroughly demoralised. a:4.eed, it is a question whether as a force they will ever eealam be ieduced or even fit to encounter us in the open Dispirited by their frequent defeats, it is far more 'robable that the rebel forces, in keeping with their Oriental <3/4aracter, will melt away, and cease to offer any effective °l,PPositices to our advance and occupation of the country. It 4t4'l only the other 4ay that several promineut officers t4taolled to the Commander-in-Chief's general staff predicted roat they would dine in Cairo before the 21st of the present I:4th. They then stood facinv a powerful rebel army frsted under the shelter of akilfully thrown-up earthworks, 4:111 whence frowned the muzzles of a numerous well-equipped artillesy. Now that army has t -e*(;lPsecl, those defences are held by the English tths Ps, and there is nothing save the unforeseen to prevent tee victorious army from occupying Cairo at all events by r;te 2lst. Ever since that first action at Kassassin, when ereneral Graham's sturdy infantry so grimly held their ' and the Household Cavalry and Dragoons under • bierleral Drury Lowe so gallantly charged the enemy's -o,a3sea by moonlight, Sir Garnet has been busily engaged in 4111Ptoving the transport service and in concentrating with la Possible rapidity the troops at the front. By Saturday vtBt 80111 e 17,000 men, representing all branches of the ser- e, Were either stationed at Kassessin or were on the letell from Ismailia. That splendid body of troops, the Allghland Brigade, commanded by General Sir Archibald leaelst°l3, were the last to leave the base of operations on the cgs of the Canal for the front. The brigade, which con- of the first battalion of Royal Highlanders, 42nd I(;?f?alitry ( ' ckWatch), the second battalion Highlend Light 74th) the first battalion Gordon Higblrinders iefsithy), and the first battalion Cameron Highlanders (70th), tteTh"mallia on Friday last, and reached the front after a dglg march under a scorching sun. Unquestionably the which Arabi made on the British positions on Satur- ua,Y, svith the bulk of his infantry, was intended to double dePf or roll back the army slowly concentrating on his be:elle" at Tel-el-Kebir. His effort, if ever it could have le,-" Successful, at all events came too late, and it will doubt- Lilt be fresh in the memories of all who are familiar • h h the progress of the war with what gallantry and corn- eas t• th a 11743 ease over 20,000 of the enemy's troops, including bO5 famous black regiments' from the Soudan, were forced eK behind their entrenchments by the conjoint efforts of Capall body of Marines and Rifles, supported by the House- -4°41 Cavalry and Bengal Lancers, and the effective fire of e: Artillery. The incidents of Saturday's fight must have alsirineed the enemy of their inferiority and their utter in- itY to meet our troops in the open field. At the time, a haticieral belief seems to have been prevalent that if our troops tre „Pushrd home their advantages and followed up the re- ea,,a,ung forces, the position at Tel-el-Kebir could have been it.-K,ltred with comparative ease; and by critics at home earilYrareet has since been somewhat severely blamed for re- tithing the British troops, both infantry and cavalry, when the 4 flushed with success. It is, however, only fair to give (A_general commanding on the spot—especially if he be an (err in whom implicit confidence can be placed—the credit aneb°Nring how best to carry out the plan of operations, it left far a success should be followed up. Apparently l til_Jrarnet Wolselev felt he would 60 able to strike a far Ter.e de cisi v e blow by assaulting the enemy's positions at ter ,111-ICebir when he had completed his final arrangements 044 .e advance, rather than by making an onslaught on a dis• te7etlised foe with forces which, though they might cap- ' dekatthe fortifications, were yet insufficient to inflict a 4itien °re° crushing a character as to render further oppo- tviA to the British advance hopeless, if not impossible. 131.0"ntly the plan was, so to speak, to finish the campaign defen" masterly, deadly stroke, and not only to carry the ersti,Dee themselves, but to capture with them Arabi and his leeti" or to route the Egyptian troops in so thorough a ilostini:r.." to prevent their-re-appearance in the field as a \elm rorce. The events of Wednesday have proved the Pres°4l and far-seeing strategy of Sir Garnet. At this Aret;'ll.lt moment Tel-el-Kehir is in our possession, while (43, ri 4tteri and the rebel troops have fled in wild confusion, vsed 'Y demoralised and hopelessly beaten. The period that tv th b e Brit. et ween the fight Satutdey and the time when isi attack was made, slaortly after four on Wednes- ernteg, s one of absolute quietude. Scarcely a shot 4rreie..e° exchanged between the distant outposts of the two tarth2: Arabi's troops sought sullen shelter behind the orks and entrenchments, while in the British lines the

• troops still on the taarch were hurrying up and the disposi- tions were being made. On Wednesday, Sir Garnet and his divisional tomnianders went over the grouuct and con- certed the final details of the plan of attack, and late in the day the Imeg-expected general order for the forward inove- talent of the whole army was issued. By that time the troops, including infantry, cavalry, and artillery, had taken up the positions assigned to them, and only the word of command was required for the advance at once to tommence. It is estimated that at the time of attack Arabi's position was held by nearly 30,000 men, including his picked Egyptian regiments acd a numerous cavalry, while at Salabieh, a few miles to the north of Tel-el-Kebir, lay some 5,000 infantry, a portion of whom had participated in the engagement on Saturday. The position defended by the rebel army was beyond all question an extremely strong one. It is described by Sir Garnet Wolseley in his telegram announcing the defeat of the enemy as " a every extensive and very strongly fortified position." The works were of a formidable character, with a front of full three miles, and bristled with heavy ordnance skillfully placed so as to com- mand and sweep the country round. It is well known that for some time past Arabi has had 60 guns of more or less calibre in position at Tel-el-Kebir, and it was rumoured at the front at the end of last week that his earthworks had been further armed with 40 additional pieces of artillery brought up from Cairo. Whether this was true or not, the rebel leader, at all events, was not deficient in artillery, and had Tel-el-Kebir been resolutely defended, the entrenchments and earthworks could not have been carried except at a great sacrifice of lives. The actual force at Sir G. Wolselev's disposal for the attack comprised 11,000 infantry, 2,600 cavalry, and 60 guns. A distance of fully six miles of difficult country intervened between the British positions at Kassassin and the enemy's earthTorks at Tel-el-Kehir, and it was obvious that an assault delivered in broad daylight could only have been carried out at a risk of a serious loss of life. Hence it was that the general, as was anticipated, decided to attack by daybreak with a view to less exposing his troops to the artillery and rifle fire of the enemy. An additional motive probably for the advance in the early morning was the dread with which the Oriental soldier is known to contemplate a night attack. The preparations for the assault seem to have been carried out with a skill and completeness well worthy of Sir G. Wolseley's reputation. In the evening the enemy struck camp at Kassassin, and bivouacked on the high ground overlaoking the camp. There the troops rested until half-past one on Wednesday morning, occupying a line from Kebir to Karaim, nearly three miles in length, erred immediately facing Arabi's position. Our most advanced line was then distant about four miles from the Egyptian front. Every soldier carried 100 rounds of ammuni- tion and two days' rations, with the exception of meat,while the water bottles were filled with tea. The regimental tran- sport, which followed the army on the north bank of the canal, carried two full days' full rations and 36 rounds of ammunition per man. In the dead of the night,and while the country lay shrouded in darkness, the British troops marched te within a mile of the enemy's position. On the right of the attacking line was the cavalry division, upwards of 2,000 sabres strong, led by Major-General Drury Lowe' and composed of the Household Cavalry, the 4th and 7th Dragoon Guards, and the Bengal Lancers. Accompanying them were two batteries of horse artillery. The cavalry were instructed to round the enemy's line at daylight, and take the Egyptians in the rear. To the left of the cavalry stood the second infantry brigade, commanded by Major-General Graham, and consisting of the 2nd battalion Royal Irish (18th), the 2nd battalion York and Lancaster (84th), and the let battalion Royal Irish (87th), mustering over 2,000 bayonets. Supporting the infantry brigade came the brigade of Guards, under the Duke of Can- naught, while to the left of the Guards were massed seven batteries of artillery under Colonel Good- enough. Immediately facing the enemy's positions stood the Highland (third) brigade, commanded by Sir A. Alison, and the fourth brigade under Lieutenant-Colonel Ashbnr- nam. The latter brigade was composed of the first and second battalions Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry (46th), and the second battalion of the King's Rifle Corps (60th). To the left on the sandhills and south of the canal was stationed the Indian contingent under General Sir H. T. Macpherson, which was constituted of the first battalion Seaforth Highlanders (72nd), the first battalion Manchester Regiment (63rd), and some regiments of Indian Infantry. The Naval Brigade were disposed along the railway and had charge of the 40-pounder, which was worked on the truck. The West India Regiment, the 19th Hussars, and two com- panies of Royal Engineers were left behind to guard the *amp. Our troops appear to have advanced within a mile of the enemy's line before their prescence was discerned in the breaking daylight. It is even said that the British artillery had opened fire upon the earthworks before Arabi's men became aware of our presence. At all events, the advancing regiments were received with a hot rifle and artillery fire, and soon the battle was fiercely raging. Taking advantage of every cover that presented itself, the British Infantry gradually crept up to within 200 yards of the entrenchments, and then with a ringing cheer and a desperate valour charged upon the Egyptian positions. With a rush and a resolution that overcame all obstacles they -swept up the steep slopes, and in the face of a perfect hail- storm of bullets they dashed into the entrenchments, and engaged in a fierce hand-to-hand conflict with the enemy. This hard advance was made without a shot being fired, our men being ordered to reserve their fire, and charge home with the bayonet. There was a race between the regiments as to who should be the first to enter the enemy's lines, and the enthusiasm of the men was indescribable. Once in the trenehesethe struggle was short, but bloody and decisive. The Egyptians refused to face the British bayonets, and fled amidst terrible slaughter precipitately to the rear, throwing arms and everything away. In this brilliant attack General Graham's Brigade on the right of the position seem to have had a most prominent part, and special mention is made by the Commander-in-Chief in his des- patch of the gallantry and dash displayed by the Royal Irish Regiment. While the trenches were thus speedily cleared and the-enemy put to flight, a large inner redoubt on Arabi's left seems to have offered more determined resist- ance, though not for long.- The work was carried by storm by the infantry, who made a terrific onslaught, bayonetted the gunners, and captured the heavy artillery with which the redoubt was armed. All this happened within a quarter of an hour of the first rush of our infantry, and we were now virtual masters of the position. As the enemy broke and ran away in the wildest disorder our troops stood and shot them down with their rides. The appearance of our cavalry on the south at once disconcerted the enemy's forces engaged with our troops, and, like their comrades in another part of the field, they immediately fled. By this time the rebel army had collapsed into a rushing stream of fugitives, all making for Zagazig, and the terror of their position was increased when M'Pherson, with his brigade, bore down on them from the south like an avalanche, and committed terrible havoc in their ranks. The Horse Artillery, too, Coming up at a gallop, unlimbered with wonderful rapidity, and were soon dealing out wholesale death in the fagitive army. The brunt of the attack seems to have fallen upon the Highlanders and Graham's brigade, for when the Fourth Brigade and the Guards came up the enemy's fortifications were already in our posses- sion. A large body of Egyptian troops were intercepted by the cavalry, who got well round Arabi's flank before the actual fighting commenced, and the prisoners, it is estimated, number several thousand. It is said that at least 2,000 Egyptians were killed in the battle. Our army captured upwards of forty guns, while in their flight the enemy left an enormous quantity of military stores of every description behind them. Arabi, who was pre- sent during the battle is said to have escaped towards Zagazig on horseback. Our loss is computed at 200 men, including a large proportion of officers. General Willis, commanding the First Division, was amona the wounded. Beyond all question, Arabi's army is thoroughly demoralised and crushed by this brilliant victory of the British troops, and it is questionable whether it will again be in a condition to meet us in the field. The Indian contingent and the Highlanders are marching on Zagazig, while the cavalry have proceeded to Belbeis, probably with the view of pre- venting the retreat of the rebel forces on Cairo. As the re- sult of this decisive victory, it is confidently anticipated that our troops will have occuped thd Egyptian capital by ote etizi of the week.

AN UNPLEASANT INCIDENT. An Alexandria correspondent records an unplcrant in- cident. While the body ot the murderer Hassan, whd was • hanged oil rrthrstiay, :it suspended ford the gallows and guarded by 20 native policemen, the mob was harangued by an Arab in violent language, who called upon them to save the country from farther degradation. The policemen were then overpowered—it is said that this was a very easy matter—the body seized, and the rope disposed of. It is stated that the murderer's clothes have been sent to a mosque as relics, and that his body is to be embalmed as that of a saint. This triumph of popular passion over the native police, whether with the connivance of the police or not, is highly unsatisfactory, and European residents regard it with uneasy feelings. It is believed, too, that though the military position is perfectly secure, the British force would not be equal to dealing simultaneously with an attack from Kafr Dowar and an outbreak in Alexandria. Possibly these fears may be merely the outcome of nervousness, but the general attitude of the natives suggests that they have similar ideas.

div.head: WAR AND THE COTTON CROP.
div.p: THE WAR AND THE COTTON CROP.

A matter of very considerable interest at the present time is the probable effect of the war upon the E2yptian cotton crop. An Alexandria correspondent has been inves- tigating this matter as far as is possible, but does not pro- fess to be able to give exact information. He finds that much uncertainty exists because of the lateness of planting, the bad spring, and the neglect of the crop after the bom- bardment of Alexandria. If, however, the war be concluded within a month, it is believed the crop will yield from 112,000,000 lbs. to 115,000,000 lbs., but a continuance of the struggle would materially alter these figures. ALLEGED ILL-TREITMENT OF PRISONERS.

The Khedive has sent, through Sir E. Ma let, a w-aternent in regard to the allegation of the correspondent of a London paper that certain prisoners of war had suffered ill-treatment. His Highness admits that there has been an instance of thumb-screwing in the case of a spy who refused to give information, but he asserts that upon hearing of its occurrence stringent orders were immediately given that in future no prisoners .should he put to any torture or suffer any ill- treatment. The Khedive declares that the other statements of the correspondent are unfounded, that all the prisoners war are on boar," a frigate, and that the captain in charge of them, a European, had received strict orders to treat them humanely. It is understood that no prisoners mf war handed over to the local authorities will be dealt with for the present.
T

KEELHAULING. Itt a despatch to the Foreign Office, Sir E. Malet giYes - Vac; facts of the case of keelhauling mentioned in several newspaper telegrams from Alexandria. Three Arabs, he says, fell out over some loot, and two of these attempted to murder the third. These two were ordered to be keelhauled, according to the Egyptian naval code but are both alive. The Khedive, it is added, has given orders that no sentence of keelhauling shall in fnture be inflicted. TEIE BALLOON PARTY. The men of the Royal Engineers who are ordered to pro- ceed to Egypt with the balloon party, were inspected at the Royal Engineer Barracks, Chatham, on Saturday, by Col. Harvey, Assistant Commandant of the School of Military Engineering. The men, who have been specially selected for their knowledge of the various branches of science to which they belong, have passed through a course of in- struction at the Royal Engineer Institute, in connection with School of Military Engineering. The detachment, which will consist of 35 of all ranks, will be made up chiefly of telegraphists, electricians, photographers, and balloonists; it will be under the command of Captain Lee. GOOD FOR THE CANAL. The Daily IVeros, talking of Canal matters, says :—The sompany has not done badly with our Ismailia expedition, viewed as a commercial speculation. We gather from an official source that between the 20th of August and the 9th of September, this year, more than 100 English warships and transports have come through the Canal, many of large size, and that 22,000 soldiers have been landed at Ismailia. This makes up, what with tonnage and passenger dues, a claim of 2,400,000 francs against the English Government, which is not a bad profit for the company, and is some set- off to any feeling unfavourable to the expedition. LORD CHARLES BERESFORD. Sir Garnet Virrolseley having declined to allow Lord Charles Beresford to go to the front in any capacity, his lordship returnol to Alexandria without demur, and having resigned his appointment on the staff of the Kliedive, leaves for Europe. Persons here, and especially the natives, are at a loss to understand the general's refusal. The Khedive asked Lord Charles to join his staff in order to show His Highness's appreciation of the manner in which he had organised and conducted the police service after the bom- bardment. His Highness then asked Lord Charles Beresford to go to the front, so it was not the same position as that of an amateur seeking an appointment. THE MILITARY CONVENTION.
