OCCUPATION OF ZAGAZIG. MARCH ON CAIRO.

A Central News telegram from Kassassin,dated Thursday, 1 a.m., says : —" Macpherson's Brigade entered Zagaz,g last night without resistance from the inhabitants, who sur- rendered themselves. They captured five trains with engines. Sir Garnet Wolseley has left for Zagazig. The cavalry follow. The Indian contingent has reached Abou- Essen. The Heavies have started for Cairo. They go by the south side of the Canal, and join the Indian contingent near Hamid. We captured yesterday a number of camels, mules, horses, and complete provisions for 20,000 men for one month. The present estimates give ten of our men dangerously, 35 seriously, and 102 slightly wounded. The official list has, however, not yet been issued, but it is ex- pected in the course of the day."

PROBABLE END OF THE CAMPAIGN. A second edition of the Daily Telegraph contained the following telegram from Tel-el-Kebir: " Hundreds of fugitives are giving themselves up, including generals and other officers. The enemy's losses were consideably heavier than expected. Our casualties number 150, including 30 killed, among whom eight are officers. Fighting may be now looked upon as more or less finished. To-day's work cannot be too much praised, the operations having been carried out admirably by all concerned. The Egyptian wounded are b2ing tended with all care. The Indian cavalry, we find, made great havoc, and the enemy was quite demoralised, their reserves being unexpectedly cutup." A later telegram says:—" The Indian cavalry are in occu- pation of Zagazig. General Drury Lowe is at Belbeis. The Highland Brigade, under Sir A. Alison, has marched out to- wards Zagazig. The headquarters follow to-morrow. We are now in possession of the railway line to Cairo. The 2nd Cavalry Brigade captlared five trains full of stores, also engines. Altogether it was a glorious day's work, extending between Kassassin and Zagazig, a distance of 40 miles. So far as regards fighting, to-day's success will probably end the campaign. Arabi escaped on horseback. All his papers have been seized kere."

Dervish Pasha and Baker Pasha have not, as intended, left for Egypt. Their departure is postponed until the signature of the Convention with Turkey, which awaits the decision of Earl Granville. The difficalty is said to have arisen in connection with the landing of the Ottoman troops at Port Said. The Porte maintains that this was arranged by the Convention, while Lord Dufferin holds that what was meant was that the Turkish troops should be first sent there, but their port of debarkation would be afterwards arranged by the British commander. Lord Dufferin warmly repudiates the insinuation that England hangs back because, having secured publication of the proclamation, she has no further object to serve in securing Turkish co- operation. His lordship declares Britain to be still anxious for that co-operation, but adheres to the original agreement as to the port of debarkation. Lord Dufferin, it is said, does not object to the wording of the proclamation, but merely to its alteration and publication without his consent. The correspondent of the Times has been seeking for a reason for the unexpected haste with which the Imperial proclamation declaring Arabi a rebel 'ism published in the Vakyt without the knowledge of Lord Dufferin, and he thinks that the true explanation is this—that the English authorities in Egypt had discovered important correspon- dence between Arabi and certain personages in Constanti- nople, which would, if published, seriously compromise the Turkish Government.

HE EXAMINER, SA_TURDAY, EPTENI.BER 16 1882. ISCELLA_NE)tTS. Lest month the value of the priuted books exported was £100,312, against £98,604 in the corresponding menth of the previous year. Toe Earl of Egmont has giwn £1,003 to the Dean and Chapter of Cork to erect vestries for the clergy and choir of the cathedral. At Swansea, on Monday, four volunteers were sentenced to six months' hard labour for assaulting the police with their belts on Saturday night. In the month ended the 31st of August, the value of the cured fish imported was £156,688, of the herrings exported £302,950, and of other fish £39,805. While fishing on the Bucks shore of the Thames, on Sund ty evening, an angler was seized with a fit, and, falling into the stream, was drowned a few minutes after his immersion. There has been an inereass in the importation of oranges and lemons. Last month the value was £16,802, against £ll.OOO in August, 1881. in the last eight months it was £1,115.230. A BIG OATFL—In an assault case heard at Congleton on Monday, against Isaac Chappell, a county court bailiff, that , functionary said he was ready to swear he did not strike the complainant "upon all the bibles in Chester Cathedral." The Parliamentary register now in force in England and Wales includes a total of 2,591,402 voters. It is expected that the number will be considerably increased by the next registration. which will be co:npleted by the end of October. The Right Hon. Sir George Grey, G.C.8., died at his seat, Falloden, Northumberland, on Saturday evening. fie was born in 1799, and was in his 84th year. After having been a member of several Liberal Administrations, he retired from public life in 1874. At Leek on Monday the foundation stone was laid of a building which is to serve as a free library, art gallery, museum, and school of art. The donor is Mr. Joshua Nicholson, silk manufacturer. The amount of the benefac- tion will be about £20,000. In committing for trial, on Monday, the secretary of a Bolton miners' beneit society on a charge of embezzlempt, the Rev. J. S. Birley remarked that "these benefit societies managed their business so carelessly that it was no wonder they were rogued •, they were all rotten." At the Deptford Railway Station, on Monday, a domestic servant named Priscilla Harvey, aged nineteen, who had been spending her birthday with some friends at Rother- hithe, stepped from the carriage before the train stopped, send was drawn under the wheels and killed. The death is announced at the advanced age of 100 of Mrs. Mary Ashley, of Oxford. Mrs. Ashley, who enjoyed very good health almost up to the time of her death, was the widow of Thomas Ashley, a boatman, who died a few days since at a very advanced age. The remarkable age of the deceased has been verified by the registrar of births, deaths, and marriages. Fish was cheap enough in London last week. At Bil- lingsgate the glut of fresh haddocks was so great that purchasers could scarcely be found at any price, and 36011)3. of fish were knocked down at auction for one shilling. It would be difficult to find more conclusive evidence of a want of some means of better distribution than Billingsgate affords. ENGLISH SAILORS EATEN Br SAVAGES.—Neirs has ~reached Glasgow of the safety of the mate of the Glasgow ship which founded on a voyage from Mexillones (Bolivia) to Liverpool. The mate•effected a landing with four of his comrades, after being a considerable time at sea. His corn- radee were murdered and eaten by the Patagoniaus, but how the mate escaped is not stated. The mate will shortly reach Liverpool. SHOCKING DROWNING CASE AT WEST BROILWICIL—On Monday a shocking discovery was made at Hall End, West Bromwich. About 020 a.m. a man named Thomas Jutson found the dead body of a female child, apparently about 15 months old, in the Birmingham Canal in that neighbour- hood. This matter was reported to the police, and Police. constable Bakewell proceeded to the place and commenced to search the canal. At 7.45 the body of a respectably dressed woman was brought to the surface, about 100 yards away from the spot where the child was found. EXPLOSION AT A Contemetv.—On Monday morning an explosion took place at Gelli House Coal Colliery, Rhondda, where 150 men were employed. The gas was fired by a naked light which a lad named Edwards had in his cap. A -rush of wind followed, and the men's lights were extinguished and the ventilation doors shaken out of place. Wm. Price, an elderly collier, and his two sons, working in the stall next to that where the gas ignited, were badly burnt, espe- cially the father and the youngest son; their recovery is doubtful. The rest of the men escaped uninjured. A correspondent writes to the Times :—" Some years ago a woman named Lovegrove (a vendor of meat pies at Kings- ton-on-Thames) laid claim to the Derwentwater estates ; but want of means prevented her from bringing her case before a court of law. A son of Mrs. Lovegrove, who had not been heard of since 1857, has recently written from New Zealand, where he says he has acquired considerable property, expressing an intention of returning home for the purpose of prosecuting his claim to the estates." THE PRINCESS OF WALES AND HER SERVANT.—A monu- ment, with the following inscription, has recently been erected in Brompton Cemetery: In memory of Elizabeth Jones, who died May 18th, 1881, for fourteen years the faithful servant and friend of Alexandra, Princess of Wales, by whom this monument is erected. Life's race well run, Life's work well done, Life'scrown well won, Now eomes rest. Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord.

MR. BRADLLUGH ON MR. GLADSTONIL—Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., sneaking at a Liberal demonstration at Kirk-lourton, near Huddersfield, on Saturday. said it would be an insult to Mr. Gladstone to measure him against a wet-nurse politican like Sir Stafford Northcote, or a Don Quixote like the Marquis of Salisbury, and though the country might return Mr. Gledstene by a grand majority, he was so tied by ducal traditions, by ignoble precedents, and hampered by Court influences, that it was not surprising that the voice expressed in the ballot-box was not expressed in the Ministry. WOMEN AS REGISTRARS or BIRTHS AND DEATHS —An application was recently made to the Local Government Board by the Guirdians of the Wycombe Union to sanction the appointment of Mrs. Russell, of Great Marlow, to the office of registrar of births and deaths, vacant through the death of her husband. The guardians had been memorialised by the ratepayers of the district to make the appointment, and were themselves unanimously in favour of it. Some correspondence has passed, the Registrar-General making several inquiries as to the ability of Mrs. Russell to perform the duties. At the Guardians' meeting on Monday a letter from him was read, in which he sanctioned the appoint- ment for twelve months. A CALLOUS FELLOW.—Jonas Fellows, who was sent to gaol by Mr. Reifies, the Liverpool stipendiary, on Tuesday, for three months, for starving his little girl to death, showed a callousness which was deplorable. The man's wife is dead, and his three children, aged respectively ten, eight, and three, have been allowed to run wild. The eyoungeet, Julia, fell ill, and when taken to the Southern eflospitel, was found to weigh only 13ilbs., and to be in a sadly eineciated condition. Fellows declared that since Christmas he had only been able to get a day and half's work per week. He could not, he said, afford to pan anyone to look after the child, and he supposed it would' not `do for him to steal. Mr. Riffles severely censured the man, saving that drunkenness was the cause of his neglect, and that the child had been starved. Three months' imprisonment is certainly a lenient sentence for such a crime. THE LAST OUTRAGE ON THE THAMES EMBANKMENT.—At the Westminster Police Court, on Tuesday, Henry Smith and Joseph Reardon, labourers, were charged on remand with assaulting and robbing Mr. Henry Wil'iam Tayler, an attaché to the Netherlands Consulate-General, on the Thames embankment. On Monday night week the prose- cutor had left Lord Cairns' house and went towards home, intending to travel by Grosvenor-road to Victoria and thence to the city. As he passed Chelsea Bridge the man Reardon came to him and demanded money. Mr. Tayler tried to move off, when Reardon put his finger to his mouth and whistled. Smith came up and caught him by the arm, while Reardon hit him on the mouth, cuttiqg both his lips. A man passing on a tricycle went for a constable, and Reardon was locked up, and Smith, who escaped, was after- wards apprehended, One or the other had stolen the prose- cutor's watch, and that had not b2en recovered. The prisoners were committed for trial. ATTEMPT TO SWIM FROM PORTSMOUTH TO RYDE —On Saturday morning, at nine o'clock, Mr. Philip Evans, of Bristol, started from Southsea Pier with the intention of smimming, to Ryde Pier, a distance of noarly five miles, for a gold medal offered by the Portsmouth SwimMlng Club. Mr. Evans claims to have accomplished this feat two yearl since, and a Portsmouth pilot states that be aeCtUreperileel him. Evans started with the tide figalnst him, swimming about 40 strokes per minute; the first quarter of a mile being i completed n 11 wutes. He proceeded off Southsea C.astie, and tl'..en made for the Spit Fort, about a mile from the shore, after passing which the sea was so rougk he was obliged to discontinue. The officials of the Swimming Club expressed their belief in Evans' ability under more favourable conditions to accomplish the feat. Though at times he was engulfed by the waves and swallowed a good deal of water, he did not appear at all exhausted. THE NEW PARCELS POST.—The Postoffice authorities are very actively engaged in perfecting their arrangements for the establishment of the new parcels post. The undertaking is obviously a somewhat gigantic one, but there is not the , least doubt, with the resources at command, that whatever difficulties exist will be successfully surmounted. It is intended to make Euston-square a principal centre, not only for the arrival and despatch of parcels, but for the ordinary letter service. For this purpose a spacious new building will be erected close to the London and North-Western Rail- way Station, from which all parcels and letters arriving by that route will be sent, after assortment, to the various postal districts of the metropolis. This will greatly relieve the pressure of work which would otherwise fall upon the officials at St. Martin's-le-Grand, and also facilitate the whole business of the deptrtment. Mr. R. W. Johnston, who has for several years held the responsible position of Postmaster of the eastern central district, has been promoted to the control of the Euston-square office; and that gentleman will thus have more ample scope for developing the energy and power of organisation which he has uniformly mani- fested during his regime in the elev. He has already entered upon his new duties, but some time must necessarily vet elapse before the parcels post is in operation. Mr. Johnston's place as head of the eastern central dis- trict has been filled up by the appointment of Mr. H. Mellish, formerly eub-controller of the inland post. --ON Pros.

div.head: OFFER TO SURRENDER KAFR DOWAR.
div.p: OFFER TO SURRENDER KAFR DOWAR.

An Exchange Company's telegram from _Alexandria, dated Thursday morning, says :—" The rebels at Kafr Dowar have offered to surrender. Arrangements are being made to occupy the works by the British." Another tele- gram from Alexandria states Toulba Pasha, Com- mander of Kafr Dowar, sent a flag of truce at 7-30 this morning to General Wood offering to surrender. General Wood has telegraphed to the Commander-in-Chief asking for instructions and the terms to be offered. Cairo so far is safe. Deputation from the capital is now at Ka.fr Dowar waiting to come on to Alexandria. It is the general opinion here that Arabi will be delivered up to our troops by natives."

The following telegram from Sir Evelyn Wood has been received by the Secretary for War:—" An officer from Kafr Dowar has brought a letter saying that all the military chiefs wish to submit to the Khedive. They have given orders to open the canal dam. They ask me to open the telegraph, and say that the army has ceased all hostilities."

div.head: DAMIETTA AND KA.FRDOWAR.
div.p: DAMIETTA AND KA.FRDOWAR.

It is said that the Exyptian officers commanding at Damietta and Kafrdowar offered to surrender to the Khedive on condition that the British troops did not advance, but General Wolseley refused to treat. TELEGRAM FROM THE QUEEN. The following official telegram has been received from Balmoral :—" The Queen was mach gratified at receiving yesterday morning the announcement of the great victory of her troops at Tel-el-Kebir, as well as the special mention made by Sir Garnet IVolseley of His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught, and the admirable manner in hieh His Royal Highness led his brigade to the attack."

div.head: MILITARY CONVENTION.
div.p: THE MILITARY CONVENTION.

The latest phase of the Military Convention difficulty received from Constantinople is that Lord Dufferin has recAved instructions from Earl Granville to sign the Con- vention after a slight modification in the copies of the Sultan's proclamation intended for publication.

div.head: ARABI AT CAIRO.
div.p: ARABI AT CAIRO.

An Evening St4ndard telegram from Alexandria, on Thiarsday. says :—Arabi arrived at Cairo yesterday after- noon and Toulba arrived in the evening. Both are virtually , prisoners. THE LOSSES AT TEL-EL-KEBIR.

The official list of our losses at the assault on the enemy's positions at El Karaim and Tel-el-Kebir shows that nine officers and 45 men were killed, and two officers and t2O , men wounded. For the brief tours that the enemy resisted the list is sufficiently heavy, and that it is not more so is due to the accuracy with which General Sir G. Wolseley's plan was curled out by General Hamley commanding the storming line. Hamley himself assurel a correspondent that his being able to do so was due to the guiding pickets -showing the direction which had been pointed during the night by Major Fraser of the Engineers, and the skilful leading by the stars by Wyatt Rawson, naval aide to General •gir G. Wolseley,

TIIE PRESTON GUILD.

What has uscioubtedly been one of the most successful guild festivals ever held in Preston was concluded on Satur- day. The weather was again beautifully fine, and the number of passengers brought from the surrounding districts by rail was about the same as on Thursaay and Friday. At noon the Guild Court met, and the formal ceremony of con- clgding the guild, sealing the books, and adjourning the guild court for a period of twenty years, took place in the Guildhall Amongst those present were Lord Winmarleigh, Mr. J. Addison, Q.C., the guild mayor, and Colonel Stanley, r,f.P. Lord Winmarleigh, in moving a vote of thanks to the zarild mayor for his hospitality tinting the week, said he represented large number of the nobility, a considerable number of member; of the House of COMMOIIP, and the inhabitants of the county ,7euerally, in moving the vote. When it was recorded that on on day 170,000 persons Lad visited Preston and Preston's mayor, ho felt sure there was that said which could not be said of any other mayor in England. Speaking from his own experience, and he had now been present at four guilds, he could assure the mayor that, despite the magnificence of some of them, they had been entirely eclipsed by that they were now concluding.—The resolution was seconded by the High Sheriff of the county (Colonel M'Corquodale), and carried, with an additional vote of thanks to the. Lai! Mayoress. Other compiinientary votes of thanks followed, and thus concluded the official celebration of the guild. Later in the day there was a monster meet of bicyclists who had assembled from all parts of England in answer to the invitation of tke Preston Club. After a parade through the town the bicyclists, who numbered about 1,000, dined to- gether. A juvenile calico ball was held in the new public hall, and was a brilliant success. The juveniles, all dressed in fancy costumes, made the large ball a picturesque scene. The closing event of the festivities was a splendid torch- light procession. The torchbearers were formed into the most ludicrous and grotesque groups, and this, the most amusing feature of the week's festivities, was witnessed by thousands of people.

The Longton (Staffordshire) Town Council have refused, in response to a large petition of ratepayers, to allow Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., the use of the Town-hall, which he had taken from the official in charge for three lectures next Sunday. div.head: MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS..
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS..

As to the proclamation against Arabi, while it has greatly gratified the Khedive, Arabi himself has prohibited its ciicu- lation among his troops. Four of Arabl's officers have surrendered at Ramleh. They say that more wished to desert, but were held back through fear of the consequences. The force at Sir Garnet Wolseley's disposal is to be rein- forced by three batteries of Royal Artillery from India— two field batteries and one mounted battery. A telegram from Port Said states that the Chief of the Staff has arranged with the Water Company at Ismailia that the farmer place shall receive 900 tons of water daily. Hopes are now entertained of the release of Messrs. Pal- mer, Cbarrington, and Gill, who, according to information received by the Admiralty, were a few days ago safe in the hands of Bedouins in Arabia.

The Egyptian Government propose to submit the •ques• tion of indemnity for losses sustained during the present crisis to a Commission, Ind has addressed a Note to the Consuls-General of the six great Powers upon the subject. General Wood has made a careful reconnaissance of the coast from Ramleh to Abourkir. He was accompanied by one of the office's who recently surrendered, who states that one of the three regiments at Mandara is ready to desert. Labourers engaged for the service of the British army in Egypt had been arrested in Constantinople by order of the Porte, but after strong recommendations from Lord Dufferin they have been released. It is stated that his lordship in- tends despatching 200 of these labourers. On Tuesday, at the conclusion of an inspection of the let Gloucestershire Engineer Volunteers, the inspecting officer invited recruits for Egypt, about 150 offered themselves. Only 56, however, answered to the army conditions, and they were enrolled in the Royal Engineers, all ranks to be retained.

The opening of the dams to allow the sea to flow into Lake Mareotis is proceeding, and shortly this lake will answer the double purpose of protecting the British position from an attack on that side, ad of affording a means by which an advance by water can be made against Arabi's left flank.

The correspondents at the front are now all ready for marching, but it is not possible for all to go, as Sir Garnet has decided that correspondents here at headquarters must consider Ismailia their permanent base of operations, and not follow the advancing troops beyond a moderate ex- cursion from the town.

According to El Jewaib, the " inspired " organ of the Yildiz Kiosk, had the proclamation against Arabi not been published European intervention in ‘Fgypt would have been the result. A counter-blast from Arabi against the Sultan is expected in Constantinople. Heavy firing having recently more than once been heard somewhat to the south of Lake Mareotis, it was conjectured that there had been quarrelling between Arabi's troops and the Bedouins; but it appears that a strong body of the latter forced their way into Fort Mex on Saturday, and had to be dislodged at the point of the bayonet. A New York correspondent informs us of 7a rumour that was circulated there that the Irish dynamite operators were trying to blow up the Anchor Line steamer Castalia that was loading with mules for Egypt. It was not believed that there waa any foundation for the rumour, but active precau- tions were taken to frustrate any such design, According to a report in the National Zeitung of Satur- day, a secret understrnding has been or is about to be arrived at between England and Turkey on the Egyptian Question, which will secure for the Porte an important financial concession, in return for which England will receive a guarantee for the maintenance of her interests in Egypt. , Intelligence comes from Calcutta that the Corm-of-Mer- in-Chief in India has issued an order thanking Qv; offieers engaged in the despatch of the Indian division to Egypt. Indian tents are to be provided for the fresh force of 5,000 men about to be despatched from this country, and addi- tional camp equipage for 2,000 additional men will also be supplied by India. A correspondent at the front, who was present during the attack on the English position on Saturday, sends a detailed account of the affair. It appears that the enemy were forced back within two and a half miles of Tel-el-Kebir, and the correspondent is of opinion that had the Highland brigade been at hand at that period of Cie engagement, the British force might have taken possession of that place. The news from Alexandria, though unimportant, is rather strange. A party of Egyptians tried on Saturday to enter the town by crossing its rampart between the Rosetta Gate and Fort Silsileh, that is, about three miles in rear of our outposts at Ramleh. Nothing could better illustrate the necessity of (longing Lake Mareotis than the impunity with which such a party of I;;;; enemy can penetrate to the very CPtre of the ground which our forces are supposed to protect. Commenting on the course of events in Egypt, the Republique Francaise remarks that, although it considers France was mistaken in refraining from taking part with England in her military action there, still it would be a serious error to suppose that France had relinquished the "rights required in the past of exercising in Egypt the influence which justly belongs to her,"
LATER DETAILS.
SURRENDER OF CAIRO.

A telegram from Tel7el-Kebir (vid Ismailia), dated Thurs- day, says :—News has just been received at head-quarters of the surrender of Cairo. General Sir G. Wolseley, with his Staff, proceeds to that city by train to-day, and the military operations will virtually terminate. The Guards will leave for Cairo.

A telegram from Alexandria is as follows :—The Khedive has received news from Cairo that the city is safe. Butros Pasha has arrived at Kafr Dowar, en route for Alexandria, as the delegate of the inhabitants of Cairo charged to declare their loyalty to the Khedive. THE BATTLE OF TEL-EL-KEBIR. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT UNDER FIRE. The Daily Chronicle, in a second edition, pu6lishes a telegram which states the Duke of Connaught was at one time under a heavy fire. A bugler close beside him was shot.

div.head: OUR WOUNDED OFFICERS.
div.p: OUR WOUNDED OFFICERS.

A Central News telegram from Tel-el-Kebir, dated 2 a.m. on Thursday, states :—" The number of our killed is still uncertain. Among the wounded are Lieutenants Melwood, dangerously, and Corey, slightly; Colonels Meansland and Richardson, the latter seriously, Balfour 2nd Grenadier Guards, Captain Cumberland of the staff; Lieut. Barclay, 19th Hussars; and Captain Dallare, R.A., the four last slightly.—A detachment of the Grenadier Guards proceeds at daybreak by train to Terapon to cut off the fugitives' re- treat in that direction. Our force at Tel-el-Kebir occupies Arabi's late camp."

div.head: DESPATCH FROM SIR GARNET.
div.p: DESPATCH FROM SIR GARNET.

A despatch from Sir Garnet Wolseley, dated September 13 (midnight), says that between 50 and 60 guns were taken at Tel-el-Kebir. Zagazig was occupied at four o'clock yesterday afternoon by the Indian contingent under Major General Macpherson, who captured five trains with engines.

Three of the five men injured by the explosion at a Irlamgow iron foundry on Friday died o.i Saturday morning. The freedom of the burgh of Selkirk is about to he ~oted to Mr. Trevelyan, Irish Chief Secretary, at the instance of the citizem, in recognition of his s;:rri.ns in the onerous office he is now tilling.

John Saunders, the burglar, who shot a groom at Stam- ford Hill last week, was on Wednesday brought up at the Clerkenwell Police Court and again remanded. It was stated that the injured man was not yet out of danger. Sir J. Whittaker Ellis, Lord Mayor of London, bas, it is stated, accepted the invitation of the Mayor of Live! pool to a banquet at the Town Hall on an early day. During his visit to Liverpool Newsham House will be placed at the disposal of the Lord Mayor. Birkenhead is about to add to the list of its distinguished inhabitants the name of Dr. Knight, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Shrewsbury, who, finding the Shropshire capital too inaccessible for the convenient discharge of his-duties, has decided to remove his residence to Birkenhead.

Liverpool has at lenath decided upon an attempt to con- trol the "street arabs " who infest some of the principal thoroughfares in that city. The Council on Tuesday adopted a resolution asking Parliament for powers to deal with the children who wander about the streets until late at night under the pretence of selling newspapers and other articles. _ . .

The Duke and Duchess of Albany arrived at Aberdeen at two o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, on board the Admiralty yacht Lively. The Provost and magistrates gave their Royal Highnesses an informal reception. The duke and ' duchess then drove to the railway station, leaving at three o'clock in a special train for BADater, en route for Balmoral Castle. The auctioneers employed to dispose by auction of the goods seized in respect of the vicar's rate, at Coventry, made another atteruNon Wednesday to effect a sale,but were unsuccessful. The auction room was packed by people opposed to payment of the rate, and several ugly rushes took place. There was an indescrib dale noise, and much groaning and singing, in spite of the efforts of a large body of police to keep order. An immense crowd gathered outside the building, and the sale was eventually adjourned sine die. THE CONVICT ARTHUR ORTON.—The Rev. Philip Gast, of Charles-street Chapel, Goswell-road, having written to Sir William Harcourt requesting permission that the convict Arthur Orton should be made acquainted with the fact that a conference of Christian ministers and other sympathisers with the claimant is to be held shortly, has received a reply declining to inform the convict of the proposed conference, or to permit him "to write a statement of those points of his case which he would desire to be discussed." Ernest Henry &Hey, described as an ex-officer of the Indian Marine, has been committed for trial at Portsmouth on a charge of defrauding tradesmen by means of fictitious cheques drawn upon the London branch of the Bank of Australasia. Among the prisoner's papers there were found a cheque-book of the bank named and a loose cheque for £5,000; but it is but fair to Mr. Bailey to state that his advocate said that this cheque was only filled up in fun. A carter named O'Brien was on Wednesday committed for trial by the Heywood magistrates for assaulting his wife with intent to do her some bodily harm. He beat the woman most savagely about the body and head with the handle of a collier's " pick," inflicting injuries which at one time threatened a fatal issue. It must be added that the wife had been away from work, drinking, and had taken refuge in a neighbour's house for the night when the prisoner adopted this violent method of reclamation. _ .

John Cartwright Snape, hawker, was committed for trial at the Longton Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, on the charge of attempting to murder a policeman named Nash, on the 2nd inst. Prisoner was being arrested for dis- orderly conduct, when he stabbed the officer in the neck with a clasp knife, inflicting a very dangerous wound, and also stabbed through the officer's clothing several times, voiving he would murder him. After a desperate struggle with several people the prisoner was secured.

_ FRENCH MONKS IN DETON AND CORNWALL.—The expul- sion of the orders from France has resulted in the establish- ment of various orders in England and Wales. Their recent movements include the settlement of the Fathers of the Society of Mary at Paignton, where the foundations of a monastery and church have been laid on St. Mary's Hill. The Augustinian Canons of St. John Lateran have settled down at Bodmin, and taken in hand a little missionary chapel and sacristy, which they are converting into a monastery. It is said the same body was settled in Bodmin in pre-Reformation times. MR. JOHN BRIGHT AND THE "CLAIMANT."—In connec- tion with the conference of the " Claimant's "sympathisers, which took place in Clerkenwell, the Press Association has received the following copy of a letter from Mr. John Bright, M.P.:—" Dear sir,—l may say that my view of the Claimant's case is as unchangeable as yours, and that I do not see the chance of any good result from an interview. As to reducing the term of imprisonment, I suppose the usual rule will be adh,red to. In my opinion no case can less merit any special consideration, but if you wish any memo- rial to be sent to the Home Secretary I will willingly present it for you.—'l am, very truly, yours, JOHN BRicarr." SAD Dnowerwo CASE.—i painful death by drowning occurred in Ramsey Harbour, Isle of Man, on Wednesday. As the tide receded the body or a boy, named Frank Southard, an orphan, aged nine years, was found lying near one of the fishing boats. He was an inmate of the Wesleyan Children's Home, having been transferred from Stevenson's Home, London, and left with other children to attend the Wesleyan day school shortly before two o'clock. He had been seen rowing about in a small boat with other boys before dinner, and it is supposed that he went along to the boat again on his way to school and fell into the harbour. TEN FISHERMEN DROWNED.—The French fishing boat Reine des Anges, of Boulogne, was wrecked on the Middle Cross Sand, opposite Yarmouth, with the loss of the captain and nine men, early on Wednesday morning. The remain- ing eight lashed themselves to spars and barrels, and were picked up by a Hamburg steamer and transferred to the Caister lifeboat, which was launched in answer to a signal from the boat. The rescued men were in a very exhausted condition when picked up, and were brons.r,ht into Yarmouth Harbour, and conveyed to the Sailors' HORI2. The son of the captain was among the saved. GALLANT CONDIJOT OF A POLICEMAN.—EarIy on Wed- nesday morning, when it was still dark, a county constable named Oliver Young, who was on duty in Aigburth-road, Liverpool, beard the noise of breaking trees in the garden of Mr. James Haddock, and presently five men came out in- to the road, laden with fruit. The officer seized one man, and was attempting to handcuff him when the others assailed him with kicks and stones. Young gallantly kept his ground, handcuffed his man' and knocking another down with his truncheon, handcuffed him also. He then whistled for assistance, and a borough officer coining up the other three men escaped. Young was very much bruised and knocked about, but with his brother officer he took the two prisoners, who were labouring men, into custody. They were each sent to prison fora month.

ENCOUNTER WITH A BURGLAR: A BRAVE WOMAN.— On Saturday morning a desperate encounter took place with a burglar at Belgrave, near Leicester. Mr. and Mrs. Dowell, living in Down-street, saw a man crawling from the foot of the bed towards the bedroom door. Mr. Dowell jumped out of bed, and the man, rushing from the room leaped from the top of the stairs to the bottom. Mr. Dowell followed and seized the intruder. A desperate struggle ensued, and Mr. Dowell finding that be was getting the worst of it, called to his wife, who, although an invalid, seized a poker and dealt the man a heavy blow on the front of the head. Mr. Dowell was then quite exhausted, and Mrs. Dowell gave the burglar another blow, which cut open the back of his head and felled him to the floor. He was then given into custody, when be gave the name of William Shepherd, and his address 27, Whitechapel-road, London. RUMOURED PROBABLE MINISTERIAL CHANGES .—T h e Press Association "understands that there is a probability that several changes in the Cabinet will be announced by the Prime Minister shortly after the reassembling of Parlia- ment in October. The precise time and the nature of the changes will, however, depend upon whether peace and order have been fully restored in Egypt. If the victory at Tel-el-Kebir should result in an early close of the Egyptian campaign and a settlement of the Eastern question, Sir avinCeoai made erettchlh, that since n fe ahe Charles Dilka is likely to be promoted to Cabinet rank and a new appointment be made to the Under Secretaryship for Foreign Affairs. The offices of Lord President of the Privy Council and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, now held provisionally by Earl Spencer and Lord Kimberley in addition to their other official duties, are likely to be filled up by fresh appointments before the new session of Parlia- ment by which time Mr. Gladstone also will probably have irseseirpgneedateleLe zuCrh.aencheillldoerrsshiwpilolfsutclece,ee,, Exchequer, to which, it A TERRIBLE MOTHER-IN-LAIC—At the Thames Police ae Saturday, a meek-looking little man, who ap- MTr .h Le nshi g applicantton for protection t b eagainst his isBhutleo'thalerp-liinel atwo. rinri.edstlh.ee lilliinkequaeenyllasihoande burdensf a firstto round his neck, and ruled both him and his wife with a rod of iron. On the previous night she Mine to his house and turned him out of doors.—Mr. lalsbinetou: What, out of your own house ?—The Applicant: Yes, sir ; and I was glad to get out safe. You would be glad to run if you had such a motherain.law. She said she would " spifflicate MP," and I know she would have done so if she had got hold of me. After I had gone she turned round and thrashed her daughter, my wife, and made my own mother, who happened to be in the house, fly for her life. She has said that she will murder the lot of us, and I ant afraid she will.—The magistrate directed Police-sergeant Gibson, the warrant officer, to go down and see the person complained of, and caution her as to her future behaviour. . A Scam{ IN A Poracu COURT. —On Monday, at Clerken- well, John Welch, aged ten, was charged on remand with "being of such a disposition that his friends were unable t. o control him," he having been found by a constable wander- ing and not under proper guardianship.—Mr. W.ilis, indus- trial school officer, rem-Irked that Welch was an Illegitimate child who was not taken proper care of. His mother lived in common lodging-houses, having no permanent home. It was thdught by the coinmittee of the School Board who looked into these cases that this was an instance in which the boy should be sent to an industrial school for a few years.—Mr. Paget: Ido not think so; I discharge the laev. —Mr. Wills: Very well, your worship; I shall bring him before another magistrate (leaving the witneEs-box).—Mr. Paget: Here, come back. Do you think that this is a re- spectable way to treat a magistrate who has adjudicated upon a case?—Mr. Wills: Well, your worship,' ----Mr' Paget: Was not that a very disrespectful remark to make? —Mr. Wills: Well, rather perhaps. (Laughter.) Mr. Paget : I think it was most disrespectful, sir, most disre- spectful. You are not fit to be an officer. Mr. Wills 1,01,, very well, sir. (Leaving the court with the boy.)

The announcement is made in the Times that two of the leading manufacturing firms at Wolverhampton are about to tran,fer their husinnses to London. A t.ireat Eastern coal-truck, in process of shunting, fall ev.r a well in London, on Thursday morning, upon the roof of a public-house, passing through into a bedroom. A man who was sleeping there, escaped uninjured. On Thursday morning the boiler of the steam tug Willing Mind, of Hull, exploded whilst she was towing a barque up Ow Humber. The tug was blown to pieces, and the engineer, Robert Turf, was lost. Three of the tug's crew were recuell by the barque. At the Ashton Mess Colliery on Thursday morning, by the giving way of a wall, a man named Stone was instantly killed and another man was injured. The accident disabled the engine which worked the winding gear, and as a result the miners in the workings were confined undergroutd. throughout the whole of the day. Arnold.Brownhill, a boy four years of age, son of James Brownhill, wheelwright, -Chorlton, died at Chorlton-curn- Hardy, on Wednesday night, from the result of a dog bite. On the 28th July the little fellow was bitten by a dog, ant was attended by Dr. Pownall, but symptoms of rabies set ia on Monday, and he died as above stated. The Clitheroe Town Council, on Thursday, unanimously declined to consent to an application to tbe Board of Trade by the Hammona Electric Light Company for a license to supply electricity in Clitheroe. Tbe reading of the address caused much laughter, as the Clitheroe Corporation mann- facture the town's gas. The Council resolved to purchase laud for £750, to construct a. new reservoir, in order to in- crease the water supply. A sad case of drowning was reported on Thursday morn. ing to the Bolton county police. A boy named Percy Charles Whewell, aged nine, residing in Park-road, Sharpies, was playing on the banks of a reservoir, and in attempt- ing to reach a piece of woed floating in the water he fell in. An alarm was raised, and a man named Aspinall gal- lantly jumped in and got the boy out, but life was then extinct. Mits. GLADSTONE AND THE GOOD TEKPLARS OF WALES. —About one hundred of the members attending the session of the English Grand Lodge of Wales at Mold visited Ha. warden on Thursday. After they had—through the kind- ness of Mr. Gladstone—visited the Castle, they repaired to the coffee tavern for lunch. In the curse of the afternoon Mrs. Gladstone called to inquire if they had enjoyed the outing. Unfortuately the members had just dispersed, bat Mrs. Gladstone was assured they had enjoyed themselves much. The Duke and Duchess of Westminster arrived. at Eaton.

Hall on Thursday evening from London. They will remain at the Hall a short time before proceeding north. The bracelet from the citizens of Chester to the Duchess on the occasion of her marriage will be privately presented by Mrs. Jacobson, on behalf of a committee of ladies, on Saturday. The Town Council of Chester will present an address of congratulation to the Duke. On Thursday morning a wheel came off a wagon in the front of a long train of iron ore waggons, as it was passing over the Dement Viaduct of the Cleator and Workington Railway, near Workiogton. The engine and three wagons in front kept the metals, but the rest of the train was thrown off the line, smashing a number of wagons and tearing ma the permanent way on the viaduct. The guard had a nar- row escape. Both lines were blocked, and passengers had to. walk along the viaduct. Three boys named Bromley, Critchley, and Morland were charged at Oldham, on Thursday, with interfering with a I railway signal on the London and North-Western Railway. The lads were playing on the line near Clarksfield Bridge, when they pulled the wire of a signal and " larked " with the lever. The case was adjourned in order to bring ,for- ward another lad who was implicated in the affair,; the • Bench saying the case was one of great importance. About three o'clock on Thursday morning be retaining wall of a coal shed connected with the boiler house of the Ashton-under-Lvne Moss Colliery fell upon the front of the boilers. Two firemen were buried alive beneath the debris and about eighty tons of coal. One man named Stone has ' been killed, and the other is very seriously injured. The men in the pits are entombed owing to the smashing of the steam pipes connected with the engines, and the men can- not go down, Information received from Lloyds, on Thursday morning, states that the steamer Armenian, of Liverpool, 1,123 tons register, which sailed from Middlesboro' for St. Petersburg with a valuable cargo, several weeks since, has not yet passed Copenhagen, and there is no doubt but that she has foundered off Lemvig, as a quantity of wreckage has washed' ashore on the Swedish coast, marked "s I. Armenian, Captain Elder," also one or two bodies recognised as belong- ing to the missing steamer. The captain and crew num- bered 25 hands all told. THE TICHBORNI CLAIMANT AGITATION. A conference of sympathisers with the Tichborne claimant was held in Goswell-road, London, on Thursday, at which about 60 persons attended, including Mr. E. Kimber (presiding), Rev. Dr. Thomas, Rev. Philip Gast, Captain Parker Snow, Charles Orton Jean Luie, Mr. Privett, son of a sister of the Dowager Lady ,Tichborne, and a number of delegates from metropoli- tan Magna Charts and Tichborne Release Associations. I Resolutions were unanimously adopted that a memorial to I the Home Secretary should be prepared, praying for a remis-

sion of the sentence. • A YORKSHIRE MEMORIAL TO LORD F. CAVENDISFL—A large number of the leading constituents of the late Lord Frederick Cavendish met at the Bradford Law Institute on Thursday afternoon, to consider the project of raising a monument to the memory of the deceased nobleman. Mr. William Foster, of Hornby Castle, presided. Resolutions were passed to the effect that it was desirable a monument should be erected, and that it should take the form of a pillar, obelisk, or like memorial, to be erected on some con- spicuous site in the neighbourhood of Bolton Abbey. An influential committee was formed for carrying out t.laS scheme.

LORD DERBY ON THE EGYPTIAN WAR.—Lord Derby has sent the following reply to a Manchester gentleman who wrote him with reference to the Eeyptian question : Knowsley, September 12, 1882. Sir,—ln answer to your ' letter of yesterday, I shall probably take an opportunity rome time in autumn or winter of expressing an opinion on the Egyptian question. In the meanwhile it is enough to say that I am satisfied that neither Mr. Gladstone ner Lord Granville would have engaged in a war without the fullest conviction that it was inevitable.—l remain, your obedient servant (signed) DERBY." The Earl of Derby attended a meeting of the County Sessions at Preston, on Thursday, and opened the new ball and offices erected for the trans.action of county business. His Lordship said the northern towns required ornament, and they could afford the handsome and decorative public buildings for which there was a growing taste in the North. In regard to the new ball, he said it was well that the ad- ministration of affairs by what was really a small provincial parliament. should be carried on amidst surroundings culcue lated to inspire respect. The new building .has cost about £58,000. THE BANK OF ENGLAND.—The Bank of England on Thursday raised its rate of discount from 4 to 5 per cent. It had stood at the former figure since August 17. At the half-yearly meeting of the proprietors of the Bank on Thurs- day, the question was asked upon what basis the Directors determined dela rate of current interest. The Chairman kMr. H. R. Grenfill) said there were various considerations • involved, all of which could not be made public. The only wish of the Directors was to arrive at a cenclusion which would be satisfactory to the proprietors of the B ink, the country at large, and the great commercial body of which the Bank was a great centre. TILE DOTEEEL EXPLOSION:—The Committee on Gas Explosions who were appointed to investigate the circum- stances attending the loss of the Doterel completed their report at Chatham on Thursday. The Committee find that the theory advanced by the Court-martial which inquired into the loss of the Doterel that an explosion of gas generated in the coal bunkers was the primary cause of the ignition of the powder magazine leas not been borne out by the result of their experiments. With respect to the storage of exero- tine siccative it has been proved that even assuming its pre- sence on board the Doterel did not tend to bring about the destruction of the vessel, yet its stowage on board ships is attended with great risk. At Accrington on Thuredav a grocer named Hodgsm, living at Osiraldtwistle, was summoned under two inferma- tions ter breaches of the Licensing Act. Defendant holds a licence to sell beer and spirits to be consumed off the premises. His house was watched on Sunday, and a girl was seen to be supplied with ruin, and on the previous Sun- day about 20 persons were observed to go into the entry adjoining defendpt's house. The Chairman said this was the worst case of the•kind they had had. It was one which would show the public the great amount of mischief and incentive to crime these licences were doing. Defendant was fined 60s. and costs, and his licence was endorsed. Jane Ellis, summoned for aiding and abetting, was titled Is. and oost3. , W. LANYSON ON TAB EGYPTIAN WAIL—Sir W Law- son, M.P., addressed a meeting at Aspatria on Tuesday night on the Egyptian question, and read that whatever reasons might be given for the war in Egypt the true reason was to secure the finances of that country for the payment of interest to the bondholders of this country for money lent ,to the Khedive. The cry raised had been that the status quo ante of that country must be maintained, and that Arabi Pacha was a military adventurer, and should be Out down. lie had no doubt the Egyptian newspapers would say that Sir G.Wolseley was a military adventurer. The only difference , which he saw was that Sir Garnet Wolseley was an aggres- sive adventurer in is country in which he had no claim, while Arabi was an adventurer to guard the hearths and homes of his country. He objected to people making Mr. Gladstone a political Pope. MR. LEATHAM, .P., AND HIS CONSTITtENTS.-11.1r. E.. A. Leathern, M.P., was present on Tuesday evening at the opening of a Liberal club near Huddersfield, and acknow- ledged a vote of confidence in the Government. Speaking as an " independent" member, he said he had exercised the privilege ef his independence o felt O n occoVtline,.,GbouNt,,t,rhnem e n dif- ficulties which bad been cast in the way o refrain from ember- were so great that be had bonund to whole he could look upon the Governm • embar- rassing them in that way. ent policy without reproach. In Ireland gong seem that their conduct bad been it might t° some P"' bad followedut Irish legislation, • consistent, but good effects in and there were symptoms every v day that the unnatural and unwholesome system which had prevailed for some years in that country was breaking U. As to the Egyptian war, he said it was not one of aggreseion or aggrandisement, and it had his support on the ground filet it was incurred for a definite and justifiable object—the protection of our com- merce with the great dependency of India. By this time the people of England knew tbat a Liberal Administration was not cowardly or weak, but reedy to defend British in terests when they were really assaiied.
