div.p: THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 16, 1882.

---- ith,44' id now over a month since Parliament adjourned, two or three weeks hence it will have nbled again for the purpose of reforming its stne ti,t,ps of procedure; yet up to the present time we been troubled with very few extra -Parliamentary littk:rance3. The chief members of the Administration 414: been silent, for the very suffieient reason that kr Policy, either home or foreign, has not been ; but why the leaders of the Opposition have t'een exerci,ing their privileges of criticism we kre Ac to understand. It is the function of an %alo.sition to attack and to criticise at every point; tiei• it is the duty af the Governmen‘, of course, to tit:all4. When the Opposition, however, take up an at- tiil;t",e (3f pap,ive indifference we are entitled to assume ttiti;ll°r.e is nothing being done by the Government t%lb, Which they can find fault, and it is unnecessary, ter to 8 '4ore, for the members of it to seek opportunities for 1/eak to the NAtion. Several very potent reasons tlot extreme reticence of the Coliservatives are ittw.4.ttr to seek. Just before the adjournment they effe'`illed a crushing defeat in Parliament, from the tblZtl'l of which they have not recovered. On the t tl'oo whether certain of the Lords' amendments ti)ct," Arrears Bill should be agreed to, the Opposi- ihg, „Were cutnumbz•red by a majority so overwhelm- %tit 'Qat it is necitess for them to appeal to the con- INtlelloies on that score, in tho hope of finding many PELthisers. The division then demonstrated eon-

elusively that the Bill was one which the Nation would not allow the Lords to destroy, anxious as they were to do this. Irish affairs ()aside Parlia- ment, too, on which the Conservatives were wont to harangue and to blame the Government for, as they alleged, making concessions to agitation, can no longer be selected as a suitable theme for Tdry decla- mation. The most recent returns show that there is a gradual diminution of crime all over the country. In isolated spots, it is true, a dreadful murder or outrage is now and again committed, as for instance, at Cong ; but on the whole there is on every hand a greater feeling of security alike for life and fez property. The sentences passed at the recent Commission Court, held in Dublin, have had a very deterrent effect, as it was intended they should have, upon evil-doers, and that being the case the establish- ment of that tribunal is more than justified. But apart from that aspect of the Irish question, land- lords and tenants live on more amicable terms; rents are paid without demur, and the benefits of the Land Act with the kindred measure for dealing with arrears are generally hailed by all parties as a per- manent settlement of a great and troublesome diffi- culty. Had the rebellion in the Irish constabulary been allowed te spread, and had there been a general strike, it would in all likelihood have formed an excellent handle for Tory orators; but that was, ex- terminated at one stroke with a firm band, and in a way highly creditable to the Executive. The right hon. E. Gibson, the Attorney-General for Ireland in the late Administration, in one of his recent speeches was bound to admit that there was an improvement observable in the state of the country—that there are fewer outrages, and that there is a greater tendency to pay rent ; and only on Wednesday, the Dublin Express,in an able leader, accepts the visit of the Lord Lieutenant to the West as a sure indication that peace and tranquillity are returning to the country. So far as regards the condition of Ireland, then, the Opposi- tion have no cause for grumbling. In Egyptian affairs there is as little. The war is behag prosecuted with vigour, and after the defeat of the enemy on Wednesday we may hope that we have at last seen the beginning of the end of the struggle. There are those who do not disguise their eager anticipations that the campaign will be a protracted one, and the Government will have again and again to come before Parliament and ask for the ways and means with which to carry it on; but happily there is now no pro- bability of this being the case, and these well-wishers of the Government are consequently doomed to dis- appointment. He is a bold politician who would dare to assert that the Government has not, in restor- ing order in Egypt, the support of the country, but politicians of this stamp are not wanting. Sir Wilfrid Lawson is one of these, and from him and such as him the Government seem to have more to fear than from their avowed enemies. At Glasgow the other eight he received a significant rebuke when an amendment approving the policy of the Government in Egypt was carried in preference to a motion con- demning that policy; but undaunted by this rebuff the facetious baronet has, we observe, been address- ing a meeting at Aspatria, convened by himself. The worthy baronet gave utterance to the now stale argument that the war was being pursued in the interest of the bondholders only. He hinted that there were no British interests involved i the conflict, and he twitted the Government that it could not find a respectable ally. He seems to think that the massacre of the 11th of June should go unpunished; and that when Arabi pointed his guns at our fleet the vessels ought at once to have got out of his range. This is all very good in theory, but in practice it is bad, and England could not afford to act in that fashion. Mr. E. A. Leathern, the Radical member for Huddersfield, —and no one will accuse him of being an advocate for armed intervention in foreign affairs—opened a Liberal Club at Salford the same evening that Sir Wilfrid was speaking at Aspatria, and he supplies a very good answer to the junior member. for Carlisle. Mr. Leathern said that if the war in Egypt had resetnbled the wars in Afghanistan or the Transvaal, or even in Zululand—if it had beeu one of aggression and aggrandisement—he should have said precisely about it what he said of them. But he added, "It was net until British subjects had been foully massacred under the very guns of a fleet powerful enough to have blown the city of Alexandria into atoms—not until, in spite of every denial and pledge, fortifications were being heaped up for the destruction and injury of the fleet— that the Government consented to strike the first blow. Then came the bombardment, and the rest logically followed." It is undeniable that our road to India, said that our commerce must be protected, and so Mr. Leathern says that " so long as our commerce penetrated to every part of the world it was essential that the strong arm of British protection should go with it, and so long as we had India—and India was one of the chief markets for the proceeds of our industry—it was essential that that great highway should be kept free and open, and free and open it Gould only be so long as there was a friendly Govern- ment in existence upon the banks of the Suez Canal." The existence of this highway, it will not be gain- sayed, was seriously jeopardised by the military insurrection which deposed our friend the Khedive, and 'substituted for him a blood-thirsty incendiary. Mr. Leathern thus very accurately sums up our object in going to Egypt:—" We have gone," he says, "to re-establish a government which should keep order upon the banks of the Suez Canal, to restore to an industrious population that prosperity of which, until the savage outbreak of the soldiery, they were in full and peaceable possession. In doing this we had gained the universal approbation of Europe, which was no mean testimony as to the candour and truth- speaking of our Ministry. When we attained all this we had achieved one of those great and historic aets of which, from the days of Cromwell to our own, the people had always felt justly proud." If there are those of the Liberal party who take a delight in damaging the Government in the eyes of its suppor- ters, it is a satisfaction to know there are also others of that party who are prepared to defend it, and that, too, with a greater show of reason than its assailants have. At the same time, we think it would be more becoming in Sir Wilfrid Lawson and others of his ilk to leave the Opposition to attack the Government, than for him and his friends to undertake that task. We may be sure the Opposition will not neglect to do so should an opportunity arise; and their silence at the present time can only be accepted as an evidence that the policy of the Administration meets with their approval. At no time, indeed, since the I general election have the prospects of the Government been so bright as they are now, and at no time have its principles and policy been so much in accord with the feelings of the nation. Hence the silence of the Tory party. We are promised a County Franchise Bill in the next session, and with an unbroken majority at the back 9f the Government there should be no difficulty in carrying this, especially after the rules of procedure have been reformel.

ONE of the most brilliant feats in modern warfare has been accomplished by Sir Garnet Wolseley. By one decisive blow he has so completely routed Arabi and the Egyptian Army that it is questionable whether the rebels can be so rallied as to again offer resistance to the British arms. At dawn on Wednes- day morning, Sir Garnet attacked Tel-el-Kebir—the stronghold of the Egyptians, and the only obstacle to the gallant general's advance on Cairo—and so skil- fully was the attack planned and so stealthily executed, that in the course of only a few minutes our army was complete master of the situation. This has been done, too, against tremendous odds. The British force consisted of 11,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry, and GO guns; while Arabi's forces are estimated at 20,000 regulars, 2,500, cavalry, 6,000 Bedouins and irregulars, and 70 guns, loeated behind formidable redoubts and entrenchments. These, however, were insuffi3ient to deter an assault, and with that indomitable pluck

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 16, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 16, 1882.

which is the distinguishing characteristic of the British soldier, the enemy's defences were scaled at a bound and the Egyptians charged at the point of the bayonet. The rebels were unable to withstanl this, and the consequence was they deserted their poets, threw down their arms, and fled, leaving their guns, provisions, and everything else on the field of battle. Some of the Egyptians more daring than others were bayonetted as they stood at their guns. After the first rush confusion reigned supreme, and as the enemy fled in terror they were hotly pursued by the cavalry, while the artillery pounded the retreating foe with shot and shell. It is estimated that over 2,000 Egyptians have been killed, while as many have been taken prisoners, and it is a matter of regret that Arabi is not one of these. The loss on our side happily is not great, and it is not expected it will excnpd 200. The pre- sent vint-ory is so ,complete that Sir a lrnet's reluctance to attack at an earlier stage of the campaign has been more than justified. It is evident his object has been to strike one blow which should end the struggle. Tiais he has now done most successfully, and he has thereby added ifnensasely to his reputation. The valour of the British arms on this occasion has not been equalled since the Crimean war; and the victory which ha e been achieved ought to speedily end this war.

The schooner Minnie Coles, bound from Runcorn to Peter- head, ran into a Peterhead fishing boat on Saturday, and cut it in two. The boat was transfixed by the schooner's jibbootn, and was thus borne up till both vessels reached the port. COLLAPSE' 07 I PROSECTITIOX AT WIDNES.—At Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Lawrence Kenny, who was remanded a week ago, was placed in the dock.—Mr superintendent Barker said the prisoner was taken into custody on the morning of Tuesday, the sth inst, on a charge of maliciously wounding Ann Rawlinson, on the 31st July. He had made careful inquiries into the case, and his opinion was that the evidence would not support the charge. He therefore asked that the prisoner might be discharged.— Mr. Husband, who appeared for the prisoner, aaid he stated so a week ago, and it was rather hard that the prisoner, who was a working man, should have been detained in gaol a week.—Mr. Superintendent Barker said an action for a common assault could be taken.—The prisoner was dis- charged. It will ba remembered that the woman was with difficulty prevailed upon to take the oath a week ago. ASSAULT AT Ruscoarr.—On Monday, at the Ran- corn Police Court, a married woman, named Elia tbeth Pendlebury, was summoned for having, on the sth instant unlawfully assaulted Elizabeth Yarwood.—Complainan state 4 that on Tuesday evening she was passing by the Navigation Inn, when the "defendant and the man she lived with" came out and commenced to curse her; also striking her in the face with her fist. —Defendant made a statement to the effect that the complainant was the aggressor, and that she (defendant) only pushed her away. —The Bench fined defendant 23. 6d. and costs.—Defendant: What imprisonment, please ?—Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk) : The magistrates say seven days.—Defendant : I hope you are not offended, gentlemen, but what am I to do with her? she won't leave me alone.—The Chairman : If she assaults you, you must take a summons out against her. —Defendant: Thank you, but I will go to gaol.—Mr. Johnson : Have you any goods? Yes, I have a few, but they are not worth much. (Laughter.) ST. MICHABL'S, DITTON Ilann.—An interesting ceremony will take place at St. Michael's Church, Ditton, on Sunday 24th inst., when the new pulpit, which has just been erected, will be unveiled. The pulpit has been planned and executed by Mr. Hubert Pilzer, of Cologne, who has already distinguished himself by the successful execution of several important commissions, amongst which a special mention is due to a more than life-size statue of the Blessed Virgin under the title of "Stella Matutina," which was lately erected at the Jesuit College at Feldkircb, Vararlberg, Austria. The new pulpit is executed in a tasteful romanesque style, with some very slight transitions to the Gothic, which the style of St. Michael's Church seemed to require. It is of Caen stone, supported by a hexagonal pillar, flanked on Oast side by a half column of black marble, and richly decorated with an ambient colonnade of marble columns and half columns. The cornice of white marble gives an elegant finish to the upper part of the pulpit, which is ado.ned with some very striking representations of SS. Ignatius, Francis Xavier and Aloysius de Gonzaga, and of Blessed Peter Canisius.

AN IMPECUNIOUS RAILWAY TRAVELLER AT ViTIDITES. —James Southern was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, to answer a charge of riding on the London an North Western Railway Company's line without a ticket, with intent to defraud the 'company.—Mr. Ferrand appeared to prosecute, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Husband.—Mr. Ferrand said that on the 31st August the defendant was seen by a guard, named Thomas White, to enter the 3 p.m. train from Widnes to St. Helens. He alighted at Appleton, and when asked for his ticket be re- plied that he had been " seeing a friend off," and that he had no money. The station master requested his name and address, which he gave as John Unsworth, 51, Widnes-road, Whines; and stating that he would return the following morning and pay the fare. He did so, but the money was refused, and it was discovered that he had given a false name and address; his name being Southern and his home at Rnncorn. He had been in a respectable position as a sur- veyor, but had fallen from it.—Mr. Husband, in addressing the Bench on behalf of his client, said the defendant's offence had been caused by his impecuniosity. He understood that the defendant was rather under the influence of drink at the time.—Mr. Ferrand remarked that the defendant lead been oonvicted of a similar offence seven years ago.—Mr. Husband said that would not affect the present case.—The Bench fined the defendant 20s and costs, or, in default, a month's imprisonment. Runomq BURIAL BOARD.—The usual monthly meeting was held at the Board's offices on Wednesday, when there were present Messrs. Coleburn (in the chair), Handley, Moss, Mellor, Littler, and Salkeld (secretary).—The Secre- tary reported that the interments for five months to August 25th were 136; corresponding period last year, 110; increase, 26. The fees received to August 25th amounted to £127 13s. Bd.; corresponding period last year, 'llO5 193. 4.; increase, £2l 14s. 4d. The Finance Committee reported that the fees for August amounted to £37 17s. There had been paid in wages £ll 163., and a balance paid into bank to the credit of the Board £26 2s. Accounts amounting to £l7 14e 01, including quarter's salary to secretary, were examined and passed for payment. Interest falling due to the end of September amounting to £5B 7s 6d was passed for payment. The committee also reported that they had considered the reso• lution referred to them by the July Board meeting, and recommended that in future the annual instalments in repayment of debt on the cemetery should be invested in a sinking fund, which should accumulate until it amounted to the whole of the debt. The Secretary said the bench in front of the cemetery gates had been broken by a number of roughs and half of it carried away, probably for firewood. Mr. Ford hall informed him that it had been the means of causing people of a rough character to assemble there, and give him great trouble and annoyance. The Board decided they would not re-fix the bench, and the meeting ended. Imerenn MILK AT WIDNES: A WARNING TO FARMERS. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. J. Brock, Charles Brassington, farmer, Crow Wood, was summoned under the Food and Drugs Act, to answer a charge of selling adulterated milk. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—Mr. Husband, who prosecuted on behalf of the Local Board, said this case bad been taken with the object of getting at the fountain of the adulteration of milk. On the morning of Sunday, the 13th Augest, Mr. Dickson, inspector, went to the shop of Mr. Dean, Major Cross-street, , where milk was sold. He waited outside until there arrived , the cart of the defendant, in charge of a boy named William Beasley. In the cart were two large cans of milk, which were carried into Mr. Deans' shop. Mr. Dickson obtained sample from each can. One can was from the farm of Jas. Knowles, and the milk it contained was found to be a fair sample; but the milk from the defendant's can Mr. Dick- son, by the lactometer, discovered was not of the required standard. He consequently took the measures, a pint and a half, required by Act of Parliament, and gave the lad a sample, telling him the other would be sent to the analyst, Mr. Campbell Brown, to be analysed. The analyst certified that the milk contained 19 per cent. of fat, 73 per cent, of other solids, and 22 parts of water had been added to every 100 parts of milk. Nearly a quarter of the milk was water. He (Mr. Husband) might mention that it was Sunday when the sample was taken. ft appeared that though thedefendant supplied milk to Mr. Dean each day, he sup- plied an extra quantity on Sunday. :Whether this increased supply was wanted because of the working men's libations of Saturday night, he did not know. (Mr. Hall : They are all at home on Sunday). It might be that the de- fendant required to make up the extra quantity of milk by adding an extra quantity of water instead. He did not knew that this was so, but at any rate the milk, which bad to go to the working classes, contained 22 per cent. of water. —Mr. Dickson then gave evidence, and remarked that he had on two previous occasions taken samples of the de- fendant's milk which were deficient in quality.—The prisone said the servant girl put up the mill: on the morning in question, and after Mr. Dickson had taken the samples, he inquired what she had done to the milk. She said she had added the ricsings out of the cans.—Mr. hall: You see Mr. Dickson has complained before of the state in which you sold milk.—The prisoner said be had sold milk in Widnes for five years, and he had never bad a complaint before.— Mr. Hall said the Bench looked upon the case as a very bad one. The Bench had never got hold of the right person I before, the person who was really responsible, and a fine of £lO and costs £1 2s. 61. would be inflicted, or, in default, two months. The advocate's fee of half a guinea was allowed.—The fine was paid.

WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL.—TWO sermons in aid of the schools were preached in this chapel, on Sunday, by Mr. Rothwell, of Liverpool. There were good congregations. THE RESTORATION OF FARNWORTH CHURCH TOWER.—SO successful has been the appeal for subscriptions in order to restore Farnworth Church tower, and repair the peal of bells, that the work has now been commenced. To Mr. Taylor, of Leftborough, has been entrusted the work of tuning the bells, and replacing the cracked tenor bell with a new one.

GOOD TEMPLAEY AT WIDNES. - At the ordinary weekly meeting of the Star of Widnes Lodge, 1.0.G.T., Brother Bold gave an interesting lecture entitled "Old Shoes." It had reference to the Temperance question. Brother Rescorl occupied the chair. RUNCORN NATIONAL DAY Soitoor.s.—The managers of these schools have just received Her Majesty's Inspec- tor's report upon the examinations held in July; and it is a very satisfactory one. The grant amounts to .£526 165., being an average of 16s. Elid. cry scholar in average attendance. The number of rs at present on the tolls is 773.

SEMIS Cnoss PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—The Bev. W. Thornley preached two sermons in this chapel, on Sunday last, and collections were made on behalf of the trust fund. On Monday evening a tea party, which was well attended, was held in the school-room. Afterwards a public meeting was held, and addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Morton, of Warrington, and others.

PIC-NIC FROM WIDNES.—The members of the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple (1.0.G.T.) had their annual pic-nic on Saturday, when they proceeded by train to Hough Green. The juveniles, who were in charge of Bros. H. Hufton, Tar- ton, Birkhall, and Rescoil, numbered 110, and were accom- panied by about 80 adults. The Star of Temperance brass bind was in attendance during the afternoon, and the weather being beautifully fine, a very enjoyable time was spent in various amusements. Mr. Longton, of Ditcbfield Hall, kindly placed a field at the disposal of the brethren. A good tea was provided.

ALLEGED HOUSE ROBBERY AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, at Whines Police Court, before Mr. G. Pilkington, Henry Bar- clay, a labourer, living in Wellington-street, was brought up in custody charged with stealing a cupboard door, of the value of 2afid, from an unoccupied house in Wellington- street, belonging to Joseph Sherlock, of St. Helens.—P.C. Brown stated that he was on duty in Wellington-street about five o'clock that morning when he heard a noise, which caused him to go to the back of the houses there, when he saw the prisoner pullingoff the cupboard door.—Mr. Manley, the agent for the property, said he visited the premises on Thursday, and the door was then safe. This morning it had gone.—The prisoner was remanded.

FAENWORTII AGEICULTURIL Sizow.---On Thursday next, the annual Farnworth agricultural show will be held, and if favoured with fine weather will no doubt be as great a success as in former years. The entries in all classes are very very numerous, and the dogs are expected to be a spt.cial feature in the show ; while the leaping of hunters and driving of horses, which is to take place at two o'clock, will be very attractive. At one o'clock there will be a public luncheon, at which Colonel Blackburne, M.P., will preside. Daring the day the band of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers will perform a selection of popular music, under the leadership of Mr. John Ravenscroft. It may be well to mention that this year the show will only be held on one day. Last year it was open on two days, but the committee taking into consideration various circumstances, have concluded that a one day's show will best meet the wishes of the pubic. ASSAULTING A WITNESS AT WLDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and J. Brock, Patrick Walsh, Mary Ann Walsh, and Rose McCabe were brought up in custody to answer a charge of assaulting James Ploughman, at Widnes, on Wednesday, the 7th inst.—The complainant stated that on that day he was a witness in a case at the Petty Sessions in which Walsh and McCabe were concerned. On leaving the court, and whilst on his way home, he was met by the prisoner Patrick Walsh,and a number a women, among whom were the prisoners. They attacked him in a savage manner, kicking him on the ribs. McCabe sent a brick at him, and Mary Ann Walsh struck him. He had not given them any pre- vocation.—P.C. Strickland deposed to apprehending the prisoner on the previous night. In reply to the charge Patrick said, " We had a row," and Mary Ann made a similar statement. McCabe stated she was not present.— Three witnesses were called, who each stated the women were present among the crowd, but took no part in the row. They all aweed that Patrick kicked the complainant. —The Bench dismissed the case against the worm n, and sent the man to gaol for 21 days.

FOWL STZALING AT STOOKIIIM. Od. Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. S. B. Chadwick, a young man named Peter Rogers was brought up in custody to answer a charge of having, on the 3rd September, at the township of Stockham, feloniously stolen two hens, of the value of 55., the property of Joseph W. Baguley, farmer.—Joseph Hughes, a labourer on the farm, stated that on the day named, about half-past four, he was in the shippon, when, in consequence of something he heard thrown against the shippon door, he went outside. On doing so he saw the prisoner coming out of another shippon. He (witness) noticed that the prisoner had something bulky under his coat. The prisoner then leaned over the rails next to the road, and asked witness where the man was who had been with him. Witness replied that he did not know, and returned to the shippon, when on returning he saw the pri- soner standing near a dead fowl, which was on the ground under the hedge.—Mr. Bagnley said on hearing of this he went to the prisoner and charged him with killing the fowl which he denied, and walked away. Another hen, which had its leg broken, and appeared to be injured internally, wag also found. The prisoner had on several occasions worked, for him. The prisoner had had some drink, but knew what he was doing.—P.S. Lowndes, of Halton, stated he received the prisoner into custody at Walton Gaol. He charged him with committing the robbery. Prisoner replied, "I don't remember it. I think I must have been drunk ; " and asked the officer to inquire from Mr. Baguley if he would take pay for the fowl.—Prisoner now pleaded guilty, and was com- mitted to gaol for a month. Feuer 13 AN QUET AT Rusconw.—ln connection with Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association, a fruit banquet was held in Bethesda School-room on Monday evening, and was in every sense a thorough success, which must be very gratifying to the promoters. Dr. Steele, the president of the Association, occupied the chair:and amongst the large number of members and friends present, were noticed the following, vice-presidents and ministers :—Mr Robert Shaw (ex-president), Rev. Wm. Preston, M.A , Rev. G. Hack, Rev. John Billington, Rev. J. D. Thomas, Rev. J. Pickwell, Messrs. Thomas Norman, J. H. Humphries, S. C. Beckett. C. G rnett, 'l'. Handley, Sr:. The decoration and arraugement of the room had been admirably carried out. Running down the middle of the room, from end to end, were a number of tables, and on a alight elevation in the centre were grouped a collection of choice plants, whose bright green foliage greatly enhanced the appearance of the room. For a centre piece there was a splendid specimen of the dracena tremanilis, flanked by two specimens of the pandanas variegatus, while the fruit, which con- sisted of grapes, nectarines, and almost every other kind in season, was displayed on dishes placed along the table. A number of palms, and one or two capsicums bearing fruit graced a cross table which had been erected. The plan,s were lent by Mrs. C. Hezle- burst and Mr. P. Speakman. The committee were also indebted for liberal donations of fruit to Messrs. C. Wigg, G. 0. Jackson, George S. Hazlehurst, John Simpson, T. Hazlehurst (Beaconsfield, Runcorn), and Mrs. Davies (of the Mount, Halton.) To add to the pleasure of the evening's entertainment, a musicale programme had been provided. The first item was the song and chorus," Come where my love lies dreaming." by Messrs. C. and J. Pownall and R. Morris, Miss Horton singing the solo part in a very pleasing manner. Mr. John Birkett sang in good style the song "Sailing" (Godfrey Marks), and in response to a hearty encore he gave "Every ballet has its billet." Molloy's charming song " Kerry dance," was sung by Miss Wright with much effectiveness of expression, ant she received an encore, which she acknowledged by singing in a no less Praiseworthy manner "The three old maids of Lea." , Miss Horton, who possesses a soprano voice of purity and tone, which she uses to advantage, sang very ably "The summer song" (H. Ponlet), and she was loudly applauded. With oil his old force, Mr. R. Morris gave the song, "The boys of the old brigade," and in response to an enthusiastic encore, he sang" The tar's farewell." Next followed the trio "Come, sail in our light canoe," sung by Messrs. 0. and J. Pownall and R. Morris in a clever manner. Miss Harrison is deserving of all praise for her clever performance of the pianoforte solo "Air Hongrois," for which she was encored. She responded by repeating a portion of the piece. "The lullaby" (Mr. J. K. Emmett) was sung bye Mr. J. Pownall with admirable correctness of expression, which may be also said of Mr. C. Pownall's rendering of the I'Vellings' song, "Some day." Miss Aslin, who made her first appearance before a Auncorn audience, excellently sang " Daybreak " (by Balfe). She has a contralto voice of sweet expression. and sings with true feeling. The quertette " Ye banks and braes "be Messrs. C. and J. Pownall, R. Morris, and A. W. King, concluded the programme,but Miss Wright graciously complied with a double encore which she had received early in the evening, by singing "Barney O'Hea," with a vivacity which carried the audience with her, and she was warmly applauded. The entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem. THE VoLuErEEHB.—In considerrtion of the excellent results of the recent examination in tactics, the Government has decided to grant a special allowance of 10s. for each officer of volunteers who is in possession of a certificate showing that he has passed his examination for every year in which he earns the ordinary capitation allowance of 30s.

PEARSON IND KNOWLES COAL IND IRON COMPANY, LIMITED.—The directors of this company state in their report that the net profits for the year ending 30th June last, amount to £52,560 Bs. 6d., aid the balance brought forward from last account was £4,383 13s. Bd., together £56,944 2s. 2d. An interim dividend, amounting to X 15,715 103. was paid in March last, and the directors now propose that the usual dividend at the rate of 6 per cent, per annum be declared on the "A" shares, and a dividend at the rats of 4 per cent. per annum on the B shares, both free of income tax. This will leave a sum of £22,451 12s. 2d., out of which the directors recommend that £17,000 be carried to the reserve fund, and the balance, £5,451 12s. 2L1., to the next account.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE TELEPHONE COMPANY.— Mr. Charles Moseley, the deputy-chairman of this company, presided over the annual meeting of shareholders held at the offices of the company in Faulkner-street, Manchester. There was a large attendarce of shareholders. The report stated that the profit realised on the business of the company during the past year was £14,733, including the sale of stores, and out of this it was proposed to pay a dividend of 5 per cent., and, after allowing. £l,OOO for directors' fees, to carry forward the balance of over £1,700 to next year.— The report was adopted, and the retiring directors and audi- tor re-elected.

ASSAULT BY A LODGER. —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Ana Dowd was summoned for assaulting Elizabeth Sproston at Earlestown, on the Ist inst. —The complainant stated that the defendant lodged with her, and had been in the habit of taking drink. Some time ago the defendant's brother-in-law came to Earlestown, and because she (the complainant) would not allow hira to stay in the house all night the defendant had frequently used abusive language. On the previous Saturday she threatened tc bite her nose off but was prevented from doing so. She, however, bit her on the hand and scratched her face.—After several witnesses had been called on both sides, P. C. Lloyd stated that the complainant came to him after the assault. She was then bleeding from the hand and face. He and ' another constable went and found Mrs. Thwd very dis- orderly with a crowd of people round her.—She was fined ss. and costs.

LEwts's "I'min-1r READINGS."—This is the title of a little volume consisting of 123 pages which has just been Issued by that enterprising firm, Messrs. Lewis and Co., of Market-street, Manchester. It far eclipses anything which has been published in the same line before, and the price Wing only one penny, the volume is a marvel of cheapness. The selections are from the very beet poets and prose writers, from the best speeches, and from original literary composition. There is, indeed, scarcely any author of note who is not represented in the volume, which we should imagine must -very soon attain an enormous circulation. Accompanying the " readings" is a chronological list of in- ventions, discoveries, Jrc., from 17C3 to 1862, and this of it- self is well worth the money, and will be found very useful. It is manifest that the publishers nnot have any profit on the publication ; their object, which we hope will be at- tained, is thus stated in the preface : "We are actuated by a desire to put into circulation a sound, amusing, and in- structive kind of reddino, which shall be within the reach of every section of the com:nunity." " Lewis's l'enny Readings " certainly are within the reach of all, and we advise all to secure a copy.

SI:ZGITLIR ACCIDENT TO THE CARRIAGE OF THE HIGH SnERIFF.—Early this week whilst a carriage and pair be- longing to Lieutenant-Colonel M.Corquodele, of Craig-y - don, High Sheriff of Lancashire, was being driven towards Bangor Railway Station, the driver being accompanied oa the box by the engineer of Mr. M'Corquolale'e yacht, one of the horses took fright, and, in suctieuly turning, broke a portion of the shaft. The two men were thrown bodily upon the ground, and when assistance could be rendered it as found that the engineer had been severely injured, so much so that his removal to the infirmary was deemed advisable. In the meantime, the horses dashed into Upper Bangor and along the Menai Bridge road, followed by some hundreds of persons, but before the Suspension Bridge was reached one of the animals rushed madly against the wall, and coming in contact with a portion of the broken shaft it fell down and bled to death. The driver of the carriage, who was only slightly bruised, followed the frightened animals in a car. The other horse was shot a day afterwards. It is rather sur- prising that the carriage' which was a valuable one, received bvt slight damage. The engineer, who received injuries through the accident, has since his removal to the infirmary returned home, and is gradually recovering. Lour, .Batexamers, &c.—(From Friday evening's Ga:ette.)' ALLEGED Burtrat SCJIMAL.—An occurrence of a most unusual and extraordinary character took place in connec- tion with the faneral of a child, whose remains were in- terred in a burial ground within one hundred miles of Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. So far as we have been able to ascertain the facts it would appear that a certain rev, gentleman had seized the opportunity to take a course which cannot be looked upon as a wise or judicious one, and one which by Christian people at least cannot be regarded as denoting a very liberal spirit towards those who differ from him in matters of religion. The other week we recorded the fact of a brother clergyman to the one alluded to inviting the co-operation and assistance of a Wesleyan minister at the interment of one who did not belong to the Episcopal Church, and the service on that occasion was conducted with all due reverence and solemnity both inside and outside the precincts of the church. But on Tuesday last an opposite course was taken, the rev, gentleman referred to standing upon the rules of the church and actually refusing to allow any portion of the burial service to be conducted inside the building because the deceased had not been "baptised." The deceased child was only about three weeks old, and the interment was arranged to take place during the afternoon, but from no fault of the parents the mourning coach arrived at the ground aleout half an hour late. The clergyman and sexton were then waiting, and the former, it is ' said, asked the reason of the delay. An explana- tion was given, and as a result the rev. gentleman reprimanded the driver of the conveyance. It is said that the clergyman then asked if the child had " been admitted into the church ?' The parents replied that it had not, whereupon the clergymen then said "Then we proceed at once to the grave, because, according to the laws of the church, we cannot read the burial service in the church." We are informed it was explained that the child, before its death, had been " baptised " by a neighbouring congregational minister. The child had been so ill that the parents feared to remove it outside the house, and the con- gregational minister was sent for, and he duly performed the ceremony inside the dwelling. Toe clergyman, however, was firm, and in the end the mourners, sexton, and clergy- men proceeded to the grave side, and there the customary i service was gone through, after which the body was de- posited in its last resting place.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
[HE WAR IN EGYPT.

WHAT HAS BECOME OF ARABI ? Yesterday, the Daily News, in a stop-press edition, publishes a telegram from Tel-el-Kebir saying that an Egyptian regimental doctor, who is a prisoner there, states that Arabi, while making off in a railway carriage to Zagazig from Tel-el-Kebir, on Wednesday morning, was shot at by one of his own officers. Another officer who was , present asserted that Arabi was wounded. A Reuter's telegram from Alexandria, despatched at 10-20 yesterday morning, says :—Arabi Pasha and Toulba Pasha have been arrested by the Prefect of Police at Cairo, it is re- ported for having attempted to incite the population to in-i cendiarism and plunder. Al! Roubi Pasha has been handed over by the Egyptian authorities to Sir Evelyn Wood, in I order to share the fate of the other prisoners of war. A second edition of the Daily ( hronicle contains a tele- gram, dated Zagazig, Friday, 6-25 a.m., which says:— Arabi was seen to ride through Belbeis, attended only by twenty horsemen. The fugitive rebel leader as he dashed past waved a sword red with blood, appealing to the natives with the cry, "Egypt is ruined ! " They, however, paid no heed to him, and his cause is everywhere considered hopeless. SURRENDER OF 'ARABI—OFFICIAL DESPATCH.

An official despatch received in London yesterday morn- ing from Sir Garnet Wolseley states that Arabi and Toulba Pashas and 10000 Egyptian troops surrendered to the British on Thursday at Cairo. The following is the substance of the despatch :—" From Sir Garnet Wolseley to the Secre- tary for War.—Benha, 15th S.ptember.—Just arrived. General Lowe occupied Cairo yesterday afternoon. Arabi and Tonlba Pasha surrendered unconditionally. The troops there (about 10,000 men) laid down thar arms. The Prefect of Polic has undertaken to maintain order. Igoon to Cairo at once."

The Daily News, in a stop press edition published the following telegram :—Tel-el-Kebir, September 14. The official return gives our loss yesterday in the storming of Kehir at 9othcers and 46 men killed, and 22 officers and 220 men wounded. The Royal Marines had two officers killed; the Royal Engineers seven men killed, and one officer and 46 man wounded; the Royal 'Highlanders, two officers and seven men killed, fire officers and 35 men wounded; the Gordon Highlanders, one officer and four men killed, one officer and 39 men wounded; the Cameron Highlanders, three officers and eleven men killed, five officers and 72 men wounded. News has reached here that the Egyptian com- mander at Kafr Dowar agrees to surrender on :condition that the English troops do not move. The following additional telegram, "Tel-el-Kebir, Septem- ber 14, evening," is published by the same paper train leaves here immediately for Zagazig, with Sir Garnet Wolseley and staff. It was delayed here five hours in con- sequence of a stoppage on the up. line. An Egyptian regi- mental doctor, who is a prisoner here, tells me that Arabi,l whilst making off in a railway carriage to Zagazig, from Kebir, yesterday morning, was shot at by one of his own officers. Another officer who was present asserted that Arabi was wounded. There are 1,100 prisoners here, the vast majarity being strong able-bodied men, and all apparently not sorry to find themselves in comfortable quarters. Many Egyptian stragglers are arriving from the country between this and Zagazig, where our walkover seems to have given a deathblow to any opposition at Cairo. Among the prisoners here is Mahomed Bey, who lea the fighting at Mahsameh. The complete collapse 01 Arabi's part is owing to the admiral forethought with which yester- day morning's _plans for the surprise of Kebir were con- trived. Twenty minutes later the Egyptians would have been prepared, and the task of storming Kebir might have been far more formidable, thus encouraging the opinion that Arabi was supported elsewhere. The advance of the differ- ent corps, however, was ac well timed that the front lines reached the entrencliments before day light, the enemy not being aware of their approach. Praise of Sir Garnet Wolse- ley's generalship is universal. The account given by the prisoners as to the number of Arabi's army at Kebir vary. It was probably about 25,000. The most trutworthy report is that about 700 of their men were killed. Sir Garnet Wolseley and his staff leave here presently for Cairo. The Scots Guards are nearly ready to start for the same destination. HOW ARABI WAS CAPTURED.

The Daily Telegraph, in a third edition yesterday, pub- lishes the following from its correspondent :—" The report that Arabi was captured is fully confirmed. A Epecial des- patch which I have just received states that some of our Royal Cavalry surrounded the house to which he had gone, and succeeded in taking bins prisoner. With regard to the surrender of the entrenchments at Raft Dowar, I have not heard that any conditions were made. No special corres- pondent has yet been allowed to visit the enemy's camp. I was therefore fortunate that I rode over there yesterday when General Wood met the rebel chiefs. THE BALLOON EQUIPMENT._
Orders were received at Chatham and Woolwich on Thumlay night from the War Office stopping progress with the balloon equipment. FURTHER REINFORCEMENTS STOPPED.
Tekgranis from the War Office were received at Chatham' yesterday morning countermanding all previous orders for the despatch of reinforcements and stores to Egypt.
A SMMD OF HONOUR FOR GENERAL WO LSE C.EY.

A proposal was mide yesterday to form a committee in Dublin to collect funds to purchase a sword of honour for presentation to Sir Garnet Wolseley on his return from Egypt. It was at first suggested that the subscribers should be confined to the residents of Monkstown, where Sir Garnet Wolseley passed his youth and was educated. hut it is now proposed to make the subscription a general one.

div.head: VICTORIA. CROSS.
div.p: THE VICTORIA. CROSS.

List night's Ga:ctte says the Queen has been pleased to signify her intention to confer the decoration of the Victoria Cross upon Mr. Israel Harding, gunner of H.M.S. Alexandra. The following account is given of the act of bravery for wtrich he was recommended :—"At about nine o'clock on the morning of the 11th July, whilst Her Majesty's ship Alexandra was engaginc, the forts at Alexan- dria, a ten-inch spherical shell passed' through the ship's side and lodged on the main deck. Mr. Harding hearing the shout, There is a live shell just above the hatchway,' rushed up the ladder from below, and observing that the fuse was burning, took some water from a tub standing near, and threw it over the projectile, then picked up the shell and put it into the tub. Had the shell burst, it would probably have destroyed many lives.

WAR ITEMS. We (Central News) understand the Duke of Connaught is desirous of remaining in Egypt until the withdrawal of the Post Guards, when he will Accompany his brigade to England. We (Central News) hear it is the intention of the Admiralty shortly to provide for Lord Charles Beresford, whose recent services are considered to give special claim to employment. The Paris Temps of yesterday gives full credit to England for the victory of Wednesday, and considers the war now at an end; but says that the national question in Egypt is not yet solved, and that Europe is waiting to learn the opinions of England on the subject. The Secretary of State for War has despatched a most flattering telegram to Sir Garnet Wolseley, in which he refers in terms of admiration of Sir Garnet's service, and of the admirable behaviour of the officers and men of the forces under his command.

THE MASSACRE OF AN IRISH FAMILY. It is now believed that the horrible mutilation of the murdered Joyce family in Connemara was the work of pigs, and that the dogs acted as the protectors of the dead bodies instead of as their mutilators. Tne Lord Lieutenant of Ireland on Thursday night visited the hovel in Maamtrasna where the Joyce family were recently massacred. The Viceroy had a strong escort of Fusiliers, and mounted police and constabulary were also stationed at intervals along the route between Lienane and Maamtrasna. SUDDEN DEATH IN THE STREET. Yesterday afternoon a very sudden death occurred at Saddleworth. A man named 'Joseph Lawton, aged 56, avms standing in Waters-lane talking to some companions, when on turning to leave them he fell heavily to the groutd. His companions at once ran to his assistance, and found blood issuing from his mouth. He died before medical assistance could be obtained. THE COTTON TRADE. The end of the campaign in Egypt has caused much satisfaction. in Bolton, as threatened cotton famine is now considered to be averted. As the railways in a great portion of the cotton growing districts are now in our possession the safety of the bulk of the cotton crop is assured, though there is a falling off in the Egyptian crop as compared with ' last year. The deficiency will doubtless be remedied by the use of the better grades of America. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A WOMAN. On Thursday moraing, at the Darwin Police Court, Alice ' Briggs, a married woman with four children, was charged with attempting to drown herself that morning at a lodge in Cotton Hall. A police officer saw her throw herself in the water, and he plunged in and brought her to the surface. She was quite exhausted. The evidence proved her to be mentally deranged, she having been twice in a lunatic asylum, and she was accordingly sent to the Blackburn 'Workhouse.

div.head: NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE MINERS.
div.p: THE NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE MINERS.

The representatives of the North Staffordshire Miners' Association have resolved to give notice of a 10 per cent. advance in wages, and thus act in unison with the colliers of Lancashire, Yorkshire, and North Wales. A ballot has been taken on the subject, and out of 5,375 men on!y five voted against the notice being given.

div.head: WRECK OF H.M.S. PHCENIX.
div.p: WRECK OF H.M.S. PHCENIX.

We learn that confirmation has been received at the Admiralty of the report from Prince Edward's Island that H.M.S. i'hcenix is ashore and full of water at a somewhat dangerous point. The crew have been saved, and a ship of war from Halifax has gone to the assistance of the Phcenix. FATAL ACCIDENT T.) A CARTER. Late on Thursday night a shocking accident occurred at Saddleworth. Two carters, employed at the Dobcross Iron Works, were proceeding from Standedge just before 12 o'clock in charge of a heavy lurrv, draws by two horses. One of the men was leading the first horse when the tarry j gave a jerk, and on going to ascertain the c'ause he found his companion, William Wortley, aged 50, lying in the road dead. Be bad fallen from the shaft, and the hurry had passed over his body.

MURDER AT THE ALEXANDRA DOCK, LIVERPOOL A CALIFORNIAN SAILOR KILLED BY A JAPANESE. Yesterday morning, the body of John Broden, a Cali- fornian seaman, was deposited in the mortuary at the Bootle Hospital, he having died from the effects of a blow inflicted upon him on Thursday night by a seaman—a Japanese. The deceased and his assailant were seamen on board the sailing ship J. B. Thomas, which docked on Thursday night. Whilst the vessel was being got into position they quarrelled, and the Japanese struck the deceased on the head with the c tpstan bar, inflicting injuries which resulted in death. The Japanese has disappeared. THE YORKSHIRE COAL TRAFFIC TO LONDON.

div.head: IMPORTANT PROPOSAL.
div.p: IMPORTANT PROPOSAL.

An important circular was on Thursday issued to the leading coalowners in York.hire,!requesting their attendance at a lepresentative meeting at Sheffield on Tuesday next, for the purpose of receiving th. 3 reports of the interviews between a deputation of coalowners and the directors of the Great Eastern Railway Company and the manager of the Midland Company relating to the tonnage rates for coal from Yorkshire to London. It is understood that owing to the Great Northern refusing any concessions new routes will be proposed. _

div.head: WELSH COLLIERS.
div.p: THE WELSH COLLIERS.

On Thursday evening a mass meeting of the Welsh col. Hers was held in the Ruabon district, when it was unani- mously resolved, in accordance with a resolution passed by the miners in the Wrexham district on the previous even- ing, to give notice for an increase in wages of 15 per cent., and, in the event of coalowners refusing, to stand out. It is believed this demand for increase of wages will extend throughout North Wales. ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A BUILDING SOCIETY TRUSTEE.

Thomas Yeats, of the firm of Yeats and Looney, account- ants, was charged before the Liverpool stipendiary yester- day with embezzling £lOOO, the moneys of a building society of which he was trustee. The prisoner absconded at the beginning of the year, and was only arrested last week. Evidence was given of the payment of certain sums to the prisoner for which he had not accounted, and he was com- mitted for trial, two sureties of £5OO each being accepted. OPENING OF THE WEST LANCASHIRE RAILWAY. The new railway betyreen Preston and Southport was opened yesterday by a trip over the line and a luncheon. The first section of thc line, from Southport to Hesketh Bank, was opened in February, 1878. The railway opens out a district, purely agricultural, but fairly populated, but it brings into very close communication Preston and South- port. There are running powers over a portion of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. Though considerable difficulties have presented themselves in the construction of the railway, the work is now almost finisbed. It is stated that in a very short time the terminus at Preston will be ready for full occupation.

div.head: Tatter to the 4tito.
div.p: Tatter to the 4tito.
ENGLAND AND EGYPT.

Sir,—ln political as in domestic meters it requires a fire to keep the pot boiling. Public businees would become stale and disieteresting if it dia not, chameleon like, change color in the shifting light. Of course, in an empire ot the matured character of Great Britain, politics are never at a standstill, as they rarely lack the charm of variety. So many interests are alive, some new, some old ones, and so many daily being barn and added to the historic list, that it would be a miracle if each day did not produce some topic Of exciting account. Apart from our coinmercial activity and the great home questions which cluster round it, we have foreign posseseious that demand us they involve constant attention. And so long ae our empire remains intact, we cannot possibly have an idle Government; we may have something worse—a foolish one; but our affairs are too I, complicated and absorbing to permit of such a thing as idle- ness at head quarters. In the medley of interests which inflict upon Parliament so much work, the Egyptian item is now the most conspicuous. Irish grievances, if not less outspoken, are less noticed than prior to our quarrel with that " simple fellah," Arabi Pasha. Tnis is not right, if it be granted that Irish tenants have more real interests at stake than our Egyptian bondholders. And Pat might dis- play a strong negative to the aovernment's idea of the matter, if he could be persuaded to do so in words. Unfor- tunately for him and his country, he favors the habit of his superiors' and expresses his objections in knocks and blows. This has brought the "servants of the law" upon him in crashing force. What more can he do than mutter, and give vent to nasty oaths, while his aggrieved friends, who are not so muck in the mud as he is in the mire, have the satisfaction of seeing the military pound poor Arabi Pasha for imperilling their interests in the Suez Canal or some other Anglo-Egyptian stocks or shares? Leaving Pat to his suppressed interacts, and taking a front-window view of this miserable Egyptian business, we are put aghast by the gaunt pretext which has led us into Egypt. If ever we needed the protestations of virtue to jus,ify an illegal and an un- just act, it is now. Oar presence in Egypt, in the capacity which Sir Garnet Wolseley's employment suggests, is not enly an intrusion upon Egypt, since we are not at war with her, but an offence which we should have deemed unpardonable in any nation's history, save our own. What are we doing there, any way? Defending the canal? Bah! It was never endangered until Admiral Seymour and his fleet anchored off Alexandria, with our silly ultimatum. From various sources we glean this much of Arabi's character, that he is too much of a patriot to willingly and wilfully damage a construction such as the canal, which we may safely affirm has been "the making" of Egypt. We have M. de Lessep's word for this. Besides, France would not have been in the hurry she was to withdraw from what she had the prudence to see was a false and dangerous coarse if the canal had really been jeopardised by Arabi apart from hostilities being commenced against him. To protect the canal, therefore, was not a sound reason for our action; indeed, if advanced as such, it must be treated as a ruse. It is urged by same— I do not know whether they represent responsible " official " opinion or not—that it was requisite to support the Khe- dive's authority in Egypt. What have we to do with the Khedive? Is he our vassal or servant? No. Is he capable of governing Egypt to the satisfaction of the Egyptians? No. Why should we interfere, then? Surely the Egyp- tians have the same natural right that we have to develop a good home government. Reverse the situation: What should we say of the Egyp- tians ,if they invaded our territory with no better argument than that we had no right to alter our pre- sent form of government? I imagine we should send them back "with aflea in their lugs"! Why, eertainly! "But," exclaim the same authorities, "the Khedive is the Suzerain of Turkey. and therefore our step holds good." Well, if the Khedive sits on the skirts of that piece of rottenness, the ' Ottoman Empire, I fail to see why we should keep him there. That is the Sultan's "job." I can understand the Sultan's eagerness to retain such a "profitable servant" at his feet, but I can't understand why English ratepayers should bear the cost. If by any process of reasoning it can be shown that our connection with Turkey justifies it, my retort is, the quicker that connection is cut the better. Turkey, of course, is too impoverished to stand the strain of a local war. An unlimited number of scamps, alias Sultans and Sultanesses have played at profligacy and squander with Turkish finances, and emptied the Ottoman treasury. Turkey is bankrupt. Britain is rich, however, and some of her wealth being sunk—never to rise again— in Turkish and Egyptian bonds.and similar worthless scrip, we are committed to the folly of throwing good money after bad. To keep floating a futile hope of remote recuperation, . we not only recognise the Sultan as an Eastern despot, but actually undertake to fight his battles for him. It this -could be done with an assurance of imposing a tax on Turkey to meet the expenses we ' should have less to grumble about although there are hundreds of English homes and there may be thousands ere long—that will be cursing the evil '2?‘ hour which beheld our army enter Egypt. But our generosity is startling. We do not expect Turkey to bear the cost of this war ;'the British taxpayer has that pleasure allotted to him. Label it, "On behalf of British bond- holders," and ask our taxpayers what they have got to do with it. And this is the act of a Liberal Government! Our Egyptian campaign may, for aught I know or care, be popu- lar. I doubt it. I give my countrymen credit for having sufficient common sense to understand that war is a costly way of settling difficulties. lia the present case the cost is - even a secondary consideration, for we are doing what, sooner or later, must confront us as a heinous crime. We have no just reason for being in Egypt at this moment. For years we have tampered with Egyptian affairs. Between ourselves and France, we have monopolised every available office, made Alexandria the home of indecency and shame, taxed the Egyptians heavily, and manipulated the country so thoroughly well, that it is far frdrn being Egypt for the Egyptians. We carried our diplomacy too far. Arabi rose with the freshness and vigour of a young and determined patriot, and combatted our intentions with Garibaldian courage. Because he did this, because he dared to defend his people against our encroachments, we dub him rebel, reduce Alexandria to a heap of ruins, dis- grace ourselves at Ismailia by our barbarous conduct, con- sociate with Tewfik, a man of fiendish character; and pro- oeed with an arbitrary policy of repression and violence that subjects us to the scorn of Europe. To make the climax more satirical, do these things in the name of Christianity. We, who posed before Europe as the friends of the oppressed Christians of western Turkey ; we, who :send out paid missionaries to reform and civilise the natives ,of heathen lands; who boast of onr home piety and advance- ment; we so far forget ourselves as to tarnish our honour by crushing a people whose principal offence is objecting -to being preyed upon any longer by either English lions, French frogs, or European locusts in general. Is it a marvel that France, whose jealousy of our presence in Egypt would. rather strengthen than weaken her desire for an intervention of some kind, withdrew from us the minute she saw us initiating such an un-English policy ? That Turkey grew angry, and has been almost forced into abetting our ra: upon Egypt? That nearly all Europe deprecates our rasbnoss in creating a pi•Judent which Russia, or Germany, any rirst-rate power might use witla fatal consequences le speciously ordainat occasian ? It is but just to sctors that Mr. Gladstone should give an ex- :a step so liable to annihilate the confidence nby the country at large. We are painfully a grave misdirection of administrative eerns so unlike Mr. Gladstone to be engaged. jar, that it heeds all the facts of the case to be .ed before one can believe it. When Mr. Blight ante time ago, on the eve of this war, there wa'S a rumour that the Government had concluded to K upon an unwise and perilous mission. As a matter .act, Mr. Bright's religious prejudices to a great exten, aimiaished the fear which his reeignation created in public mind towards the Government's foreign policy. retracing our steps, we are inclined to think there something more than religioue bias moulding John Bright decision at the time in question, that he saw the country's good name and fame exposed to the calamity which has overtaken us, the severity of h:ch will be realised more distinctly when the fever-heat of passion and prejudice has w passed away, and left the na:ion calm enough to form an adeqaate opinion of the Government's treatment of Egypt. It is highly important we should view the position dis- passionately. The wrong done is by a Liberal Govern- ment. If this proves anything, it is that the people have chosez irreliehle men to represent them in Parliam,ent. No -member who endorses a policy entailing dishonour and •tacreased taxation is a friend to his constituency. In each 01511 he should be re-called as a traitor to the promise given e by she Liberals; s a body at the last election to stand by the party mono ofs` Peace, retrenchment, and reform." /t is

div.head: EXAMIIatrgATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 16,1882.
div.p: THE EXAMIIatrgATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 16,1882.
DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

USING PROFANE LANGUAGE.— At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, Peter Hilton, of Ashton, was scm- moned for using profane language in the public street, at Ashton, on the 2nd inst.—P.S. Savage proved the case, and the defendant was ordered to pay the costs. NORTH ASHTON BRASS BAWD. —ln aid of the funds of the North Ashton Brass Band the members of the band gave what was termed a "field dance," on Saturday afternoon last, in a field at Whitledge, which had been kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Priestner, of Rose House Farm, New-road. There were not very many persons present, but those who assembled, thoroughly enjoyed themselves. The band arrived on the ground about four o'clock, and played for dancing, which was indulged in up to dusk. CATTLE SALE.—One of the well-known periodical cattle sales by auction, by Messrs. Melling and Son, took place in their yard behind the Gerard's Arms, on Wednesday after- noon, when there was a very good attendance. There were offered for sale 5 head of horned cattle, 30 sheep and 20 lambs, and all were disposed of at fair prices. The•cattle and sheep were about the average quality, and as a con- sequence the bidding was very brisk. MONTHLY MEETING OF ODDFELLOWS.—A monthly meet- ing of the members of the Triumphant Lodge (97) of the Inthpendent Order of Oddfellows, M.U., was held at the Gerarces Arms, on Saturday evening last. There was a fair attendance of the members, and Bro. John Latham, N.G.. presided. The only business of interest was the considera- tion of the Government Actuary's return as to the valuation of the lodge, whieh was fully discussed, and a delegate was ultimately appointed to attend the next district rneetlng. After the accounts and the minutes had been duly read and passed, the lodge closed in the customary manner.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ACCIDENT. AT MR. T. DAvms' SAW MILL —On Wednes- day George Warburton, a joiner, met with an accident while engaged near the circular saw, a piece of timber being sent with some force from the saw, breaking one of his ribs and severely injuring another. The patient is progressing satis- factorily under the treatment of Dr. Robinson. MR. J. J. STEWARD'S CATTLE SALE.—A very successful sate was held by Mr. J. J. Steward at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodshatn, when the entries were choice and numerous. The following prices were realised, viz. : Fat calves, £2 183 to £4 each; bulls, £lO to £23; cows, £l6 to £10; heifers, £l4 to £l7; lambs, 27s to 445; sheep, 30s to 703; pigs, £4 to £8 17s Gd ; store pigs, 17s to 493; Shropshire ram lambs, 50s to 755; Leicester ram lambs, 603 ; Shropshire shearlings, £4 to £4 123 64; Shropshire ewe lambs (stores), 445; Shropshire shearling e.Yes, 563 to 613. There was a good attendance of buyers.

FRODSHAM AND HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD: ELECrION or NEW MEMBERS.—On Monday a general meeting of the ratepayers within the district of the Frodsham and lielsbv Drainage Board was held at the Frodsham Town Hall, for the purpose of electing new members. The functions of the Board are to manage matters connected with the drainage of the marsh land below Frodsham. Mr. Challoner took the chair shortly after seven o'clock, when there were pre- sent :—Messrs. R. Bate, J. E. Bate, Thomas Davies, and Mr. C. E. Linaker (clerk).—The Chairman expressed his serrow that there was not a better attendance, although he thought it showed the members of the late Board had done their work satisfactorily.—The Clerk read a letter from the Mar- quis of Choltnondeley, a member of the Board, stating that his lordship did not think it necessary that his name should be kept on the list. He would still like his agent, Mr. Hig- nett, to remain on, however.—The election was then pro- ceeded with, and as the result the following were appointed: —Messrs. Win. Hayes, John Higson, Ralph Bate, T. Davies, Joseph Ellams, F. Thornley, E. A Wright, Jame Reynolds, James Andrews, W. Booth, John Challoner, W. E. Davies, James Percival, Thomas Hig,nett, and H. Linaker. The retiring members were the Marquis of Cholmondeley, Mr. A. C. Talbot, and Mr. Abraham White, whose places were filled by Messrs. T. Davies, Joseph Ellams, and H. Linaker. The first meeting of the new Board will be held to-day (Satur- day.)

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

TEACLIF,Rs' QUARTERLY MEETING.—The teachers con- nected with the Golborne congregational sunday school, held their quarterly tea meeting in the schoolroom on Monday week. The scholars in two senior classes were also present, the total who sat down to tea being about 40. Mr. George Unsworth afterwards occup;ed the chair. The teachers' attendances for the previous quarter were submitted by the secretary, after the consideration of which, a conversation on school matters ensued. The meeting was a very pleasant one. _ _

_ ALARMING STREET ACCIDENT. —An alarming accident, attended by serious consequences, ozcurred near St. Thomas s schools, Church-street, one day last week. A horse, attached to an empty cart, owned by Messrs. R. Evans and Company, colliery proprietors, was proceeding along the street when, from some cause, the anima took fright. The man in charge was riding in the cart, and, as the horse dashed along the street, be was in great danger. Instead of turning in the street across the railway bridge, the animal ran down the narrow road leading to the station. When near St. Thomas's school one of the wheel's came in contact with a lamp and knocked the latter to the ground, completely smashing the glass and ironwork. The driver was thrown out of the cart, and bis face was cut and bruistd, though he was not severely injured.
HAYDOCK.

CannoN TO BICYCLISTS.—AI the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, before R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Esq., John Winatanley and Charles Burgess were sum- monad for riding a bicycle on the footpath at Haydock, on the let inst. Both pleaded guilty. A police-constable stated that about half-past five, on the Ist inst., he saw the two defendants riding bicycles on the footpath in Newton- road, Haydock.—Each was fined 51. and costa, the chair- man remarking that the defendants had no right to ride on the footpath. A SAD MISTAKE : ADMINISTERING Oct OF TAR INSTEAD OF SOOTHING SYRUP.—A mistake of a sad and shocking character was made at Haydock on Thursday evening in last week, the occurrence resulting in serious consequences to a female child named Alice May Black, 15 months old, daughter of an engine driver residing at Sutton. It appeared that the parents of the child left home for a few days, and during their absence the child was in charge of some rela- tions residing in Clipsley Cottages, Haydock. The child was brought to Haydock last Saturday week, and a few days later commenced to suffer from a slight cold. On the following Thursday evening, about nine o'clock, the child's grandmother went to the ct;.pboard with the intention of getting a bottle containing some soothing syrup, and which was to be given to the child. The grandmother took up a bottle from the capb,)ard, poured' out a teaspoon- ful of the liquid it contained and . then gave it .to the child. Immediately afterwards it was found that a mistake had been made. Instead of taking up the soothing syrup battle, the grandmother had taken one up containing a quantity of oil of tar, and administered to the child a dose. Ihe hot liquid ran down the child's throat, and caused the utmost paid and suffer- in-/. As may be readily imagined, the poor child's motath and throat were burned in a shocking manner, the tongue, lips, kc., being .much swollen. A few drops of the liquid also got on the child's chin, 111 d as a consequence small blisters soon 'made their appearance. Medical assistance was at once sent for, and the as4/tant to Dr. Ricketts, of Black- brook, soon attended to the child. The little sufferer has b2en in intense pain, and remained in a seriodS. condition for some time. It is a pleasure to note that there are signs of an improvement, though it will be some days before the child thoroughly recovers.

div.head: LYMII.
div.p: LYMII.

LAWS TESNIS PARTY AT LYMM.—Any one going along Oughtrington-lane last Friday might have beheld a very pretty sight on the tennis ground of the Ladies' Club in Lymm. The occasion was a grand party, given under the auspices of the leading ladies in Lymm, who have formed themselves into a club for the purpose of furthering the practice of lawn tennis. This gathering was propoed to have been held some weeks ago, but unfortunately, owing to the illness of some of the members, the project had to be abandoned. On Friday, no such hindrances being in the way, the enjoyable event came to pass. Invitations were sent out, and these must have been heartily responded to when we have to state that upwards of 140 persons presented themselves at the ground. Very soon play was commenced, and the scene' which might at this time have been observel—what with the beautiful and bright dresses of the ladies, and the more sombre dress of the gentlemen—was Pleasing in the extreme. Perhaps it would be invidious to mention any particular costumes, although several deserved special notice. Happily ' the day was beautifully suitable for the event, as it was not felt to be too warm for play. Still, the sun was shining brightly, and of course this advantage tended to keep both hostesses and guests in a thoroughly good humour. The members were very . careful to see that the wants of the inner man were well looked after, the pavilion of the defunct cricket club, serving for the nonce as an admirable cafe, and the ar- , rangernents connected with this department, which were , deputed to a sub-committee, were carried , out in such a manner as to be highly congratulatory to all who took part in it. Of the grou id itself, it may be mentioned that it is situated perhaps in the most picturesque spot in Lytnm, and is certainly well adapted for such a concourse of people as that assembled on Friday, for we noticed eight sets simul- taneously at play, whilst for the convenience of the elder portion of the guests, tents were erected. These tents were kindly lent by Colonel Legh, W. Battersby, Esq., and T. P. Norris, tsq. Altogether the day passed off very pleasantly indeed, and the memhers have every reason to believe that the unanimous verdict of the visitors was that they had en- joyed themselves, .if not more, quite as much, as ever they did at a lawn tennis party. Perhaps it will not lse out of place to mention some of the prominent players. Amongst these were Miss Robinson, Miss Battersby, Miss S. Battersby, Miss Myer, Miss A. M'lver, Miss Norris, Miss Godfrey, T. P. Norris, Esq., Captain Ross, Colonel Godfrey, Dr. Fox, Mr. Antro- bus, and Mr. M'lver. We need hardly say tiaat the fences were crowded by those villagers who, although not in- vited inside, yet were determined to see the spectacle, and, if we may judge from the time some of them sat there, we may safely say that they were enjoying the game quite as much as the insiders

div.head: NANTWICII.
div.p: NANTWICII.

The Nantwich Board of Guardians on Saturday rejected a motion in favour of triennial elections. ITToLENr ASSAULT NEAR NANTWICII—At the Nantwich Police Court, on Saturday, a farm servant named Harriet Eat3n was charged with having inflicted grievous bodily harm on BelljaMill Sutton, a fellow 9ervant, by striking him on the head with a poker, The prisoner and Sutton

were in the employ of Mr. Broady, of Newhall. While they were at breakfast together, prisoner gave prosecutor a piece of dry bread to eat, and when he refused to take it they quarrelled, and she took up the peker and struck him down almost senseless. Prisoner, against whom there was a pre- vious conviction, was sentenced to two months' imprison- ment with hard labour.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON 'BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. ASSLULT.—Wm. Nicholson and Mary Ann Shaw were sum- moned by the male defendant's wife for assaulting her on Sep- tember 4th.—lt appeared that both complainant and her husband were more or less intoxicated when Mrs. Shaw came Into their house and asked the complainant what names she had been calling her. A quarrel ensued, when the female defendant dragged complainant across the house by the hair of her head. Complainant's husband also struck her in the face at the same time, saying to his wife" You ought to have been my daughter and she (the defendant) ought to have been my wife" —The Bench dismissed the case. atrd recommended husband and wife to go home and live neaceable and sober lives. MoNnAv,7—Before the Mayor (Alderman Piekmere), _ .

EMBEZZLEMENT BY A FORESTERS' SECRETARY AT PNESCOT. COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONER. On Monday, at the Prescot Police-court, before Mr. Earle, a respectable-looking man, named James Mutchavas charged with having embezzled the sum of Os., the property of the Prescot District Branch of the Ancient Order of Foresters; and also with embezzling another sum of £ll 7s. 11d., the property of the Court Horn Lodge of Foresters.—Mr. Mac- kenzie prosecuted, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. Mr. Mackenzie, in opening the case, said he appeared on behalf of the trustees of the Court of Foresters to prosecute on the two charges against the prisoner. The first case was that of embezzling the sum of nine guineas on the sth of May of last year. It appeared that the prisoner was at that time secretary to the Prescot District Foresters. The district, the Bench would understand, comprised seven courts, all of which contributed to a certain fund called the district fund. There were a secretary and a treasurer appointed for the pur- pose of getting this money; the treasurer holding the money and the secretary making certain orders to him for the pay- ment of accounts which became due from quarter to quarter. 'On the sth May, 1881, the prisoner went to the treasurer with one of these orders for the payment of nine guineas due to Messrs. Gaume, Son, and Hatton, London, and the secre- tary in due course handed him over that money. He (Mr. Mackenzie) was prepared to prove that that money had never been accounted for, it not having been paid to Messrs. Gaume, Son and Hatton, 'her in fact to anyone on behalf of the society. He would also prove to the Bench that on the 11th May, six days after receiving the money, the prisoner wrote to Messrs. Ciaume, Son and Hatton stating that he had received their account, and that he would bring it before the delegates at their next meeting on the 4th July. The Bench would observe the felonious intentiou of the prisoner ; he had the money in his hands, and yet made excuses for not paying it. Then, on the 22nd March, 1882, be wrote further letters in which he aggravated his felonious intent, and cast upon the trustees and others in that society a certain amount of dishonest abuse. In fact he, to clear himself from any blame, places it upon the shoulders of thoss who had the management of the society. If he proved a prima facie case of embezzlement he should ask that the prisoner be committed to the assiaes.—Edward Dyson was then called, and stated he was secretary to the Corporation Gas Works, St. Helens, and resided at Church-street, Prescot. He was one of the trustees of the Prescot District Branch of the Ancient Order of Foresters, the rules of which society had been duly registered under the Friendly Socie- ties' Act. The prisoner was district secretary in May, 1881, and was paid a salary. His duties were to receive money from the treasurer for the payments of liabilities against the lodger. In order to obtain the money he had to fill a form in the cheque book he kept for the purpose, of which form a counterfoil remained in the book. This form he handed to the treasurer, whose duty it was then to pay him the amount. They firet saw Day and George Cosgrove about 9-30 in the morning, and they were then playing. They then went into Viaduct- street, where they watched the defendants for an hour and half pitching to a mark. At eleven o'clock the other ee defendants came up, and they played.
