div.p: L GABORNE SWIMMER IN A.MEI;ICA.

DEFEAT OF THE CHAMPION OF PITTSBURG. The following is taken from a letter dated Newcastle (United States), August 28th, and receivara few days ago : —"Wm. Lawson, the well-known swimmer of Golborne and champion of Lancashire, won the great race at Geaugua Lake, Pennsylvania, on Saturday last, August 26th, with great ease, the distance being half a mile. Nine swimmers, iacluding the champion of Pitlsburg, started for the race, the men starling from two boats. A great race ensued for 200 yards, when the Pittsburg representative led for that , distance, but it was plainly seen who was going to be the winner, and two Pittsburg gentlemen offered to bet , 100 dollars to 10 on Lawson, having seen Lawson win the Allegany handicap two years ago. They were satisfied that no one could beat Lawson in the race. Lawson and Harm- atrong swam well together for a quarter of a mile, Lawson watching him at every stroke. Lawson dropped back a few yards, and remained there until 600 yards were covered, when he came in with a rush, and his powerful overhand Btroke telling in his favour went on in the next 100 yards at a tremendous pace, leaving his op- ponent at a standstill, and won easily by 25 yards. This makes the 14th victory in the United States. Lawson in- tends starting for Canada to swim at .Niagara Falls on August 29th, after which he will go to Toronto to spcnd a few days there. Lawson worked bard in getting himself in condition on fair ground. He has issued a challenge to swim Riley the champion of New York, who was beaten by Captain Webb of England at Boston on Monday last. ; Lawson and his friends state they will tnake a match for 500 dollars to swill at Cleveland baths, the distance to be ' 1,000 yards. This will be his last match as he states that he will retire from water, and will give up swimming altogether after this race, if accepted by Riley

The clerk of the Ormskirk Union has just produced a return of the voting on the triennial election of poor-law guardians, of which the following shows the result :—For the triennial election, 2,483; against, 231.

„ THE CAPTURE OP PICKPOCKETS AT ORMSKIRK.—The Ormskirk police have discovered that the two women com- mitted for trial last week for picking pockets on the occa- sion of the Royal visit to Ormskirk belong to a notorious gang of thieves, and that when they arrived in the town they were accompanied by five or six desperate characters, who at once took their departure by different routes on their companions being arrested. The woman who gave the name of Mary Jones proves to be Catherine O'Neil, and, though only -18 years of age, there is a long list of previous convictions against her. RAINHILL.

HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICES AT RAINHILL. ^On Sunday last harvest festival services were held in the Parish Church, Rainhill. In the morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. H. S. Maye, 8.A., vicar of Fairfield, Liverpool; and in the evening by the Rev. E. G. Robinson, M.A., vicar of St. Matthews, Liverpool. On both occasions there were very large congregations, and the collections, which were in behalf of the Curates' Augmentation Fund, amounted to £l7 3s. 6d. As on former occasions the church was very elaborately and effectively decorated. The chancel was adorned with beautiful plants from the conservatories of Mr, H. Baxter, Mr. E. Johnson, Mr. W. H. Meadows, and Mr J. Birchall. The pillars were appropriately entwined with:corn, and the windows were tastefully set with ivy, interspersed with bright coloured flowers and plants. The pulpit was very properly made the most conspicuous object, being literally covered with corn, flowers, and seasonable fruit, both from orchard and vinery. The font, reading desk, and other portions were also similarly embellished. The display was altogether unusually neat and appropriate. The decorations had been arranged by Mrs. Barlow, Mrs. H. Horner, Mrs. Thompson, Miss Poore, Miss Gibbs, Miss A. Martin, and the Misses Bromilow.

CONCERT AT ILLINEann.—On Wednesday evening a very successful concert was given in the Wesleyan school-room, Rainhill, in aid of the organ fund of the Wesleyan chapel. The programme arranged for the evening was an excellent one, and amongst the artistes were more than one already favourably known to concert-goers in this district, including Mr. George Barton and Miss Parry, from St. Helens. The accompanist on the piano was Miss M. E. Johnson, of St. Helens, who, it is needless to say, acquitted herself in the most skilful manner. The opening piece was a glee, " Oh, who will o'er the downs? "(De Pearsall) which was ren- dered by a glee party under the conductorship of Mr. J. Thomas. The party had evidently been previously under the rod of the conductor, and as a consequence performed their part effectively, and were rewarded by a round of applause. The next was a song, "doming home from the war," by Mr. Thomas, who was also rewarded by deserved applause. Miss Parry, in giving " Sleep, my love, sleep," caught the spirit of the song and earned a hearty encore, when she sung" Home they brought her warrior dead" in a forcible and sympathetic manner, and was again rewarded by a round of applause. A solo on the pianoforte, "Moonlight stream" (Demster), was then given by Miss Johnson, and was warmly appreciated by the audience. The next song down on the programme was "Nina," by Mr. Wood, but it was announced that Mr. Wood was sulering from a severe cold, and as a substitute Mr. Barnes would sing "Tile wolf." Mr. Barnes proved him- self to be a very worthy subatitute, and, having received an encore, sung a humorous song, "The well-known man." A solo and chorus were then given by Miss Roscoe and choir, after which a lively song," Tell me, my heart," was sung by Miss Gardner. Mr. Barton then made his appearance and sung the " Death of Nelson" in his usual masterly manner, and as a consequence brought down the house, when, as an en- core, he sung with equal effect, "Nora, the pride of Kildare." "Childhood's scenes" found a fit exponent in Miss Grounds, who was accompanied by her brother on the piano. In response to the continued applause which greeted the close of this song, Miss Grounds returned and bowed her acknowledgement without, however, singing an encore song. A trio, "0, memory," by Miss Gardner, Miss Parry, and Mr. G. Barton, concluded the first part of the pro- gramme. The second part comprised a duet, "Whispering hope," by Mr. Barton and Miss Parry; and a song, "Lord, remember David," besides other songs by the artistes already named, all of which were well received.
WIGAN.

TUE VALVR OF PROPERTY AT WIGAN. On Tuesday fternooo, at the Raven Hotel, Wigan, Messrs. Melling and Son, auctioneers, Ashtovi, put up for sale by auction several lots of freehold and leasehold business premises. There was a fair attendance of gentlemen, including Mr. Clayton (representing the firm of Messrs. Peace, Ackerley, and Company, solicitors,). Lot 1 consisted of the premises known as the "Aspull Copperas Works" with the extensive sheds and the dwelling-house adjoining, situate in Withing- ton-lane, Aspull. It was explained that the property was about 30 yards from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, and could readily be adapted for any business, the site containing about 8,640 square yards of land, of wkich 4,635 yards we freehold. The first bid was one of £7OO, and as no advance on this was made the lot was withdrawn. The reserve price was stated to be £l,OOO. Lot 2 was the b2erhouse known as " Our House," in the Wiend, Wigan, now occupied at a yearly rent of £35. The bidding started at £5OO, and advanced to £550, after which there was no further offer. The auctioneer stated that the reserve was £7OO, and the lot must be with- drawn. Lot 3 consisted of a freehold shop and residence adjoining the last-mentioned lot, and was occupied at a rent of £lO. An offer of £4OO was made, but this sum was briskly advanced to £6OO. £7OO was the reserve price, however, and as no advance on £6OO was made, this lot was withdrawn. The sale then concluded.

IMPORTANT ARBITRATION CASS : HEAVY CLAIM AGAINST THE WIGAN CORPORATION.—An important arbitration suit, interesting to both corporate bodies and mine owners, com- menced on Monday, at Lancaster, before Mr. W. H. Higgin, Q.C., umpire, and Messrs. E. H. Woodcock and J. Booth, arbitrators. The Orrell Coal and Cannel Company, Limited, for whom Mr. Edge appeared, claim £22,664 12s. 7d. from the Wigan Corporation, who are represented by Mr. Leresche and Mr. R. S. Wright, for the coal mines underneath the sewerage pipes running through the land. The statement of claim by the plaintiff company, after citing the facts as to the construction of the sewer, which was made for the ' purpose of carrying the Wigan sewerage to a farm at New- burgh, a distance of seven miles, states that this pipe runs through land under which they are the lessees of the fol- lowing seams of coal :—The Wigan five feet, the Wigan four feet, the Wigan nine feet, the Orrell Yard, the Orrell five feet, and the Orrell four feet. By section 15 of the Public Health Act, 1875, it is enacted that every local authority shall keep in repair all sewers belonging to them; and sec- tion .18 enacts that where any person sustains any damage by reason of the exercise of any powers of that act in relation to any matter as to which he is not himself in default, full compensation shall be paid to such person by the local authority. The Orrell Coal Company state that inconsequence of the construction and maintenance of this outfall sewer the mines cannot be worked and gotten in accordance with the usual and customary method of work- ing without causing the subsidence of the surface, and in- jury to sewer pipes and works, and that it will be necessary to leave unworked and ungotten a large quantity of the said mines, not only under the sewer but under the land adja- cent thereto. and that the company will be hampered and hindered in working the other portions of the mines, making the cost more expensive. In consequence the company c!airn, as stated, the sum of L 22,664 12s. 7d. for compensa- tion. The corporation disclaim the right of support, main- taining that the coal company may work their mines without any injury to the sewer, which has been so constructed that it will not be damaged by any subsidence; that no support, either viftical or lateral, is required from the plaintiff com- pany ; and that they are not liable, and will not pay the amount claimed. The case—which has arisen owing to the recent decision in the suit by Earl Dudley against the local authorites of Dudley—will last, it is expected, sevez al weeks, and naturally is creating considerable interest in the mining world, as other claim of a similar nature will be made azainst the eorporation, , should this prove successful, the sewer p:pe running through a great partion Of the Wigan coal -field.

THE UNITED METHODIST FREE CHTTRCHES.—The anni- versary services of this church were held on Sunday and Monday last, when the Rev. John Guttridge, of Manchester, preached twice in High-street Chapel. The congregation in the morning was good, and the sermon, from Revelations 22 c., 9," Worship God," was a masterly epitome of Methodist doctrine and belief. In the evening the chapel was crowded to the utmost by upwards of 1,000 people, to hear the veteran preacher set forth the plan of salvation from. 1 Timothy, 1 c., 15 v., "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.' On the Monday afternoon a public tea meeting was held in the schoolroom, after which a public lecture was given in the chapel, Mr. Joseph Slater pre- siding. By some misarvangement or misunderstanding, the choir were not allowed to give their customary share to the anniversary treat, though they had amply prepared as aforetime to maintain their character as an able Christian congregational choir. No doubt the oversight will be remedied in future. The proceeds of the collections and tea auraunted to 'very nearly £5O. WINSFORD RIFLE CORPS PRIZE SHOOTING.—The annual prize shooting of the Winsford E Company of the 3,6 Volunteer Battalion of the County Regiment, took place at the Weaver range, on Saturday last. ITEMS OF CHRSHIRE NEWS. "Hospital Sunday" will be observed in Chester on Sun- day next, when the morning and evening offertories will be given to the Chester Infirmary. At Wednesday's monthly meeting of the Chester Town Council, Mr. E. J. Salisbury raised a discussion on the new Ituprovement Bill, by criticising it in part favourably and lin part adversely, and he moved that it be as instruction to the committee that the capital sum to b.) borrowed for free- ing the Dee bridges be £15,000. After some discussion, the proposal was adopted. SUICIDE AT CIIESTEM—On Tuesday, a lad 16 years of age, named James Pavey, committed suicide by hanging himself at 25, Watergate-street-row, Chester. The deceased worked at a pipe factory at Newton during the day, appear- ing in his usual health; but at ten o'clock he was found hanging behind the bedroom door, quite dead. It is said that the lad had been reading "Dick Turpin " and other sensational literature, and that his mind had become affected.

There is a singular conflict going on at Chester. The Welsh Sunday Closing Act is in force in the immediate neighbourhood of the city, but the publicans concerned are hoping that if a scheme for the incorporation of a Welsh suburb with the city is successful they will he brought within the jurisdiction of the Chester magistrates. They are therefore supporting the scheme, while their fellow- tradesmen within the city are opposing it, in the hope of preserving their monopoly of the Sunday liquor trade. It is hard to soe how, if the proposal for incorporation is carried, it will take any part of Wales out of Wales and thus out of the scope of the Act. PROPOSED NEW POST-OFFICE FOR CREWE.—At the monthly meting of the Crewe Town Council, on Wednes- day, the Mayor (Alderman M‘Noill) said he thought the time had come when Crewe should be provided with a more commodious post-offlca than the existing one in High-street. The Town Clerk read letters from Warrington and Buxton, where the Government had provided new post-offices, and ultimately it was unanimously resolved—" That in the opinion of the Council. considering that the parcels postage will shortly come into operation, it is desirable to take meass to secure a more commodious post-office for Crewe, and that application be made to the Postmaster General for that purpose." The Town Clerk was requested to see the District Surveyor with a yiew to obtaining his co-operation.

TER REPRESENTATION or WEST CHESEIRE.—At a meeting of West Cheshire Conservatives, on Saturday, the Hon. W. F. Tollemache, M.P., intimated his intention of retiring from the representation of the division at the n,2xt election. The reason he gave was not one with which we are disposed to quarrel, but it affords a curious illustration of the manner in which certain of our territorial magnates assume that the right to settle the parliamentary representa- tion of the district belongs to themselves. At Sir Philip Egerton's death, said Mr. W. F. Tollemache, "there was no person to fill his place, and accordingly his cousin came for- ward and rescued the seat from the enemy. When Mr. Henry Tollemache came forward it was perfectly understood that he himself should retire. His father felt strongly that two Tollemaches ought not to represent the same division, and he most thoroughly agreed with him." WIRRAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—The fortieth exhibi-

tion of the Wirral Agricultural Society opened on Thurs- day, at Bidston, on ground which had been prepared for the purpose with great care and cost. Thanks to the exertions Df the committee, the show is the most attractive and

interesting eir held in connection with the society, and gives evidence of a vast improvement of late years in the agriculture of Wirral. We append a few of the awards : Leapers : Jumper over hurdle and water (open competition), 1, W. Dodsworrh, Middlewich ; 2, John Halsall, Halebank ; 3, J. H. Cooke, Malpas. Pigeons: Homer, 1, R. G. Preston; 2 and 3, T. Mathieson, Beweey New Hall, Warrington. Dogs: Pointer (dog), 3, Thomas Mathieson. Clumber spaniel: 2, C. P. Harvey, Whitegate, Nortbwich. Sheep dog, smooth hair (dog or bitch): 3, George Raper, Bowdon. Sheep dog, rough hair (dog): 1, John Grocott, Haughton, Tarporley. Bull dog: 1, George Raper. Skye terrier: 2, Henry Dilliway, Denton's Green-lane, St. Helens. Any variety of rough or broken-haired terrier dog or bitch: 2, Richard Hall, Knutsford ; 3, J. J. Ashworth, Ellesmere Lodge, Al trincham.

ALARMING COLLISION AT EARLES- TOWN STATION. A LUGGAGE TRAIN RUNNING INTO A PASSENGER TRAIN. What is commonly known as the " curve" at the Earles- town railway station, was the scene of an alarming collision on Monday afternoon, and though, fortunately, unattended by personal injury resulted in much damage to rolling stock, and considerable delay and inconvenience in the working of the traffic. It appears that the passenger train which leaves Wigan at 3-10 p.m. for Warrington, arrived at the " curve " at 3-35, two or three minutes before it was due. It was timed to leave the station at 3-40, and as but few passengers left or entered the train, it was ready to start before time was up. The train consisted of three carriages with a guard's van at each end, and was drawn by an engine, which had been reversed, and was running with the "tender "in front. On its arrival at Earlestown there were only three or four passengers inside, but four females who had booked for Warrington entered, making the number of passengers seven or eight. This is a most fortunate circumstance, for, otherwise the collision might have been of a fatal character. While the train was stepping at the station a luggage train was observed approaching from Newton Bridge at a speed of about 15 miles an hour, but it was not expected that it was to be turned on to the curve for Warrington, the line on which the passenger train was standing. Such, however, proved to be the case, and it was evident to all beholders that a collision was unavoidable. The only occupants of the platform at the time were Joseph Oliphant, ticket collector, Earlestown, and the guard of the passenger train, a man named Adam Hitchmond, of Warrington. Both sought safety in flight, the former running across the lines to the opposite platform, while the latter made his escape by getting over the wooden rails and into the neighbouring field. The driver of the luggage train, when he observed the passenger train in front of him, sounded the warning" or "danger" whistle, and to avert a collision turned off the steam, reversed his engine and applied the break, whilst the driver of the passenger train put on the steam and moved his train, but before it had proceeded far the engine of the luggage train dashed with great force into the guard's van. The fireman of the lug- gage train jumped from the steps on to the platform before the collision occurred, but the driver stood at his post. The crash that took place is described as tremendous, the car- riages were pitched violently forward, and were turned up on end, then banged down on the ground. One of the passengers, alarmed at the whistling of the luggege train, looked out of the carriage window, and observing the col- lision to be unavoidable, he jumped froth the train and escaped the severe shaking which the other passengers received. All persons inside the carriages were precipitated from one side of their compartments to the other and it is stated that several ware very badly shaken. It cannot be ascertained definitely that any cuts or wounds were re- ceived by anyone through the severe shock to the system of some of the passengers added to the fright and alarm which were occasioned are sufficiently serious. The effect of the collision upon the passenger train was of a serious character. The guard's van and the carriage next to it suffered the most, the former being much smashed, and the latter had its end knocked in, while both were thrown off the metals. The buffers of the van and the lamp were crushed into in- describable shapes, and the end of the van was lifted on to the front of the engine. A composite carriage was nnich damaged. In addition to the buffers being twisted, the end was smashed in, while parts of the woodwork were knocked into matchwocd. The second carriage from the guard's van—the middle one of the train—also bore marks ef the collision, one of the buffers being crushed, and the woodwork staved in. Two of the wheels of this carriage were off the line. The carriage next to this one was comparatively uninjured. The second guard's van, however, was thrown off the line and was much damaged. The buffers were twisted and the wood work was staved in. The engine was not much damaged. As far as the luggage train was concerned none of the waggons appeared to have suffered, though the engine was seriously damaged. The passengers mane their way to the booking office platform, and were conveyed to thole destination on the next train. In the meantime Mr. Young, the station master, had arrived. Information of the collision was telegraphed to Warrington, and a break-down gang was asked for. Before the gang ar- rived the assistance of several men employed at the viaduct waggon works, belonging to the railway company, were ob- tained, and an effort was made to clear the line so as to have as little delay in the traffic as possible. The luggage train was blocked on the Liverpool line, and the.shunting engine "Earlestown " assisted in the removal of the carriages. About half-past four the breakdown gang, under the charge of Mr. Mountfield, arrived from Warrington with a powerful travelling crane, screw jacks, aec. By the directions of Mr. Young, stationmaster, who worked hard and perseveringly to get the lines clear, Mr. Mountfield, of Warrington, Inspector Peters, of Liverpool, and other officials, the men set to work. After about an hour's labour the carriages and vans were placed on the line, and were shunted out of the way. While the line was being cleared, both the up and down trains were run on one line at much inconvenience. As to the cause of the collision, it is stated that the signals were right for the luggage train to proceed. The driver of the train states that was so, and that on nearing the "curve" he saw the passenger train in the station, but owing to the sharp turn the rails make he was unable to see on which line it was standing. On seeing that nis train was on the earns line as the passenger train, he commenced his warning whistle, thinking it might be the means of sending the passenger train forward. He reversed his engine, and turned off the steam, while the break was also applied, but it was too late. It is said the collision is due to some fault in connection le ith the signal. The lever for the signal to be up was all right, but from some cause or cther unexplained the signal did not act, and consequently hung down, giving the engine driver of the I approaching luggage train the idea that the line was clear.

div.head: CARDINAL MANNING AT WIDNES.
div.p: CARDINAL MANNING AT WIDNES.

CATHOLIC DEMONSTRATION. A demonstratinninoonnection with St. Mary's Temperance Leagueof the Cross eva.s held in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, on Mosiday evenirg. Additional importane was lent to the gathering by the presence of His Eminence, Cardinal Manning, Catholic Archbishop of Westminster, who arrived in the town'froen Liverpool about a quarter past six. He was received at the London and North Western Railway Station by the Re,. Father Clark, incumbent of , St. Mary's; the Rev. W. Ryan, curate of St. Mary's; and the Rev. T. Fine- gan, pastor of St. Bedes, Appleton; and proceeded to the residence of Father Clark. At seven o'clock the members of the League, 1,000 strong, assembled at St. Mary's Catholic School. Thence, headed by the band of the society, and the guards, who wore a bright green regalia, they paraded the principal streets of the town. The meeting was an- nounced for eight o'clock, but fully three-quarters of an hour a surging crowd blocked up the entrance to the build- ing._ The spacious hall was filled to its utmost capacity, the back of the hall and the side passages being occupied. On his Esainence entering the room there was an outburst of cheering, which continued for some time. His Eminence was accompanied by the Rev. Fathers J. Clark, A. M. De Haze Radlrtz, S. J. Y. Finegan, M. Ryan, Blake Cody, 0.5.8., Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. H. W. Deacon, P. Talton, J. Tallon, G. J. S. Wells, Carey, and others. Without intro- ductory Ceremony of any description, His EMINUXCE, who was loudly cheered on rising, said be should first of all tell the audience that his coming to Widnes that night was a visit to the workingmen of Widnes. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The secretary of the League of the Cross told him that if he were to come to Widnes the workingmen would give him welcome. (Cheers.) He therefore said, "I will come and see." Well, he was there to ascertain whether the secretary told him the truth or not; and he was bound above all to say that he had come to make a visit to the League of the Cross of Widnes— (cheers)—and he hoped that before be had done, and before they separated, that there might be a great many more members of the League of the Cross. (Cheers.) Perhaps it would be well for him to say exactly what the League of the Cross was, what it had done, and what it was doing.; and he would therefore relate how it arose in the beginning. In London there was ten years ago only one temperance association in ex-stence—he meant in the unity of the Catholic Church, for with the temperance associations out of the unity of the Catholic Church he could have nothing to do, but bade them all success in their work--(hear, hear)—of putting down drunkenness. But he was unable to enter into any co-operation with any one without the unity of the Catholic Church, to which they were all, as Catholics, bound. (Cheers.) Well, he called together a large meeting of his people at the largest schoolroom he could find, to see whether they could not found a Catholic association of total abstiuence. And the first thing he did was to say "Let any man here who took the pledge from Father Matthew lift up his hand," and there were about 16 hands held up. He wondered if he were to ask that any man present that night who took the pledge from Father Matthew should stand up and hold up his hand, whether there would be found one among them. If there be, be asked him to show himself. [Four men of elderly ap- pearance then stood •up, amid loud cheering.] He (the Cardinal) was glad they had begun so well. The League of the Cross in London, which now had 30 branches on every side of London—on the north and on the south side of the Thames—branches in England, in Wales, in Scotland, and he was happy to tell them one in • Ireland, too—(hear, hear)—that League of the Cross he al- ways said was nothing but a graft upon the root Father Matthew planted in London. It was his work, and not their work; he looked upon it as Father Matthew's work come to life again; and they in Widnes had four who took the pledge from Father Matthew, and the League of the Cross in Widnes sprang from the work of Father Matthew, from that man holy and venerable, and in benediction in the heart of everyone who heard him, every Catholic, every child of Ireland, and even those who were neither one nor the other, nevertheless venerated the name of Father Matthew, the apostle of total abstinence. (tleer, hear, and cheers.) The first thing that happened iu that meeting was that a good man said to him (the Cardinal) "Father, ask our good priests to put themselves at the head of us, and then we will do anything." "Well," he replied, " I will put myself at the head of you, with all my heart, and I will be your chaplain, and will do my best with my other good priests to see that they shall do the same.' They had got their priests at their head, who were guiding them to the League of the Cross, and if they would faithfully follow, then be sure that the League of the Cross would prosper in Widnes. (Cheers.) He had just said that he heartily wished success and prosperity to all temperance societies that were outside of their unity. In saying that be wished to explain his meaning. The Leaeue of the Cross, and anything else that was founded on the Catholic religion, and under the laws of the Catholic faith and its Unity, was absolute, and as the world would say, as exclusive as the Catholic Church itself; because, as he told those good men, he could deal with the members of his own flock for they would listen to him, but he could not deal with those who were not members of his own flock, for they would not listen to him. He could deal with his own flock when they prac- tised their religion and were faithful Catholics; he could not deal with any men who did not give Lam some pledge. Therefore the League of the Cross was absolutely indepen- dent of everything else. They heard of armies of all sorts and kinds, and all manner of colours, names, and titles. They could have nothing to do with any other body that was external of the League of the Cross, because it was external • to the Catholic Church, no more than an army would admit e-. volunteers into its ranks, or members of any other army on the face of the earth. Every army must have its discipline, and the League of the Cross had the discipline of the Catholic Church. (Cheers, and an interruption from behind.) Having said so much—he was ready to hear and answer anything that might be said from the end of the room—having said so much about the League of the Cross, let him tell them where it existed. First in London, as they knew; next it was to be found in York, Newcastle, Norwich, Manchester, Birmingham, Liverpool ; in all the great cities and centres it was to be found, and also in a multitude of other places, and all the unity together was :under one rule, and that one rule was total abstinence. - ,They did not receive any partial pledges whatsoever ; that .was what were called temperance pledges, and the reason of it was this : 'Every man who was a Christian was bound by the vows of his baptism to be a temperate man, and they did not therefore give a pledge to a man who was pledged already. He was already bound, and they thought it better and safer to leave him under the obligation of his baptismal vows and duty. It was perfectly, absolutely free for a man to do or not to do according to his conscience, and therefore to take the pledge of total abstinence was to do something more than they were bound to do; and to do it for reasons he would not enter into at present. First of all he wiehed them to think of what they all were as God had made them. They were all men, and man was the most perfect and he would say the most beautiful work that the Creator ever made. It was quite true that a men had not the speed of the antelope, or the strength of the horse, and he could not fly in the air like a bird, nor live in the water like a fish ; and therefore it would seem that man was less perfect than the other creatures round about us. But a good man could do something which neither antelope nor horse, nor fowl, nor fish could do, and that was he could reason. He had got intelligence, brain, heart, and he could love that which was good and hate that which was evil, and he had got a will which was like the rudder of a ship by which he could . govern himself; and therefore a man, though lie had not got the fleetness of some of the creatures, nor had he the strength of the others, he had got gifts above them all. He w s the likeness of God himself who made him, and having that he ought to be happy. If he had a good conscience he would be happy. He might meet with a great many sorrows and cares, but if his own conscience was good these would not destroy his happiness; and a man who was happy might have a happy home. He might haves roof over his head where he would be happy with his family, and he would have a day of rest. There were too few days of rest for the hard-working people. He wished the days of rest were more in number, but happily there was one in every week, and that day of rest, if it were kept as a day of religion and of repose by a man who was happy in himself and happy in his home, was a happy day indeed. (Cheers.) He would go further, and say that man was the best and greatest work that the Creator ever made. A working man stood very high, for God sent us into the world to work, not to be idle. The first man was to till the ground or dress the garden. He was not to be indolent or unintelligent. A workingman who used his strength and intelligence to do his work whereby he gained his bread, was as honourable in his calling and in his way of life as any man that trod the face of the earth. (Cheers.) They were all working-men, he hoped. Well, such was man. The man he had sketched as God had made him. What was man as man made himself? Was it not a wonderful thing and a mournful thing that the bright sky over our head was just as bright as it was in the day that It was created; the earth under our feet just as green as it was in the time when it was made; the flowering trees bore their fruit, the flowers, the lilies and the rose, sprang out of el. the earth; all these were in their full beauty just as Gcd made them in the beginning. And more than this, all the creatures that he bad spoken of—the oxen in the fields, and the sheep upon the dcwns, and the fowls of the air, and the fishes of the sea—were all of them as they were made. They had never sinned agamnBt God; they had never departed from the perfection in which God made them. They were to-day as they came from the hands of His goodness and wisdom. There was only one creature that He had made that had destroyed himself; only one creature of all His wisdom and goednesa that was miserable and unhappy; and that by his own doing—who committed self-murder in body and soul— aid that was the creature which He had made in His own likeness and image, and is the highest and most perfect of all the work that God ever made. Man and man alone could destroy himself, deface, disfigure, murder himself i; nuke himself miserable and wretched n this world; and God's mercy alone could preserve from an eternity of misery. (Cheers.) All sin destroyed the beauty of man; but There was one sin, which beyond all other sins, darkened, destroyed, disfigured, the happiness and the perfection of Alan, and the beauty of the head and the heart that god tad given him, and that one sin was drunkenness, by which the brain was made to reel and the conscience became dark, the heart inflamed and passionate, and the will became weak and wilful; and all that which he said in the begin- ning ought to be the happiness of man was destroyed. Then In that state there was not a law of God that he might not break; there was not a sin that he might not commit; , there was not a passion that was not set on fire; there was nothing he might not do;. and he did not knor what he was doing, (Chow ) Eramense related one or two instances

to show this, He wished to say most strongly that if drink wrecked a man and made man miserable, none suffered by drink so much as woman; and for this reason. The poor mother who had many children saw her children naked, famishing, shivering with cold, starving, because the hus- band and father spent his wages in drink. The poor wife having a drunken husband was of all women on the face of the earth most to be pitied, and it often happened that for the purpose of saving her husband she would go to the public-house where he was sitting late at night. She could not prevail on him to go home with her. She sat •lown patiently waiting in the hope that he would listen. Perhaps she was herself tempted to taste intoxicating drink, and it often happened that h. wife who had gone in the hope of saving her husband had herself fallen into the same habit and become as bad a drunkard as he. (Cheers.) He would not there speak of those horrible things which they read of continually in the newspapers, of that most brutal and unmanly act which was constantly brought before the magistrates of the country, where the husband lifted his hand against the wife, using the strength and violence of a man, cruelly to inflict pain upon a poor defenceless woman. No men who had not lost his reason, his will, his heart, could commit such a crime, and yet they knew it was committed every day throughout the land; and the chief cause of it was intoxicating drink. And if weak women were to be pitied, should they not all pity the poor children? Could they conceive anything more horrible or more fright- ful to a little child than to see his father lying on the ground unable to speak, with his own countenance changed so that the child could hardly recognise him? If there was anything more terrible than this it was when that child saw the mother in the same state of degradation. Such then was the condition to which man brought himself. How happy might man be if he would only remake himself; if he would only undo this evil. There was time. When it went on too long it might be beyond his p,wer, but there was time. If he would only return and re- in tke himself, he might get back to that which he was in the beginning. There was one thought which passed him, which he could not help expressing. He said man might be happy in himself, in his home, and on the day of rest. Now what a terrible thing it was to know that it was just that one day of rest on which intoxicating drink made the greatest havoc. It was that one day of rest on which a man who had toiled six days before, and who needed to be refreshed and strengthened, would, if he had this terrible habit upon him, drink on Saturday night and through the Sunday, and would on Monday morning be unfit to go to his work. He wasted, destroyed, and desecrated his day of rest, and on the Monday morning be arose, not refreshed and strengthened to go about his work, but rendered more incapable—with hands tremulous, and eyes unsteady. And they knew this: that in Manchester, for instance, there was not a day in the week in which so many persons were brought for accidents of a dangerous kind into the Infirmary, as on Monday. What then had to be done? There were two remedies for this evil. One was a parliamentary remedy. Perhaps they would say "You cannot make a man sober by Act of Par- liament." No; that was quite true, but Acts of Parliament multiplied the temptations and facilities of drunkenness, and Acts of Parliament could undo that which an Act of Parlia- ment had done. (Cheers.) He did not know whether in Widnes there were any members of the United Kingdom Alliance; but it would be a good thing to know what the Alliance was. In every great city, borough, town, and vil- lage there were agents who were making people understand the wreck and misery which came from intoxicating drink, and were stirring them up to use their vote at the next elec- tion to return to Parliament such men as will give their full strength and full intelligence to the endeavours to obtain for the people of this country what was popularly called the power of veto; so that no public-house should be put down in any place contrary to the will of the people of that place; that neither magistrates nor any other authority whatsoever should judge for them whenever they desired to have a public house put down in the midst of them; but that the ratepayers should have the power of saying "No," if they did not wish it. (Cheers.) That day he had received in Liverpool, a paper—he supposed from the author— which contained a statement he could not help mentioning, because it would show the importance of the subject upon which he was speaking. In Toxteth Park, in Liverpool, there were three distinct divisions or districts. In one of them there was a population of 25,000, and in that popula- tion there were 100 public-houses. In the second division there was a population of 45,000. and in like manner there were 100 public-houses. In the third division of 50,000 there was no public-house at all. (Loud cheers.) Now, what was the fruitful result of this? In the first division of 25,000 there were between 900 and 1,000 paupers. In the second, of 45,000, there were between 500 and 600 paupers. In the district of 50,000, where there was no public - house, there were• only 45 paupers. (Great applause.) Who was it that paid for the support of these 900 paupers in the first district? The sober working- men who had to pay for the drunken paupers. Was it not then fair and just that the working-men who paid the rates should have the power of saying " Yes " or " No" if a public-house was to be put. down in the midst of them? Why were such houses put in the centre of them now, as the people did not ask for them. He would tell them. He did not wish to speak a word which should be understood as an attack upon anybody. He was not going to attack brewers, distillers, or publicans—he hoped this would be well understood—.but he did say this, that brewers and publicans. with the enormous capital of £130,000,000 Or £140,000,000, which was engaged every year in the pro- duction, distribution, and sale of intoxicating drinks, exer- cised an influence which bad the effect of multiplying pub- lic-houses, because the multiplication of those houses made their trade more profitable. The more public-houses there were and the more drink there was sold, the greater was the profit to those who produced that drink; and the more drink there was sold the greater was the Intoxication, and the heavier were the rates for the police, the administration of justice, and the maintenance of madhouses. In the same ratio did those rates become more burdensome to the workingman. (Applause.) It was merely justice, then, that they should have the vote and the power, when any body of licensing magistrates was prepared to give a licensed house to a man, to come in and say "No; in order to preserve our homes and the streets in which we live from the evil which a public- house always brings with it, we object to the license." (Cheers) In Widnes if there were not a hundred public- houses, there were something very near it. (Laughter). Now, there were two ways of curing this. One was to shut the doors of the public-houses. He believed one was shut in Widnes the other day, but it was open again. (Laughter and cheers.) They had Rot at this timo the power of shut- tieg the doors, hut they had the power of not putting their feet over the threshold. The League of the Cross was a great army, not of reformed drunkards, for he was the presi- dent of it—(laughter and cheers)--and his good griests were presidents of every branch of if. (Cheers.) His Eminence then described the aims of the League, and in urging those present to join, be remarked that the other day 2,000 physicians, the first in the land, signed a declaration carefully drawn up by themselves, in which they declared that stimu- lants of every sort or kind had net the power of ordinary wholesome natural food, for any healthy man did not require it; that it was injurious to health; and that its use was the source of misery, sin, crime, wretchedness, shame, and degradation to our country. (Cheers.) He touched upon the evil which had in many instances resulted through medical men recommending stimulants as a medicine; and spoke of the importance of parents training up their children without tasting intoxicating drink. In conclusion, he said he did not know whether he should be welcomed in Widnes again. (Loud cheers.) Let every man and every woman who had already taken the pledge renew it with him. If there were any who had taken the pledge in time past, and had broken it, let them come back to the ranks, and take it again with him. (Cheers.) If there were any whose hearts had been waver- ing, and their conscience saying " What he says is true, and will be good for me if I had only the courage to do it ; " if there were any who had been thinking they would do it at some future time, he said to those people, do it now. Let those who had been convinced and half persuaded, rise up too, and take the total abstinence pledge with him. (Cheers.) Almost the whole of the large assembly stood up in their places, and repeated after the Cardinal, the words of the pledge. The Cardinal then resumed his seat, amid prolonged cheering, havingspoken for about an hour. Mr. H. WADE-DEACON who was warmly received, remarked that the Rev. .I:Clarke was kind enough to ask him to be there that evening. He wrote back to him what he knew already, that though be strongly and heartily- ap- proved of temperance, he could not approve of total abstin- ence. He told Father Clarke that at the time, but he still asked him to come, and he therefore was there that night. It seemed very ungracious, no doubt, to say anything which did not agree with the able address they had beard from Cardinal Manning. (Cheers.) He was sure that everyone, and none more than himself, agreed very much indeed with what Cardinal Manning had said. He went with him entirely on the temperance question when he said that a man should keep sqber and a woman should keep sober, and not drink more than was good for them. But he could not go with him to the end. He could not stand up when the others or some of the others, stood up and took the pledge. He thought that each man must judge according to his own conscience. Coming under these circumstances, he could not go away without this explanation, and without thus enunciating his views. Dr. O'KEEFE said they had been so well entertained by a prince of the church, who had honoured them by coming amongst them that night, that he thought it would be un- necessary, a work of supererogation, for him to say anything further than had been said already by his Eminence. While he agreed with what Mr. Deacon had said in regard to temperance and sobriety, he also thought that total absti- nence was exceedingly necessary. (Applause.) He knew that their priests in Widnes had laboured hard to establish a branch of the League of the Cross, and this League had proved a great instrument of good amongst them. As his Eminence had told them, medical men, both in Widnes and elsewhere, were agreed on the great evils of intemperance. He thought the large essembly who had been honoured by the advent of his Eminence would go away bearing in their hearts an indelible impression of the good advice which they had received from him, and he trusted that all those who had stood up to take the pledge with him would endeavour to make as many others take it as they could (Applause.) • The Rev. M. RYAN !proposed a vote of thanks to his Eminence, which was accorded with great cheering, during which he left the room, accompanied by the clergy and almost all the gentlemen who had occupied seats on the platform. proceedings conc watch," concluded withwa was sung musical by Messrs. entertainment.yons A The, larboard and Mullen. This was followed by a humorous song, entitled "Pet and the widow," given by Mr. Mullen, who Theduet, succeeded in convulsing the audience with laughter.

THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' ELECTION. - ;US ANOMALIES.—No. 3. In our first sketch we mentioned an anomaly which we now more particularly ref 3r to, it being of so extraordinary a character as to warrant more than a casual notice. We mean that clause in the Runcorn Improvement Act which enacts as an indispensahle qualification for a seat on the , Board a residence within the limits of the Runcorn Improve- ment Act district. The area of the whole district is but 1,490 statute acres, and yet out of this area the number of mem- bers up to sixteen must, be found, and with a further quali- fication nearly double of that required for a seat on the L3cal Board of a town of even a larger population. We have been puzzled to find a reason for this, but suggest the following: that as the Act was obtained in 1852, when there seemed not the slightest probability of its being opened to the outer world by railway communication, it must have been thought that Runcorn was a world of itself, and was and would re- main for an indefinite period the depository of sufficient in- telligence and wisdom to guide its destinies for all time. But the railway has come, fresh life has been introduced into its veins, and we venture to prophesy that 'ere long the in- habitants will demand that this anomaly be removed. In fact we have been told that three or four years ago a mem- ber;of the Board of Commissioners brought the matter under the notice of his fellows, and an elaborate report was drawn up for transmission to the Local Government Board advo- cating the adoption of a seven mile radius residential quali- fication, but which, on being submitted to the whole Board, was rejected by a narrow vote. We wonder if that report is still in the" pigeon holes" of the Commissioners' "corner cupboard." It might be of some service if admitted to the light of day. We suppose some of the members must have seen that if they voted for it they would—if current rumour be correct—have been giving themselves muni- cipally the coup de grace, or, in plain words, the "happy dispatch," and we should have been surprised to have heard that the vote had been otherwise. But now, surely, wider considerations ought to prevail, the custom of to-day being for wealth and position to choose suburban residence, a cus- tom recognised by law, both in the case of Corporations and Local Boards. As we have before stated, a member of a Local Board may live anywhere within a radius of seven miles, and, we believe, a member of a Town Council may reside within a radius of twelve miles and still be qualified for a seat in the local parliament. It may, perhaps, be of in- terest to note that the Law-clerk to the Commissioners never has resided within "the charmed circle," and yet we have not heard that his legal acumen has been impaired by a residence at Frodsham, and this during the time when such valuable members of the Board as the late Chas. Hazlehurst, Esq., John Simpson, Esq., original members of the Board, the late Mr. W. H. Ockleston and Mr. James Handley had to resign their places, though only living within a short distance of the town, and others, who were able and willing to give their services, were prevented from the same cause. We have somewhere heard of a hymn commencing: We are a garden walle 1 around, Chosen, select, peculiar ground," • bat which is of such an exclusive character as to be refused admission in modern collections. We may add a few general remarks which have occurred to us during the penning of these sketches. First, as to the Act itself. It does not seem large enough in its scope. As Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst remarked a little while ago, it is time Runcorn grew out of "its swaddling clothes " and ordered a "Corporation suit." The Act does not give even sufficient money power, to purchase the gas works' though it contains all the adminis- trative clauses needful ; and is entirely silent as to the erection or purchase of water works, thongh we fully believe it would be an immense advantage for both these undertakings to be in the hands of the town. Next, the anxiety of the works for certain persons to be on the Board, seems born of a misapprehension. Depending, as Runcorn does, for so much of its employment on the works; and as a consequence the tradesmen class deriiing their living from the results of that employment, it would be impossible to return men to the Board pledged to do any thing of an arbitrary nature affecting the works. The thing might be surely left to take care of itself, and all the unpleasant rumours of " intimidation " and "strong influence " being brought to bear at election times, and which were not entirely stifled by the collapse of last Thursday week, would be a thing of the past. As to the other matters—the "scale of voting," "nomination of members," "ballot ''—we have heard that a return has been ordered by the House of Com- mons from Boards of Improvement Commissioners, which we think points unmistakably to the advent of an era which we hope may lead up to a "purer and a higher life."
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday, at tbe Board's offices, Alforde Chambers. There were present :—The Chairman (Mr. F. H. Gossage), D. O'Keeffe, and Messrs. Carey, Pankhurst, Handley. Wright, Midwood, Manley, Johnson, Webster Sadler, Kershaw, Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Roberts (gas engineer), • and Dickson (nuisance inspector).

instructed to suggest that each club, or the friends of a patient, should appoint some person to visit their patients in the hospital at least once a week, so that a report, if neces- sary, may be made upon the treatment received."—A state- ment was presented showing the average cost of food for twelve months to be 9 8 pence per head per day for patients and staff.—Mr. SADLER moved, and Mr. MARTLEY seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Sadler said the circular letter was to be sent with the intention of keeping the Board clear from all liabilities in the future. The Board had already received a bill from a certain medical man in the district, which had been before the committee several times, and was still under consideration; and it was thought best to issue that letter setting forth the aim of the hospital so that there would be no such claims in the future.—The motion was carried.

BREAKING INTO A PUBLIC-HOUSE AT PARR, ST. HELENS. On Monday, at the St. Helens Borough Petty Sessions, two labourers, named Thomas Tierney and James Wynn, were charged, on remand, with having broken into Mr. M. Har- risons, Black Horse Inn, Parr, St. Helens, on the night of the 2nd instant, and stolen therefrom the sum of £8 or thereabouts.—Mr. Swift prosecuted, and Mr. Riley defended Wynn.—Ann Jane Harrison, the wife of Matthew Harrison, said she lived with him at the Black Horse Inn, Parr. At about half-past four on Saturday, the 2nd instant, she was serving in the bar. She saw the two prisoners in the •t aults, and while they were there she changed a sovereign for a little girl, and then wrapped it in a piece of paper and put it in a cigar box. She put the box on a shelf in the bar. While doing that someone in the bar asked her if that was her bank. The house was closed at eleven o'clock, and her husband went to bed about half-past eleven and witness at a ' quarter to twelve. She was the last to go to bed, and before doing so she saw that the house was securely fastened. There were four sovereigns and half a sovereign left in a cigar box in the bar, and in another cigar box there was left about £3 10s. From what her husband told he: the next morning she looked in the bar, and found that both boxes were gone but she afterwards found one of the boxes in the cellar, the money, however, having been taken out. The last thing that she did before going to bed on the Saturday night was to go down into the cellar, turn the gas low, and see that the window was all right.— Matthew Harrison, the landlord of the Black Horse Inn, said he knew the two prisoners. On the day in question he saw them in his house between half past four and half past five. They were in the bar. Witness was called into the bar by the servant, who told him, in the presence of the prisoners, that they had ordered a quart of beer, and that they would not pay for it. There were others in the bar besides the prisoners and the servant did not say who she meant by "they," but Tierney had the jug in his hand. Witness asked Tierney who was going to pay for the beer, and he replied he would pay for it if he had the money. Witness then took the jug out of his hand, and told him to 'go out of the house, to which he replied that he would not. On witness going round to put him out Tierney raised his hand as if to strike but did not do so. A scuffle ensued in which Tierney was thrown to the ground. Wynn said to witness that if he had done the same to him he would have broken his neck. Tierney also threatened that he would "do " for witness, after which both the prisoners went out, and witness did not see any more of them that night. He got up about half past six tha next morning and went into the cellar, and found a square of glass in the window had been broken, and it had been pushed wide open. Tne window had been secured by an iron- bolt, and had not been opened for about six years previous. The grid outside the window had also been displaced. Cross-examined by Tierney, witness denied that he (Tierney) had won any money from him during the past three months.—By Mr. Riley: Witness said Wynn was the son of a respectable tradesman in St. Helens, and so far as his experience went had always been a quiet young man and of a good character.—Thomas Lee, a labourer, said he knew both the prisoners. On Saturday, the 2nd inst., he went to Tierney's house, and after some conversation, asked him to go and have a pint of beer. Tierney replied that he did not like to go as he had no money, but added that he had some to get from the "Blunder." Witness sent for a pint of beer and left Tierney's house between seven and eight o'clock. He called again the same night when he found the two prisoners and Tierney's wife in the house. The next morning he again called at Tierney's house about half-past eight and found Wynn there who said he had been staying with Tierney all night. Tierney, who had not been in when witness first called, came in soon after, and having procured and drank a gallon of ale, was requested by his wife to go upstairs to bed. Tierney then went upstairs and was shortly after- wards followed by his wife and Wynn, witness remaining downstairs. Soon after they had gone upstairs he heard a noise as if some one was pulling his clogs off, and while this noise continued the police entered. Tierney's wife who had again come downstairs on seeing the policemen shouted up to the prisoners," What are you making that row about." Sergeant Ross went upstairs and brought the prisoners down, but agein went upstairs, witness this time following him. On gerting into the room the sorgeant pulled some of the brickwork of the chimney out, and took I some money from behind it. On seeing the sergeant do this I Tierny said "I have worked for the money at the 'Blunder.'" At the Parr police station witness heard Wynn say to Tierney "I put it in the bucket."—Mieliael Degnan, labourer, Prospect-row, Park-road, deposed that about 12 o'clock on the Saturday night in question, he saw both the prisoners outside the house of Wynn's father, in Park-road, about 130 yards from the Black Horse Inn. Wynn was evi- dently having some words with his father. Tierney took him away in the direction of his house in Prospect-road.— Jos. Waters, wages' clerkat Mr. Hy. Baxter's chemical works, Parr, stated that the prisoner Tierney entered Mr Baxter's employ as a labourer on the 7th August. During the first week his earnings were 3s. 7d.; in the second, 108. 4d.•, in the third, 9s. 5d.; and in the fourth he was paid 4s. 3d.; but in addition to this he received lls, from a contractor. The last week ended on the 31st August, and Tierney was paid on the 2nd September.—P.C. Carruthers said that about half-past three on Sunday morning, September 3rd, he was about 130 yards from the Black Horse Inn, and saw both the prisoners come from behind some houses fronting Park-road. They went into Tierney's house in Prospect-row. The same , evening he assisted Sergeant Ross to take the prisoners into custody. On the way to the police station Tierney said "They can't charge us with stealing," to which witness re- sponded " Have you been stealing ? " To this Tierney merely said "Do you think we are green."—Sergeant Ross said that owing to information he had received, he went about 9-45 a.m., on the evening of the 3rd instant, to No. 2, Prospect-terrace, earl., the dwelling-house of Tierney. On entering the house he heard a noise upstairs as if bricks or something of the sort were being removed. Tierney's wife shouted up "Make a less noise there; the bobbies are here." Witness at once went upstairs, leaving a constable in charge of the room blow. On entering the bedroom he found ties • two prisoners. Wynn. on seeing him, went -down stairs; Tierney was in the act of bricking up the fire-place of the room. Witness pulled down the bricks, which appeared to have been but newly put up, and behind them found Ll 18s. , Tierney on seeing him take out the money said "That money is mine; I worked for it at Paddy's Blunder. I have , not been out of this house for two days." In a bucket partly full of dirty water in the same room under a bed witness found .£2 17s. id. There was also about 121bs. of beef on the floor near the bed. Witness then came down stairs, and whilst searching the room below Wynn said " I was not out of this house last night and know nothing about the meney." Prisoners were then taken into custody, and on Tierney being searched at the police office £2 Ss. 61. was found in his pocket. In reply to the charge Tierney said, "It is all right, I know nothing about it," and Wynn also said he knew nothing about it.—Mr. Riley, in defence of Wynn, urged the fact that none of the stolen property had ben found upon him, and added that the reason for his being at Tierney's house was that his father would not ad- mit him on the night in question on account of his being intoxicated.—The magistrates, however, decided to commit both prisoners for trial at the assizes, bail being refused.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.

An adjourned meeting of this Board, for the purpose of electing Commissioners and transacting ordinary business, was held at the Public Offices on Thursday. The chairman (Dr. Stetle) presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Norman, Whitaker, Meadowcroft, Lake, G. S. Hazlehurst, Briscoe, Highburn, Taylor, Fisher, Williams, P. Speakman, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor.)

div.head: ELECTION.
div.p: THE ELECTION.

The CHAIRMAN announced the result of the annual election. Tie expenses incurred amounted to £8 35.3.1. Mr. NORMAN moved and Mr. LIGHTBURN seconded, a resolution that the expenses be paid, and it was carried.

div.head: ALLEGED NUISANCE FRO3I THE GLYCERINE .WORICS
div.p: THE ALLEGED NUISANCE FRO3I THE GLYCERINE .WORICS

The CHAIRMAN read a letter which had been received from Mr. S. Yarwood, who said he was sorry to have to invite the attention of the Board to the most fearful smell from the Glycerine Works and asking for its abatement. When the wind was in the direction of his house.the smell was so bad that they could could not get their meals, and in Church-street on Friday night, the Bth inst., it was fearful.—The CHAIRMAN observed that the Board gave the proprietors of the works a month's notice to abate the nuisance, and that notice ex- pired that day. It now remained for the Board to say what steps were to be taken.—Mr. HAZLEHIIIIST : Has the nuisance inspector anything to say about it ?—The CHAIR- MAN: No; he is very ill.—Mr. BARKER observed that he had -a report on the matter for the Sanitary Committee. At the request of the Chairman, he 'read the following: "The stench from the glycerine works is still more or less per- ceptible, but I have not found it as bad as heretofore. I have seen the foreman on the subject, and he says that they are making changes in their system of working, that the stench is considerably less, and ultimately it will be reduced to a minimum."— Mr. BRISCOB: The smell is quite as bad this morning as ever it has been. The wind is just in the direction of my house. As to any abatement, I can see none.—Dr. Mlc- DouGALL pointed out that it would be best to discuss the subject at the meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee, ard suggested the adoption of that course.—lt was agreed to. flThe Highway and Sanitary Committee recommended that the Law Clerk be instructed to take proceedings against Mr. Victor Clolas, the proprietor of the Glycerine Works, under section 112 of ale Public Health Act. The Board accepted the recommendation.

div.head: AN ABSCONDING ST. HELENS TRADESMAN.
div.p: AN ABSCONDING ST. HELENS TRADESMAN.

On Wednesday morning P.C. Cottam, an officer of the St. Helens police force, left St. Helens for Liverpool, en route for Bahia, Brazil, to bring back to England an absconding St. Helens bankrupt, Mr. Joseph Taylor, who carried on business as a baker and flour dealer, in Liverpool-road. It will be remembered that Mr. Taylor was adjudicated a bank- rupt on the 15th August last, but before a meeting of his creditors had been held he took ship at Liverpool for Brazil, South America. Thio having been ascertained by the creditors, a warrant was obtained, and also an extradition order. In- structions for the apprehension of the defaulter were then telegraphed to the British Consul at Bahia. About the end of last week an intimation of the arrest of Taylor was received at the St. Helens police office from the Home Secretary's office, and desiring that an officer should be sent out to receive him into custody. P.C. Cottam was the officer appointed for this duty, and on Wednesday afternoon left Liverpool in the steamship " Herschell " bound for Bahia. It is expected that some six or seven weeks will elapse before the return of the officer and his charge. We under- stand that on the return of Taylor some very rigid enquiries will be made into certain transactions made by him previous to his bankruptcy, by which both money and stock were transferred to other parties.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF FEVER: SHOCKING NEGLECT.
div.p: OUTBREAK OF FEVER: SHOCKING NEGLECT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported to the Health Committge that during the month of August there had been 94 births, equal to a rate of 45.1 per 1,000; and 68 deaths, equal to a rate of 32.64 per 1,000. There were 29 deaths among children under one year, and 21 among children between one and five years. Zymetic diseases accounted for 28 deaths, representing a death rate of 13.44 per I,ooo.—The NUISANCE INsPEcToR reported that there had been seven deaths from scarlet fever, 16 deaths from diarrlicea, one from typhoid fever, and one from whooping cough. Several cases of scarlet fever were reported from various parts of the town. Disinfection was being carefully attended to. The vaccina- tion returns for the half year ending 31st December, 1881, showed that 537 births were registered, and 400 children were successfully vaccinated; 61 died unvaccinated, 20 were postponed by medical certificate, 50 could not be found, and there were six defaulters.—lt was recommended that three months' notice.be given Mr. Robinson to modify the agree- ment in respect of fees for prosecution.—Mr. CAREY, in moving that the minutes be confirmed, remarked that the vaccination returns were satisfactory. With regard to the death-rate, it was for the quarter ending 31st March last, 174; for England and Wales for that period it was 21.6. For the second quarter, the death rate was 178; for England and Wales 19. The zymotic death rate, or the death rate from preventable diseases, was very low for the first half year, and he was sorry to say that the death rate from that c iuse was rising very fast at the present moment. There was scarlet fever in two or three parts of the township,•and there was danger of the disease spreading. In Accrington the disease had led to •the closing of all the elementary schools, and in other places had committed ravages of which the members could read in the newspapers from day to day. The committee found great difficulty in dealing with this disease entirely through the carelessness of many of the parents who permitted their children to go from the house before they were allowed to do so by the medical attendant. He would not mention any particular cases, because he did not want to give pain to any family, but he wished distinctly to give notice that the committee, advised by the medical officer, would really have to take some serious step and make an example of some parent in the neighbourhood, if mere attention was not paid to the request of medical men. Children were allowed to run out before the scarlet fever bad left them; their hands and face perhaps" peeling," and the result was that the efforts of the committee to stay the disease were rendered entirely futile. He supposed there was nothing else to be done but summons one or two persons under tke clauses of the Public Health Act, which em- powered the Board to prosecute people who were guilty of this careless conduct, before the magistrates, who were authorised to impose a fine not exceeding £5.. The Board would be obliged to take action if they could not get people to be more careful in the way in which they went about when the disease was in their houses.—Mr. WEBSTER Inquired if the drains were ventilated where the disease had broken out. He was afraid the disease had arisen principally through the drains not being properly drained.— Mr. MIDWOOD said he should like to know if the Market Committee were going to take any steps by shich the market could be worked at a profit instead of a loss; or whether it was to continue a serious loss to the ratepayers.—Mr. SADLER inquired if it was not usual for the medical officer to attend the Board meetingS. He had not seen him for a long perio3.—Mr. CAREY said he was glad that Mr. Webster was giving his attention to draining. It was a subject of the highest importance, and he ( Mr. Carey) should only be too glad if the drains could be more thoroughly ventilated than they were at the present time. Replying to Mr. Midwood, Mr. Carey said the loss on the market was a subject which the committee would like to have some information upon, and they would be delighted to receive any advice Mr. Mid- wood would be pleased to give them. If he would attend the meeting of the Market Committee when they had the subject under discussion, any advice as to how they could make the market pay would be gladly received, and Mr. Mid- woed must have some good ideas on the subject or else he woeld not have asked the question. With regard to the medical officer's attendance, he used to attend the Board meetings pretty regularly when he (Mr. Carey) was first a member, but his attendance was hardly ever required. He supposed the medical officer had dropped it because he was never asked any question, but if the Board would like him to attend he would no doubt very gladly do so.—Mr. SADLER : I think that when he drops his attendance we should drop his salary at the same time.—The minutes were adopted.

FINANCE COMUITTER. At a meeting of this committee a letter was read from Mr. Beasley, who asked that the remaining accounts should be sent to the taxing officer without either side being repre- sented. Recommended that this be agreed to.—Mr. 11. S. Oppenheim wrote to ask for a payment of £lOO on account of Muss Brook Bridge law expenses. The request was re- ferred to the Board.—List of empties, brickstools not worked this year, reduction in assessments and bad debts, produced, amounting to £99 3s 8d; and it was recommended that these be written off. Accounts, amounting to £283 as 4d, on gas account; £l4O 15s 8d on water account; £193 23 3d Highway Committee; £l33s Hospital Committee; £l4 us Health Committee; £7 103 market accounts; £240 2s 4,1 Sewerage Committee; and £577 7s 7d Finance Committee, were recommended for payment.— Mr. HANDLEY moved the adoption of the minutes, with the exception of that relating to Mr. Oppenheim.—Mr. MID- WOOD, in seconding the motion, referred to Mr. Oppenheim's request, and said he hoped the Board would refuse to pay the money until they had received the whole bill. He thought it a large sum of money to ask for. The Board was in a most unfortunate position. They were obliged to have a solicitor ia the matter, and when a solicitor under- took an action like that he should be prepared to carry the thing through before he asked for one penny. The minutes were passed. It was evetatually resolved to pay the £lOO asked for, oa the motion of Mr. KERSHAW, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY, on the understanding that the Board's position in the matter was to be defined.

SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. Mr. KERSHAW moved the confimation of the minutes of this Committee, who had received a letter from Messrs Part and C)., solicitors, on bAalf or the Hutchinson trustees, declining the offer of £250 in settlement of way-leave.—Mr. CAREY seconded the motion.—Mr. KERSHAW observed that the sewerage 'works were progressing satisfactorily.—Mr. SAGLER said there was a. report abroad in the town that the bricks now being used in the work were of an inferior quality. He should like to know if the Committee had satisfied themse!ves on the matter.—Mr. KERSHAW replied that the Committee would make it their duty to inquire into the matter. Mr. Sadler was one of the Committee. He (Mr. Kershaw) had seen the bricks, but had detected nothing wrong.—The minutes were passed. THZ BYE-LAWS.

Mr. KERSHAW, in accordance with his notice, moved that the resolution passed on the 28th February confirming the bye-laws be rescinded. He had adopted this rourse in order to obtain time to make some alterations to those which re- ferred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee.—Dr. O'KEIIFFia seconded the proposition, which was carried.— Mr. CAREY then moved that the Health bye-laws be passed as they stand, but eventually withdrew his resolution.—lt was decided to hold a special meeting to pass the bye-laws on Friday, the 22nd inst. THE RESIGNATION OF THE GAS ENGINEER.

The Board then resolved itself into Coramittee,and the reporters were asked to retire. After the lapse of about half- an-hour they were again called into the room, when the Chairman said it bad been decided to accept the resignation of Mr. Roberts, and also to advertise for a successor. at a c,,mmencing salary of £2oo.—Mr. WEBSTER moved, and Mr. JOHNSON seconded, the confirtnation of the deci- sion.—The motion was carried by a majority of one, 9ix voting for and five against. GRIEVANCES.

Mr. Mmwoors said the Gas Committee seemed to have a plan of making each house have a separate connection with the main, which worked rather hardly upon owners of pro- perty. Each house, also, was required to have a stone with , an iron frame fixed about a yard from the boundary wall, which was very expensive. He thought it would be well if the committee could see their way to remove this great hardship from the property owners. Then there was a "man who goes round looking for what be could find " (laughter)—as regarded leakage in water pipes. He (Mr. Midwood) knew places where the man had never been for twelve months. When be found a small leakage the man made no more ado than knocking it up with his hammer, and then left the inmates of the house to do as best they could. A case occurrtd a week or two ago, where an owner of property, who was also a plumber had a leakage in his pipe,—(laughter)—and he repaired it himself. Mr. Roberts afterwards sent a man to the house to repair the pipe, who cut off the repairs and then set to and repaired the leakage over again. He (Mr. Midwood) thought this a great hardship, and he asked if these•things were to go on. He had made one or two en- quiries, and he learned that the Gas Committee had the whole thing in their hands, and he really thought the com- mittee ought to take the matter into their consideration.— Mr. KERSHAW said the remarks of Mr. Midwood showed a very unsatisfactory state of things. If there was a leakage in a water pipe and the occupier of the house could repair it there was no reasen why he should l not.—Mr. PamtnunsT said the committee would take the matter into consideration. He suggested that Mr. Midwood should ask the man who had complained (Mr. Lathom) to write an account of the affair to the committee, who could then take it as part of the proper business.—Mr. KERSHAW : As to connections I think it is a standing rule.—Mr. PAlncHußgr : Yes. The Board then separated.

On Tuesday evening Mr. J. B. Leach, of tha firm of J. B. and B. Leach, auctioners, St. Helens and Liverpool, offered by public auction, at the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, two com- modious leasehold dwelling-houses with stabling and out- buildings, situate in Hardshaw-street, St. Helens. The pro- perty was purchased by Mr. Collins for £550. Mr. H. S. Oppenheim was the vendor's solicitor.

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers, 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Sep. 14) :—Till the announcement of the taking of Tal-el-Kebir the market kept comparatively quiet, the feeling of desire to await definite news before operating still ruling pretty generally. The prospect of money going dearer here, too, has kept figures from moving up, and the rumour of advance in the rate of the Berlin Bank put prices down early hi the week, but fluctuations have occurred since. When the news of the British victory with such a complete rout of the enemy was received, the market became buoyant, but best figures are not maintained, Bank rate being put to 5 per cent., having damped values, though, as it was vety generally expected, the effect is not severe. Egyptian stocks were quiet, but steady, up to news of the English success, when they moved forwards, the Unified showing an advance of about 14 on the week. BANKS keep firm, with a fair business passing. Values arc not changed much. INSURANCE.—Very few transactions or changes of quot itions. In the latter the balance is adverse, but the movement is not by any means decided.. COAL, IRON, &C., AND MINING.—No great amount of busin,si Is reported; but where other than solitary transactiona are , marked later figures are slightly better. The tone as evinced by the prices on revision is better. Bolckows are quiet, and are now quoted ex-dividend. The fully paid show II / ch tnge. but the £l2 paid are the turn better. Ebbws keep moving slowly upward. Canadian copper and sulphur quiet and about the same. Indian gold cones irregular and nothing done here In them. Llynoi and Tender ordinary are stronger, buyers ad- vancing more than sellers, but still not 'much business is con- cluded in them. Higher: Patent Nut and Bolt 4. Bolckows £l2 paid 4, Chillington iron 4. Ebbw Vale 4, Park Gate iron 4, Indian Glenroek 4, John Brown's 4, and Llynoi and Tender or- dinary 4. Lower: Telegraph c >nstruction and maintenance 4. Rio Tinto 4, ()animals 4, Indian Phtzenix 4, Tharsis sulphur, 84c 4, and Consolidated Telphone construction aud maintenance 4. COTTON SPINNING AND 31.ssurAnTuhrt/G.—Market continues firm and stronger with the news from Egypt; not much busi- ness, however, concluded during the week. TELEGRAPHS better almost all round. TELEPHONES are better where changed. Lancashire and Cheshires show rise 3-16, being now ex-dividend, CORPORATION, &C., STOCKS not quite so firm. HAILWAYS.—The market has produced numerous fluctua• Vous. The rise in the bank rate and other Cauca has counter- acted the good effect of the Egyptian news.
