div.head: WIDNES AND NOXIOUS VAPOURS.
div.p: WIDNES AND NOXIOUS VAPOURS.

The CLERK read the following communication : Warrington Union.—Dear air,—The Rural Sanitary Auth irity of this Union have for some time had under their consideration the means of the more effectual control of the escape of noxious vapours in and aro ind their district. They find damage caused to crops. An., is great, besides the annoyance to inhahtants of their district. The Authority are .troogiy of opinion that the appointment of an additional inspector, under section 19 of the Alkali. Ac., Works Regulation Act, 1881. is necessary. The section referred to provides that any authority or combination of authorities may appoint an additional insi,ector under toe Act, a moiety (perhaps half) of whose salary would be paid by Government. The inspector to be appointed would reside In such portion of the united district as the authorities might decide Will you kindly lay this before your authority and a‘tcertain whether they are willing to join this authority for the purpose above earned. I may state for your information _
thaft have been in communication with the Local Government Bard hereon, and that this is the only course tney cm sug- gest —Yours hithru ly, Jamms &ITT" clerk.—The Clerk, Leal Board, Widnes.

The Cmtuares remarked that in regard to this matter Widnes was very well able to take care of itself. Mr. CARRY said his view was strongly that Widnes being a very important centre of the alkali trade, deserved a special in- spector of its own, and appointed directly by the Local Government Board. In Widnes was made a large proportion of the alkali made in the United Kingdom, and it had al- ways been the contention of the manufacturers that there should be an inspector resident in the town, in order to look after the escape of noxious vapour and control it as far as possible. It had, too, always been their desire that a resi- dent inspector should be appointed by the Local Government Board, and he (Mr. Carey) did not think it would be palitic on the part of the Board to join any other board in the appointment of an inspector; or that the Board should pay any part of his salary. If the matter was left to the Local Government Board, it. was his opinion they would eventually appoint an inspector. Dr. O'KEEFFB observed that he was glad to hear such a statement coming from a manufacturer. It showed he had the interests of the whole neighbourhood at heart; and he thought it might ba fairly considered that Mr.Carev was expressing the opinion of all the manaufactu- rers in the township. The Beard, he thought, ought to take measures to help the appointment of a special inspector for the town at once. It would be a great satisfaction to the farmers in the neighbourhood, and others who are dissatis- fied, as they were asserting strongly that their crops had been injared through the escape of noxious vapours. Were the measures taken in time they would tend to tranquilize _ .

the fears of the agriculturist.—Mr. limastraw asked how the inspector would be provided. Mr. CARRY replied that if they agreed with the request contained in the letter which had been read, the lioard would have to pay either one-half or one-third of the salary of the inspector, but the manufac- turers had always held the opinion that as Widnes was such an important centre of the chemical industry it ought to have an inspector appointed by the Local Govern- ment Board, and paid for out of the treasury, and not by the community. (Elear, hear.) He might explain that in either Case the inspector was appointed by the Local Go- vernment Board, and was under its control whether paid by the Sanitary Authority or not.—The discussion was then postponed in order that the Alkali Works, &c., Act might be consulted. It appeared that Mr. Caroy's explanation was correct.—Mr. 'Unworn) surrgested that the letter should lie on the table.—The CHAIRMAN said it would be more courteous to reply, and say that the Board cold not see their way to join with the Authority.—This course was adopted.

div.head: GAS AND WATIIR COXMITTEN.
div.p: GAS AND WATIIR COXMITTEN.

At a meeting of this committee, held on the Bth August, a letter, dated 31st July was read from Mr. H. Roberts, the engineer, tendering his resignation. Its consideration was deferred until the let September, when it was recommended that it be accepted, and a successor advertised for. In his report the engineer sta.ed the rainfall for the month was 2.995 inches measured by the gas yard gauge, and 2 930 by the Pex 1111 gauge; mean 2.962 inches. The water pumped during the four weeks ending 23rd Augu,t was— Stockswell, 17,837,287 gallons ; Netherly, 17,873,190 gallons, a decrease of 25-79 per cent, in the former case, and an increase of 15.93 per cent. in the latter. The water delivered amounted to 36,405,632 gallons; corresponding period in 1831, 39,523,136 gallons. There had been 3,837,000 cubic feet of gas made, and 3,648,000 cubic feet delivered, 3 decrease of 4-30 per cent. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16 47 candles. The month's accounts amounted to £238 6s. 4d. for gas works, and £l4O 15s. 6d. for water works. It was recommended that the offer of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company to supply instruments and keep them in order for .225 per annum be accepted. In reply to an application by the Bridgewater Navigation Company, the committee offered for sale the Cameron engine at Netherly for £175, the company ta take it down and remove it. A letter was read dated the sth ultimo, from the Wigan and Whiston Colliery Co. offering to supply gas, if a main was laid by the Board to the colliery, at 7d. per thousand cubic feet. Recom- mended that the offer be not entertained. It was also recommended that the tegder of Messrs. J. W. Warini, and Co. for tar, and Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co. for gas liquor be accepted.—Mr. PANKHURST moved the confirmation of the minutes, with the exception of that portion referring to the resignation of Mr. Roberts, which he suggested should be considered by th.e Board in committee.—The motion was seconded.—Mr. MARTLEY Said seeing that the committee manufactured gas at a cheap rate, he should be glad if they would supply it at a more reasonable rate than was charged at the present time.—Mr. Minwoin objected to the question of Mr. Roberts's resignation being considered in committee, and moved an amendment that it should he discussed by the Board openly.—Mr. WRIGHT seconded the motion.—Reply- ing to Mr. Martley, Mr. Peersuun.sr said the committee could not at present reduce the price of gas. They were endeavouring to improve the qoality of the gas.—The CHAIRMAN, referring to the offer of the Whiston Colliery Co., said he did not think it an advantageous one; nor did he think it was a position the Board should take, virtually placing themselves in the hands of a private company. It would not be wise to accept the offer. Mr. Martiey, in asking his question with regard to the price of gas had (remarked the chairman), forgotten that the Board had already made a reduction.—Mr. MARTLEY : Yes; but it is still 3s. 61. nett.—The CHAIRMAN thought it would he quite out of the question to make a reduction at once, until the Board saw whether they could carry on what they had al- ready undertaken—Mr. CAREY and Mr. KERSHAW expressed their intention of supporting Mr. Pankhurst's motion —The amendment waa then put and lost; and the minutes with the exception named, were passed.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTED: IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTED: IMPROVEMENTS.

The Highw ly Committee recommended that the Board retain the work of lighting, rtc., in their own hands. The Clerk was instructed to submit an estimate for lighting to the Gas CommitteP, and to ask for an appointment to diszuss a proposed reduction of charge to £2 per lamp per year. H. Mather's account with regard to Moss Bink Bridge approaches for b dance of contract amounting to £lO3 ss. 31, and for extras £3lB 16s. 11., total .D 122 is. 4d., was presented, and the Surveyor was instructed to check and report. A letter dated the 11th August was read from the railway company, in which they promised that their engineer should inspect Waterloo level cr.,ssing on an early day. The Surveyor reported that the work of paving Lower House- lane would be at once proceeded with. The offer of Mr. Joseph Davies to give up land valued at £l2 103. at Crow- lane for widening Moorfield-lane, in consideration of a fence being erected to protect a dangerous pit, estimated to cost £lO, was recommended to be accepted. On the 28th ult. Mr. Oppenheim wrote that notice of trial had b±en given by Messrs. Teehay and Lynch with regard to Moss Brook Bridge. Mr. W. Swindells wrote to the committee com- plaining that Mr. Short had erected a shed in the back yard of a house in Widnes road, which was a nuisance to the neighbours; and the committee decided to inspect the premises. A letter was read from Mr. Wiles asking that a public lamp might be erected at the Primitive Methodist chapel, Princes-street. The committee decided to consider the request at their lamp inspection. The plans of seven houses in Martley-street for Mr. S. White were approved.— Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Mr. SHIITTLEWORTH seconded, the passing of the minutes; the former remarking that the committee might on any day be requested to meet the engineer of the company, Mr. Worthington, with regard to Waterloo-road crossing.—Mr. HAIIMLBY said he saw there was an action entered against the Board for Moss Brook Bridge, and as they were pressed by Mr. Mather for money on account, it would perhaps be as well if the Board had some information as tonhe facts of the case.—Mr. KERSHAW remarked that with regard to Mersey-road ferry approach, Mr. Midwood had thrown out a good suggestion, which was that the Railway Company be asked to contri- bute something to its repair. The committee had corres- ponded with the company, and a reply had bben received that the matter would have to go before the directors. The committee, therefore, could not say what amount the com- pany would offer the Board.—Mr. Herrin-HY inquired what was the Board's position in respect to the impending trial. —Mr. KERSHAW : We are in it, and I suppose we cannot get cut of it. (Laughter.)—The minutes were passed. THE AIM OF THE HOSPITAL.

The minutes of the Hospital and Markets Committee contained a recommendation that a circular letter explain- ing rules 3 and 4 be forwarded to the medical men and employers of labour in the district. It was as follows : "As there has been occasionally some dissatisfaction expressed as to the wrking of the hospital, especially in respect of Rule number 3, I am instructed to ask your kind attention to the following explanation: The primary inten- tion in establishing this hoqpital was to provide suitable accommodation and proper nursing for accident patients, at whose homes such accommodation and nursing are not available. The hospital, in short, isMa sub- stitute for borne and the patient employs his own medical attendant at his own cost as if he were at heme. The Board therefore wishes it to be distinctly understood that in no case will it be responsible for the fees of medical men who may be called to attend the patients. In future each patient, or employer, or person in charge of patient, when application is made for admission must provide a duly qualified medical man, otherwise the matron will either refuse admission, or if the case is admitted on account of urgency the Union medical officer will be called in and the patient will, in accordance with rule No. 4, be removed at the earliest possible moment to the Whiston Hospital. lam

MO 'CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- l. tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- conmging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Dot out on Hire, or Pnrchase, Lease, GAB COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best makers for ec,nomy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.

COWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOL.—Tbeee Schools will be OPENED for tuition on MONDAY the Oth Oarosim NEXT. M. E. J. SIMPSON. M.A., Trinity College, Cambridge, Head- master of Hinckley Grammar School, has been appointed Head Master of the boy's school, and Miss Kate Jurgenson, L.L.A., B And' ews, late assistant mistress at Norwich High School, Head Mistress of the girls' rchool. Tuition fees: boys, £8 per annum: girls, 4 per annum ; entrance fee, al. To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistresses required, intending pupils are requested to apply for admission to the schools without delay. Applications for ad- mission must be made on forms to be obtained from me, the undersiaged. Pupils applying for admission before the 7th September next, will not lie charged the entrance fee of 4. No boy or girl under 8 years adroittei. The examination for admission will be held at the schools on Thursday, the sth day day of October next, the following being the standard. Read- ing simple narrative, writing text hand, sums in the first rules of arithmetic with the multiplication table. THOMAS BREWIS, Clerk to the Governors. Town Hall, St. Helens, 10th August, 1882.

SEAFIELD OUSE, LIVERPOOL. This New Hotel, which combines all the social advantages of a ffydropathic Establishment, will be open for the reception of visitors on the 25th September. The hotel is situated on the shore, on the Lancashire side of the Mersey. seaward of- the Lighthouse and Fort at New Brighton. Its position thus secures to visitors the first of the ozone as it comes in its purity, fresh from the open sea. There are two asciendas, from which a view is obtained of the arrivals and departures of the unsurpassed extent of shipping which frequents the Mersey. The Conservatories. Winter Gardens, and Recreation GrOlands cover an area of about ten acres. The Bedroom accommodation is for about 250 visitors, to- gether with requisite Bitting Rooms. Bait Water and other Baths. Gymnasium, Re ,ding, Concert, and Recreation Rooms. Billiard Room, Five Tables. INTelephone. Special Telegraph Wire to all parts of the King- dom. Telegraphic and Cable Address—" &afield, Liverpool." Table d'Hote at 6-30. The distance from the Exchange station, Liverpool, of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, is from 15 to 20 minutes. The service is most complete. 104 trains rnn daily to and from Waterloo A new end commodious station has lately been pro- vided there. Private conveyances from the hotel will meet every train. The drive to the hotel is about 5 minutes. The Waterloo omnibus also passes the establishment every half hour to and from the Liverpool Exchange. Special terms can be arranged for permanent residents. Address— C. NAIJ, Manager. The hotel will be opened on Monday afternoon, 25th Septem, ber, at o'clock, by the Right Honourable the Earl of Lathom, on which occasion the Countess and the Ladies Skel- mersdale have signified their intention to be present.
